#6426. Scientists Discover a Hidden Immune System Difference That Could Explain Why Obesity Affects Men and Women Differently

Scientists have discovered that immune cells in fat tissue behave differently in males and females, potentially helping explain sex-specific responses to obesity.

A type of immune cell best known for its role in allergies and asthma may help explain why obesity affects males and females differently. Researchers at the University of California, Riverside found that certain immune cells in fat tissue appear to protect female mice from obesity-related inflammation, while others become more inflammatory in males fed a high-fat diet.

The findings, published in PNAS Nexus, challenge the long-held assumption that these cells, called eosinophils, perform a relatively narrow range of functions. Instead, their effects may depend on their molecular characteristics, biological sex, and interactions with neighboring immune cells.

Using high-resolution single-cell sequencing, scientists identified six distinct eosinophil populations in adipose (fat) tissue. Each population displayed different patterns of gene activity, suggesting that eosinophils perform specialized functions rather than acting as a single, uniform group.

“Eosinophils are more complex than we once thought,” said Meera Nair, a professor of biomedical sciences at the UCR School of Medicine who co-led the research with biomedical scientist Adam Godzik. “Some populations can protect against obesity, and if we can identify and activate the pathways that produce these protective cells, we may find new ways to improve metabolic health.”

In female mice, researchers identified a protective eosinophil population that communicated more effectively with macrophages, another class of immune cells found in fat tissue. This relationship appeared to be supported by RELM alpha, a protein produced by macrophages that may help maintain protective immune activity. Earlier experiments showed that supplying RELM alpha to mice had protective effects, providing additional evidence for its role in regulating the immune environment.

Male mice showed a different response to a high-fat diet. Their fat tissue tended to contain more eosinophil populations associated with inflammation, and these cells displayed gene-expression patterns that suggested weaker protective functions.

“This means the relationship between eosinophils and obesity is not simply a matter of how many eosinophils are present,” said Rebecca E. Ruggiero-Ruff, a postdoctoral researcher in Nair’s laboratory and co-first author of the study. “Their functional characteristics and how they communicate with other immune cells are also critical.”

Although eosinophils have been detected in the fat tissue of people with obesity, scientists have not yet established whether they perform the same protective or inflammatory functions observed in mice. Determining whether similar cell populations exist in humans could help researchers investigate treatments that influence specific immune pathways rather than broadly altering immune activity.

“A drug may not activate the same pathways or produce the same effects in males and females, particularly when it targets the immune system,” said co-first author Xinru Qiu, a postdoctoral researcher in Godzik’s laboratory. “We need to investigate sex-specific biology more thoroughly so that treatments can be optimized for different patients.”

The researchers are now developing three-dimensional adipose organoids, laboratory-grown structures that reproduce certain features of human fat tissue. These models could allow scientists to examine how eosinophils interact with fat cells and macrophages, and whether modifying those interactions can encourage healthier tissue responses.

“We ultimately hope to develop human adipose organoids that will allow us to investigate whether manipulating immune-cell communication can promote healthier tissue responses,” said Godzik, a professor of biomedical sciences and the Bruce D. and Nancy B. Varner Presidential Endowed Chair in Cancer Research.

Reference: “Single-cell heterogeneity of adipose eosinophils is shaped by sex and RELMα and linked to macrophage communication networks in obesity” by Rebecca E Ruggiero-Ruff, Xinru Qiu, Lauren Vance, Yuxin He, Djurdjica Coss, Adam Godzik and Meera G Nair, 24 October 2026, PNAS Nexus. DOI: 10.1093/pnasnexus/pgag365

The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health, UCR School of Medicine, and California Institute for Regenerative Medicine.

#6424. How octopuses squeeze through tiny openings, step by step

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The cephalopod how-to guide involves three or four moves, depending on a hole’s size

Octopuses are famous for fleeing tanks by squeezing through narrow slits and impossibly tiny holes. Now scientists have studied the sequences some cephalopods like this Mayan octopus use to make such great escapes.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Octopuses have made many a great escape. Remember Inky, who fled from New Zealand’s national aquarium?

The cephalopods can Houdini their way out of tanks and off boats by squeezing through narrow slits and incredibly tiny holes. Now researchers know exactly how some octopuses pull it off. These masterful getaways involve a consistent, step-by-step game plan, researchers report November 5 in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

Octopuses are mostly squishy muscle, allowing them to shape-shift, though they do have some rigid body parts. Not many scientists have studied how these animals squirm through small openings, says Robyn Crook, an evolutionary biologist at San Francisco State University who was not involved in the research. “It’s one of the most characteristic behaviors of octopuses in popular awareness, but the strategies octopuses use have not really been examined systematically.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Sneaking through small spaces isn’t just a party trick for octopuses, says Michael Kuba, a biologist at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy. The animals use that skill to find hidden food and to avoid becoming food themselves.

Kuba and his colleagues observed how three common octopuses (Octopus vulgaris) and four Mayan octopuses (Octopus maya) approached small holes. For each individual, the team measured the distance between the octopus’s eyes as an indicator of the size of their most rigid cartilage around their brain. Then the researchers designed acrylic boxes with holes that were slightly smaller or larger than that eye-to-eye measurement. They plopped the octopuses inside and watched what happened.

Octopuses have slightly different escape how-tos, depending on the size of the hole they are squeezing through. Here, a common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) wriggles through a space just a little bit bigger than their most rigid body parts. It takes just three steps for the octopus to free itself from the acrylic box.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Common octopuses used one of two escape strategies depending on the hole’s size. When the hole was wider than the distance between their eyes, the octopuses pushed themselves through it in three steps. First, they snuck one or two arms through the hole and then threaded a couple more arms through. Finally, they used the arms that they had already snaked through the hole to push against the box and yank their head and the rest of their arms through in one fell swoop. The whole operation took a few seconds.

When the hole was narrower, common octopuses added a fourth step. They shoved all of their arms through the hole first and then squished their head and bulbous mantle through.

When a hole is smaller than their most rigid body parts, common octopuses add a fourth step to wrestle their bodies through an opening.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Mayan octopuses behaved more cautiously than the common octopuses. When confronted with the narrower hole, Mayan octopuses didn’t even attempt to fit inside of it. They usually ignored it. This difference between the species could stem from their biology or how they’ve adapted to their environments, Kuba says. Mayan octopuses live in sandy, rocky areas, so while they might disappear under rocks, they don’t often need to cram through holes, he says.

The team hopes these escape artists will inspire new soft robots that can morph their shape to fit through tiny spaces, says Wenci Xin, a robotics researcher at the National University of Singapore. “This incredible capability could enable robots to overcome environmental limitations and enter spaces that are difficult to reach.”

Studying how octopuses navigate different types of holes may provide additional clues for robots, Crook says. For instance, the cephalopods may take a different tack for openings that are more like slits or tubes than holes.

Currently, robots built to fit through tiny holes tend to be snake-shaped, but further research on these eight-armed contortionists could unlock other configurations.

W. Xin et al. Overcoming environmental constraints: octopus uses 3-step or 4-step strategies to squeeze through small holes. Journal of Experimental Biology. 2026. doi: 10.1242/jeb.252825

#6423. The 6 Best Electric Snow Shovels for Quickly Clearing Sidewalks and Driveways

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

These models deliver fast cleanup with minimal effort when there isn't enough accumulation to take out the snowblower. Here are our recommendations.

Winter will be here before you know it. Easily one of the most laborious and hated chores of that season is shoveling the snow. Not only that, it can be dangerous. Beyond the strain it puts on your back, the American Heart Association says it can increase the risk of a cardiac event for those with heart issues, and the cold weather can hide symptoms that otherwise would give you pause. That’s why the best electric snow shovels not only make the task easier, but safer, too, for those at risk.

Of course, you should not mistake these for full-blown snowblowers. Because of their compact size and throwing range, electric snow shovels are best used for small homes with shorter walkways and fewer steps. Like their larger counterparts, they use augers to scoop up snow (no more than 6 to 8 inches, ideally) and launch it up to 25 feet through the air so you don’t have to bend or lift as you dig out after a storm.

They also work well as supplemental tools for clearing out outdoor stairs, walkways, patios, decks, and anywhere else a snowblower may not be able to reach. If that sounds like it could help you out of a blizzard-induced jam this winter, we can steer you toward the best electric snow shovels that can make the chore as painless as possible.

Toro Power Shovel 60-Volt 12-Inch Electric Snow Shovel

Ego Power+ EGO POWER+ 12-Inch Electric Snow Shovel

We leaned on our personal experience with snow removal machines and conducted extensive research to inform our selections. Specifically, we looked at each machine’s clearing area, weight, battery life, and throwing distance. Because snow removal needs vary from property to property, we included larger models that can clear up to 6 inches of snow from two- to four-car driveways, along with lighter electric snow shovels that are easy to lift and maneuver in smaller areas, such as walkways and patios.

Though we still include one corded model as our best budget pick, we primarily focus on cordless models because for most people these days, the convenience of battery power beats having to drag a cord around on a cold day.

Most electric snow shovels max out with a fairly narrow clearing width and low clearing depth, potentially forcing you to do multiple passes to clear a proper path. This Earthwise model is an exception.

With a broad clearing width of 16 inches and a depth of 8 inches, it’s capable of clearing paths through deeper snow. And since it launches snow up to 32 feet away, you can use this machine to clear small driveways along with your walkways, deck, and patio.

On the other hand, this electric snow shovel is quite heavy. It has wheels, though, which make it easier to push and maneuver. It’s a tradeoff, but one that pays off if you live in an area that routinely gets 6 to 8 inches of snow in a night.

You may notice that our best overall is a bit cheaper than our best value pick. This is because we felt the wide clearing width and the fact that it has wheels to support your efforts made this a solid choice for many people.

Though higher in price than some of the other models on our list, there’s a lot that you get for the price, namely power and run time. With a larger battery than most, this electric shovel from Greenworks runs longer on a single battery than any other cordless electric snow shovel out there.

It packs a good amount of power with a large 80-volt 4.0-amp-hour battery powering a brushless motor; you’ll get about 45 minutes of run time on a single charge. This snow shovel clears a 12-inch path through up to 6 inches of snow, then blows it 25 feet away, making it ideal for uncovering a large area after a light snowfall.

Just remember that with great power and runtime comes great weight. With the battery loaded, this machine weighs more than 19 pounds, so moving it around for 45 minutes can turn into a real workout.

If you want the most clearing power possible from an electric snow shovel, Earthwise is your brand. This corded model can carve a 16-inch-wide path through snow up to 8 inches high, which is significantly more than what you can expect from other brands. It’s also significantly more powerful, moving up to 430 pounds of snow per minute.

For reference, most of our other picks move around 300 pounds per minute. As a result, it can handle deeper, slushier snow than most electric snow shovels. It also has a longer throwing distance than most corded or cordless electric snow shovels out there.

At 16 pounds, it’s pretty heavy, but like other heavy models, it has a pair of wheels so you can push it most of the time. In short, it offers the best snow removal capability of any machine this side of a snowblower.

Ryobi makes several types of cordless electric snow shovels, but this model is a head attachment for its Expand-It 40-Volt String Trimmer that you can swap in when the snow starts falling. The advantage here is that you aren’t limited to just one tool; you can swap in a variety of attachments to run on the same primary unit and battery. This makes a lot of sense if it only snows a couple of times where you live, and you only need a snow thrower infrequently.

During our testing, we were impressed with this tool’s performance. In mere minutes, we were able to clear a wide path through 8 inches of snow (more than the max height of 6 inches this model is rated for) on a patio outside our office. It was not fresh snow, either; it was densely packed after sitting for several days. There were times when the shovel head froze up while trying to push through too much at once, but this was quickly rectified by pulling back and pushing through again. The snow flies quite far, too, for such a small toolhead, at least 10 to 15 feet by our estimation.

Being able to fling snow that far is a good thing because this thrower can only send the snow straight forward (some models have adjustable fins that allow you to send it to either side). You need to be strategic about the direction you push to avoid creating more work for yourself if you have a long path to clear.

We must admit, too, that while this electric snow shovel makes the job easier than a manual shovel, it does take a bit of strength to operate, especially since it doesn’t have wheels to help you stay balanced and moving. You can move it along the ground, but you may need to lift it slightly if the snow is packed or icy at the lower levels, and it doesn’t come with a shoulder strap to help you do that. If you aim to greatly reduce the physical strain of snow removal, models from our list that feature wheels and directional fins may be a better option.

Overall, if you already have the Ryobi 40-volt-compatible string trimmer, adding this attachment to your arsenal would be a good move if you only need to clear snow from a small driveway, walkway, deck, or patio. The 40-volt, 4-amp-hour battery will give you up to an hour of power, which is more than enough for a small job like that, and buying into this multitool system will keep it from being a tool that just sits in the toolshed or basement for most of the time.

The lightweight design of this cordless electric snow shovel makes it a great option if other electric snow shovels are too heavy for you to manage. Whereas most electric snow shovels weigh around 18 pounds, this one weighs just 13.5 pounds.

Along with being lighter, the Snow Joe electric snow shovel also has a dual-handle design that allows you to operate it while standing up straight, taking pressure off your back. Despite its lighter weight, it can still clear a foot-wide path of snow up to 6 inches deep. The Snow Joe does have a shorter runtime than most, which limits it to lighter-duty snow removal, such as clearing walks, decks, and patios.

With its two 20-volt rechargeable batteries, the Worx electric snow shovel is both versatile and powerful. It can clear a path a foot wide and up to 6 inches deep and throw snow up to 25 feet, so it's suitable for clearing tighter spaces.

The two-battery design gives you the option to mix and match larger-capacity 20-volt Worx batteries to increase this shovel’s run time for larger jobs, such as clearing small driveways. It also comes with a dual charger, so you can charge both batteries simultaneously for a shorter turnaround time.

Another plus is that this model's batteries are compatible with other 20-volt Worx yard machines, making it a great option if you’ve already bought into the Worx product line.

We’d be remiss if we didn’t point out that this whole category of yard machines has some limitations. Most electric snow shovels can only handle snow depths up to 6 inches—8 inches if you’re lucky—and lack the power to handle heavier slushy snow. They are ideally suited to powdery snow on walkways, patios, decks, and maybe a small driveway. If you see heavy snowfalls regularly or have a large number of driveways and parking spaces to clear, get a snowblower before you buy an electric snow shovel. For big jobs, go with a gas snowblower. An electric snowblower works for small to moderate-sized driveways.

When push comes to shove, we recommend looking for a cordless electric snow shovel rather than a corded one. Having the freedom to move without worrying about a cord makes the whole shoveling or snowblowing process much easier. That said, if you’re on a tight budget or only need to clear a short walk or a small patio or deck that’s near an outdoor outlet, you can get by with a corded model.

Much like a snowblower, electric snow shovels are rated by how much snow they can move. The wider the shovel, the fewer passes it takes to clear an area. Most electric snow shovels move a 10- to 16-inch-wide path of snow. A small, narrow shovel is lighter and more nimble, making it useful for creating pathways. Wider, larger models are better equipped for clearing a patio or driveway, but are also heavier and more difficult to maneuver in tighter spaces.

Electric snow shovels can handle snowbanks around 4 to 8 inches high, depending on their clearing depth. Technically, you can remove deeper snowfall with these machines, but you’ll have to make more passes to do so.

For an electric snow shovel to be useful, it should be able to propel the snow far enough that it’s off the deck, walkway, or driveway that you’re clearing. Most electric snow shovels launch their snow between 20 and 30 feet, which is on par with entry-level, corded electric snowblowers, but shorter than cordless and gas snowblowers that can throw snow a distance of 40 feet or more. With that in mind, consider the route you plan to take while clearing, and make sure you’re moving the snow somewhere out of the way so it can sit until spring arrives.

Electric snow shovels process and throw snow like a snowblower, so you won’t need to bend over and scoop up snow as you would with a shovel. However, you should still look for the lightest possible option. While you won’t have to lift and throw snow as you would with a conventional snow shovel, you have to hold it upright and apply some force to push it through the snow. At the very least, you should look for a shovel that you can lift easily whenever you need to clear steps or multiple levels of patio.

Electric snow shovels typically weigh between 10 and 20 pounds. As you might expect, more powerful shovels that can move more snow and feature large batteries tend to be heavier than smaller, narrower models. Some large electric snow shovels have a set of wheels mounted to the rear of the base for standing upright on their own, so you can maneuver the machine with minimal lifting.

Similar to standard snow shovels, electric models come in both straight and curved handle varieties. A curved handle allows for standing more upright while operating the machine, putting less strain on your lower back and decreasing the risk of injury. A straight handle gives you more leverage for lifting loads of snow, but since an electric snow shovel has an auger that lifts and blows the snow for you, it’s not an advantage for electric models.

Electric snow shovels operate similarly to single-stage snow blowers. The shovel end of the machine has an auger that’s powered by an electric motor. As you push the shovel through the snow, the rotating auger collects snow, mashes it up, and then propels it through a shoot that throws the snow off to the side

The average electric snow shovel can churn through about 300 pounds of snow per minute. That means a snow shovel with a 12-inch wide intake and a clearing depth of 6 inches can remove about 4 inches of powdery snow from a 1,000 square foot driveway in about 20 minutes.

Just keep in mind that a shovel’s snow-clearing ability varies depending on certain conditions, such as the heft of the snow itself.

It’s never a bad idea to have a standard snow shovel around. While the electric snow shovel can reach most spaces that a standard push-behind snowblower can’t, it may not always be able to clear hardened snow or wet slush.

Plus, a manual shovel ensures that you can always dig out in an emergency, like when you’ve lost power after a snowstorm.

#6422. Your Brain Chemistry Could Change How You Understand Language

A single word can overturn your understanding of a sentence, and your brain chemistry may shape how hard you work to make sense of it again.

Even a single word can change the meaning of an entire sentence, forcing the brain to rethink what it just read. But how efficiently the brain handles these grammatical surprises may depend partly on its chemistry.

A study published in PNAS found that increasing dopamine and noradrenaline (catecholamines) strengthened a brain response associated with untangling ambiguous grammar. Researchers led by the Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics (MPI-PL) in Nijmegen observed the largest effects in healthy adults with lower baseline working memory capacity.

“Catecholamines are known to regulate attention, working memory, and cognitive control, but their role in language remains poorly understood,” says Peter Hagoort, senior investigator and director emeritus of MPI-PL’s Neurobiology of Language Department and the Donders Institute for Brain, Cognition and Behavior.

“Our earlier work suggested that catecholamines can affect semantic aspects of sentence comprehension. Whether these neuromodulatory systems also influence syntactic processing—how the brain combines words into grammatical structures—was largely unknown.”

Understanding a sentence involves more than knowing what its words mean. Readers also have to work out how those words fit together, sometimes revising an interpretation as new information arrives. The researchers used temporarily ambiguous “garden-path” sentences to examine that process.

Consider “The fan attacked the drummer, and the guitarist packed the instruments up.” When the words appear one at a time, readers may initially group “the drummer and the guitarist” together as the people being attacked. The word “packed” reveals that the guitarist is instead performing a separate action, requiring readers to rebuild their interpretation.

To test whether brain chemistry influences this revision, the team recruited 30 healthy adults. Each completed two sessions, once after taking methylphenidate, a stimulant commonly prescribed for ADHD that increases catecholamine levels, and once after taking a placebo.

Participants read ambiguous and unambiguous sentences and answered comprehension questions after each one. Meanwhile, researchers recorded their brain activity using EEG (electroencephalography), allowing them to examine the response at the precise word that exposed the grammatical ambiguity.

After methylphenidate, participants showed a stronger P600 response at the critical word, such as “packed.” This well-known EEG signal is associated with demanding grammatical processing and reflects increased cognitive effort. Its enhancement suggests that higher catecholamine levels changed how the brain recruited resources to resolve the sentence.

The increase was greatest among participants whose working memory capacity was lower before treatment.

“The findings suggest that catecholaminergic systems contribute to the dynamic allocation of cognitive resources during syntactic processing,” says Hagoort. “Their influence on language therefore appears to extend beyond semantic processing to syntactic unification, and the magnitude of this effect may depend on individual baseline working memory performance.”

“The results support the development of neuropharmacolinguistics as a field linking neuromodulatory systems to language processing.”

Reference: “Neuropharmacology of language: ERP evidence for catecholaminergic modulation of syntactic processing” by Yingying Tan, Ashley G. Lewis, Iris C. Schmits, Robert-Jan Verkes, Roshan Cools and Peter Hagoort, 22 October 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2606806123

#6420. ZWO Seestar S30 Plus review

We tested the brand-new ZWO Seestar S30 Plus, an all-in-one smart telescope for beginners and hobbyists that makes astrophotography accessible to everyone.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There's much to enjoy about the Seestar S30 Plus. The image quality is great, it's easy to use, and it's compact and lightweight enough to take it anywhere. It's not quite as good as the more expensive S30 Pro, but it's a nice middle-ground option between the S30 and the S30 Pro that gives you a lot of features for the money.

Seestar app is reliable and easy to navigate

All-in-one workflow from shooting to sharing

2K image quality is better than we expected

Editing controls could be a little more responsive

Not suitable for smaller planetary nebulas

Why you can trust Live Science Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best ones for you. Find out more about how we test.

ZWO has just released the newest member of its smart telescope range: the Seestar S30 Plus. This all-in-one smart telescope is designed for beginners and hobbyists who want an affordable way into astrophotography that won't leave you scratching your head, and lets you capture, process and share your images in one simple workflow. It sits between the Seestar S30 and S30 Pro, and is priced at $499 for its release.

With 2K image quality, a light pollution filter and a user-friendly interface, it's a smart telescope that anyone can enjoy, regardless of your experience level, and regardless of whether you're shooting from your city balcony or a dark sky site. Like the other models, it uses dual cameras to capture a wide range of subjects, including deep-sky objects with the telephoto camera, and constellations, star trails and the Milky Way with the wide-angle camera. It's lightweight and easy to travel with, and it even comes with a separate solar filter for solar imaging and eclipse time-lapses.

We got our hands on an advance copy to test ahead of its release, so we put it through its paces on several different celestial subjects.

The Seestar S30 Plus is one of the smallest, most compact smart telescopes on the market, weighing just 3.63 pounds (1.65 kg) and measuring 8.3 x 5.5 x 3.2 inches (210 x 140 x 80 mm). Its sleek, matte white design looks identical to the other Seestar models (we compared it to our S30 Pro), except for the branding on the unit itself.

It comes in a padded soft carry case and includes a small tripod (although we always prefer to use our own), a solar filter, a 40-inch (1 meter) USB-A to USB-C charging cable, a removable shoulder strap for the carry case, and a quick-start guide. With its accessories and case, the whole setup weighs 4.89 pounds (2.22 kg).

On the unit itself, you'll find just one button, which powers it on, plus the USB-C port on the side. Super simple, although we'd have liked the USB-C port to be covered to prevent moisture or dust from getting in.

It comes with a carry case, strap, USB-C cable and solar filter.

The set-up process couldn't be easier. When you turn the telescope on, you'll hear a double beep and see the power button light up alongside the red dots on the black screen to indicate the battery level. Four dots mean the battery is full. The telescope will tell you when it's ready to connect, at which point you can sync it up to the app on your smartphone or tablet. To turn it off, you just select "Shutdown" in the app, which closes the arm and turns the unit off.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

It also features an anti-dew heater, which we've found works quite well in mild to moderate humidity. On a couple of our shoots, we noticed a tiny bit of condensation forming on the unit when the humidity was higher, so we wouldn't feel confident leaving it unsupervised for long periods on a particularly dewy evening. (We used the Clear Outside app to monitor the humidity levels.)

The Seestar App is user-friendly and easy to navigate, with just the right amount of controls: you have plenty of options to choose from but it doesn’t become overwhelming. The main Seestar page is where you'll likely spend most of your time, as this is where you can search for celestial objects to shoot, access your album, plan a shoot and read up on what objects Seestar recommends based on your time and location.

The Stargazing section is where you can select or search for the subject you want to shoot. You can use the search function to find a specific target or browse Tonight's Best, and you can also search through different types of subjects like galaxies, nebulas, clusters and more. From here, you can also select planets, track comets and photograph constellations using the wide camera.

Click on a subject and the app will display information about it, including its current altitude and coordinates, which help determine what time is best to shoot that particular object. It automatically applies the appropriate filters and settings, but you can override these if you want to.

There's very little to complain about when it comes to using the app. It has lots of information for beginners, so you don't need a ton of knowledge about the night sky, and everything is fairly self-explanatory. There were a couple of occasions when it failed to calibrate itself (for example, when we tried to locate the Pleiades, which had just risen above a tree), and other times when we chose a new target and it slewed the long way round instead of only having to move slightly. But otherwise, the app worked well.

The AI Enhance section has some good editing tools to bring out the best from your photos. You can reduce the stars, adjust the brightness, contrast, saturation and RGB curves, apply denoise and eliminate any satellite trails — although we'd love a dehaze slider to bring out some of the fainter nebulosity of certain objects. The sliders could do with being a little more responsive, especially the RGB curves, but overall, it does a pretty good job of editing your pictures to get a pleasing result.

We had about 10 days to test our review unit before its release, so we could only capture as much as the weather permitted in that time. We'll add more images to this review over the coming weeks. All our tests were conducted from our backyard in a Bortle 4 region, and captured before moonrise to eliminate as much light pollution as possible. Due to these time constraints, we aimed to capture our images for a total of 60 minutes each, although we'd have ideally aimed for longer in some cases.

Now for the fun part — the images. The Seestar S30 Plus has a focal length of 160mm, which is advantageous for capturing large subjects like the Andromeda Galaxy, the North America Nebula and the Pleiades. Large emission nebulas are where it really shines; however, the focal length is too short to capture smaller apparent objects.

For this review, we aimed to capture as many different types of objects as possible. All our images were edited in the Seestar app with, in some cases, a few minor tweaks in Lightroom. You also have the option to download the individual files to your computer to process them yourself in dedicated astrophotography software, which is advantageous if you're a more experienced user.

Everyone's favorite star cluster, the Pleiades, was one of the first targets we wanted to capture. We could see the faint blue nebulosity after as little as 15 minutes of integration time, and it only improved over time. After 60 minutes, we had a really nice image and could easily bring out the blue haze via the editing tools in the app. However, we got a much more impressive result after tweaking our image a little further in Lightroom, bringing out even more haze and reflective dust.

The Andromeda Galaxy is a perfect target for the Seestar S30 Plus. It takes up a large portion of the frame, and with long integration times, it can reveal beautiful details in the faint outer arms. We shot for around an hour in our tests due to weather and time constraints, but we still got an impressive image. As we approached 60 minutes, there was a lot of cloud cover, and we noticed it struggling to stack images toward the end of the session, so we stopped the integration at 57 minutes.

Andromeda is certainly going to be the most impressive galaxy for the Seestar visually, as most others will appear smaller in the frame and will need longer integration, so make sure you have a clear, dark night for it.

Large emission nebulas are where the Seestar S30 Plus thrives, and the North America Nebula is a great target. It covers the whole field of view, and the red hydrogen gas easily comes to the forefront of the image.

The Eastern Veil Nebula is another lovely target where you can bring out the beautiful red and turquoise hues in as little as 15 minutes, but longer integration times will yield brighter, more colorful results.

Planetary nebulas are where you will see the limitations of the Seestar's 160mm focal length. Most planetary nebulas have a very small apparent size — we've previously captured the Dumbbell Nebula and Cocoon Nebula with our S30 Pro, and they were a tiny dot in the middle of the screen. We tried the Helix Nebula, and even though it's one of the largest apparent planetary nebulas, it's still fairly small on the Seestar S30 Plus. You can still get a decent image of it, but if you want to focus on imaging planetary nebulas, you'll need a bigger scope. Because it was very low in the sky and there was some interfering cloud, we stopped integration at 27 minutes.

The Seestar S30 Plus is an affordable entry point into deep-sky astrophotography without the confusing settings and expensive setup. It's ideal for beginners, although more experienced users will likely want to upgrade to the superior image quality and extra features of the S30 Pro.

Still, for under $500, we can't complain. Not only is the Seestar S30 Plus easy to navigate and use, but it teaches you about space in a fun and interactive way, and you don't need to spend hours stacking individual frames on your computer to process — although you still can do that if you want more control over your editing.

If you can stretch your budget, the S30 Pro is a worthy upgrade. It produces 4K images and offers more pro-level features.

To see deeper into space, the Seestar S50 Pro has a longer focal length of 260mm and a larger 50mm aperture, making it better for smaller apparent objects.

If the imaging aspect doesn't interest you, the Celestron StarSense Explorer range of telescopes connects to your phone to guide you around the sky, but you observe the cosmos through an eyepiece instead of capturing it on your phone.

Read our full Celestron StarSense Explorer LT 70AZ review

Kimberley Lane, E-commerce writer for Live Science, has tested a wide range of optical equipment, reviewing camera gear from Sony, Canon, OM System and more. With over 6 years of photography experience, her skills span across landscape and seascape photography, wildlife, astrophotography and portrait work. Her photos have been featured in a number of national magazines, including Digital Camera World and Cosmopolitan. She has also contributed to our sister site Space.com and Tech Radar, and she regularly uses binoculars and telescopes to stargaze in the dark skies of South Wales.

#6418. Scientists Discover California Has Way More Bugs Than Anyone Imagined

California is teeming with thousands of insect species science has yet to name, and its wild places hold more distinct worlds of tiny creatures than researchers realized.

California is home to an astonishing variety of insects, from the deserts of the Mojave to the forests of the Sierra Nevada. But scientists are discovering that the state’s insect diversity is far greater than previously believed.

A new study in Ecography estimates that California supports more than 60,000 insect species, far exceeding earlier estimates. Scientists have formally described only about two-thirds of them. Led by researchers at the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, the study also found that nearly every location sampled had its own distinct insect community.

The findings suggest that conserving California’s insect life will require protecting a wide range of habitats. Even places with similar climates and landscapes can harbor different species, making it difficult for any single protected area to represent the state’s extraordinary diversity.

The research is the first publication from the California Insect Barcode Initiative (CIBI), a $6 million project with an ambitious goal: collect and identify every insect species in California. Although insects are the most diverse group of animals on land, they remain underrepresented in large-scale conservation assessments.

Researchers used DNA barcoding on more than one million insect specimens. The technique compares short sections of DNA to help distinguish species, giving scientists a way to investigate diversity that can be difficult to recognize from appearance alone.

The effort brought together the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, California Department of Food and Agriculture, UC Berkeley, UC Riverside, San Diego Natural History Museum, and California Academy of Sciences in San Francisco. Researchers gathered tissue samples from museum collections, deployed Malaise traps across 72 ecoregions, and made collecting expeditions to 454 additional locations statewide.

Museum specimens extended the project’s reach beyond what researchers could collect in the field. Fresh sampling added another essential piece, with volunteers helping keep traps operating week after week. Although Malaise traps capture insects passively, collecting their contents and maintaining them takes sustained effort.

“This is an example of community science. Volunteers stepped forward to help with sampling by managing traps, which we would not have been able to do for continuous weekly sampling,” says study co-author Giar-Ann Kung, the museum’s entomology collections manager.

Kung joined researchers and volunteers across California in setting traps and collecting insects. Some participants maintained sampling sites for years, providing a continuity that the research team could not have achieved alone.

“There are people like Sara Fairchild and Michael Nance who managed a Malaise trap for over three years at a site in the high desert, which is the longest continuous site for the project. That could not have been accomplished without them.”

To explore how insect diversity varies across California, the researchers compared ecoregions, areas grouped by the Environmental Protection Agency according to shared ecosystem characteristics. They used Level 3 classifications, including the Mojave Basin and Range, Southern California Mountains, and Sierra Nevada. Of these regions, the Mojave Basin and Range had the greatest number of insect species.

Although similar environments shared some patterns, each region had its own mix of insects. “The deserts are kind of more similar to each other, and the mountains in northern California are a little bit more similar to each other, but every part of the state hosts a really different insect fauna,” says Dr. Barkdull.

Those differences also appeared at a smaller scale, with individual collecting sites within the same ecoregion harboring distinct insect communities. Together, the findings highlight the need to protect a wide range of California’s wild places.

Reference: “DNA barcoding of more than one million insect specimens indicates that at least one third of California’s insect biodiversity remains undiscovered” by Austin J. #6416. This armored amphibian once lived and hunted on the seafloor

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The ancient creature differs from all other known amphibians in its ability to tolerate saltwater

A Gerrothorax maritimus fossil unearthed in China was discovered in an ancient seabed, suggesting it's the first and only amphibian known to have lived in the ocean.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Most amphibians shrivel or suffocate in saltwater. But long ago, an oddball armored amphibian may have dwelled deep in the ocean.

Scientists have found evidence that an ancient amphibian with a flattened body and upturned eyes may have once stalked the seafloor. The animal, Gerrothorax maritimus, is the first ever amphibian known to have lived without access to land or freshwater, researchers report October 26 in Nature Ecology & Evolution.

G. maritimus, which lived 237 million years ago, was rather unlike today’s amphibians, which breathe and drink through their porous skin. The creature’s lifestyle was unimaginable for an amphibian, says Ryosuke Motani, a paleobiologist at the University of California, Davis. Of the more than 8,000 amphibians known today, none live solely in saltwater.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Motani and his colleagues inspected two well-preserved G. maritimus fossils from the late Triassic Period, which spanned roughly 237 million to 201 million years ago. Each creature measured around 70 centimeters, about as long as a skateboard, and was swathed in armor made of bony plates. The specimens appeared nearly identical to their closest relatives, other amphibians that dwelled in freshwater, Motani says. But the fossils’ location was unusual: They were found in what was once a seabed, roughly 30 kilometers from any ancient land.

It wasn’t clear whether the creatures lived in the ocean or were landlubbers that got buried there after they perished. So the team performed a chemical analysis. Levels of different forms of strontium in the fossil bones matched those of the Triassic ocean. This telltale sign revealed that G. maritimus ate seafood and drank seawater. “That means it lived there,” Motani says.

For amphibians, “this is the first time that that we have hard evidence that they were actually adapted for long-term life in the sea,” says Lachlan Hart, a paleobiologist at the University of New South Wales in Sydney who was not involved with the new study. Hart and his colleagues previously suggested that a different ancient amphibian may have been seafaring but probably did not dwell in the ocean.

Scientists have long searched for a marine amphibian. The fossil record is littered with skeletal fragments revealing how some mammals, reptiles and birds have adapted to a salty lifestyle. “Amphibians were always the problem because they did not really follow the rule,” Motani says.

The same skin that makes today’s amphibians vulnerable to disease and toxins also makes saltwater fearsome. Key adaptations allowed G. maritimus to skirt these issues. G. maritimus and its relatives evolved bony body armor, probably for defense. But these hard plates would have helped the seafloor dwellers prevent water loss. And unlike modern amphibians, which typically lose their internal gills after the larval stage, this creature and its close relatives retained a fishy breathing strategy suitable for life in the depths.

G. maritimus fossils hint that the animal lurked on the seafloor as an ambush predator. Its jaw lifted upward like a toilet seat so that it could unleash a suction attack on fish and other small creatures.

There may yet be other amphibians hiding in ancient oceans, environments ignored by paleontologists studying these creatures. “Because they’re amphibians, we would be looking for them in terrestrial freshwater environments,” Hart says. Perhaps there are more amphibians that have gotten their sea legs.

#6414. Scientists Develop a Groundbreaking Rechargeable Battery That Runs on Vitamin B12

The same vitamin found in everyday foods could eventually help store surplus renewable electricity, after an experimental zinc-air battery using B12 completed up to 250 recharge cycles.

The search for safer, more sustainable batteries is leading scientists to some unexpected places, including the chemistry of vitamins. Researchers at the University of Córdoba in Spain have found that vitamin B12, a nutrient essential to human health, can also help power a rechargeable battery. Their experimental design completed up to 250 charge and discharge cycles, opening another possibility for future energy storage technology.

The researchers developed a zinc-air battery, which generates electricity through chemical reactions involving zinc and oxygen from the surrounding air. Unlike conventional batteries that store all their reactive materials internally, zinc-air batteries draw oxygen from the environment. This makes them lighter and gives them high energy density, meaning they can store substantial energy relative to their weight. They are already used in small devices such as hearing aids.

Zinc also offers advantages because it is abundant and recyclable. These batteries use nonflammable, water-based electrolytes, making them potentially safer than conventional lithium-ion batteries, whose raw material extraction raises economic, social, and environmental concerns.

Making zinc-air batteries rechargeable, however, presents a challenge. They need a catalyst, a substance that helps chemical reactions proceed, that can support both the production of electricity and the reverse process needed to recharge the battery.

Vitamin B12, also known as cobalamin, offered a possible solution because its molecular structure contains cobalt (III), a form of the metal cobalt that helps drive these reactions. Although better known for its role in nutrition, B12 is produced naturally by certain bacteria and manufactured commercially for food and pharmaceutical applications. Found in foods of animal origin, it is used to address nutritional deficiencies and has also become popular alongside other B vitamins as a hangover remedy because it can help reduce fatigue.

Researcher Antonio Jesús Fernández Romero explained that vitamin B12 “has proven to meet the necessary conditions to act as a good catalyst because, during discharge, it catalyzes the reduction of oxygen to water and, during recharging, it promotes the production of oxygen”.

The difficulty was keeping the vitamin inside the battery. Because B12 dissolves readily in water, it could not simply be added to a battery that uses a water-based electrolyte. The researchers solved this problem by attaching the vitamin to single-walled carbon nanotubes, extremely thin carbon structures that hold it in place while allowing it to support the chemical reactions. Their approach mimicked “the process by which amino acids bind together in proteins.”

The prototype was developed by the Physical Chemistry research group (FQM-204) at the University of Córdoba’s Chemical Institute for Energy and the Environment (IQUEMA). As study author Manuel Cano Luna explained, “we looked at the properties we can find in naturally occurring materials to use them in new batteries.”

This is the group’s third battery prototype using a biological molecule as a catalyst. Earlier experiments involved hemoglobin, which contains iron (II), and catalase, which contains iron (III). The key advance with vitamin B12 is that the resulting battery can be recharged, completing up to 250 cycles in the researchers’ tests.

Although the prototype remains experimental, the findings suggest that naturally occurring molecules could contribute to cheaper, more sustainable energy storage systems. With further development, rechargeable zinc-air batteries could eventually help store surplus electricity from renewable energy sources, addressing one of the challenges of transitioning toward cleaner energy.

Reference: “A vitamin B12-based air electrode for high-performance rechargeable zinc–air batteries” by García-Caballero, Valentín, López-León, Miguel, G. Argudo, Pablo, Camacho, Luis, Rodríguez Mellado, José M., Martín-Romero, Maria T., Abad, José, Fernández Romero, Antonio J. and Cano, Manuel, , Journal of Materials Chemistry A. A fresh look at Einstein's equations suggests that gravity can sometimes snap and reconnect, similar to magnetic field lines on the sun. The findings hint at a new way that gravity and matter can trade energy.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Magnetic reconnection — the process behind the sun's most violent outbursts — may have a counterpart in gravity.

According to a new theoretical study, sheet-like structures in the gravitational field can break apart and reconnect in new arrangements, much like the magnetic field lines that unleash solar flares.

Built entirely on Albert Einstein's theory of general relativity, the study spells out when this "gravitational reconnection" can happen. It also offers a way to measure how fast the theoretical reconnection proceeds, and suggests a change to how gravity and matter trade energy. The process could even play a role in black hole collisions, the researchers suggest.

Magnetic field lines are normally "frozen" into plasma — the hot, electrically charged gas that makes up stars — and carried along wherever it flows. The lines can be stretched and twisted, but not cut. Where this rule breaks down, they can snap and rejoin in a process called magnetic reconnection, releasing pent-up energy in explosive bursts such as solar flares.

"In plasma physics, reconnection has become an essential part of our understanding of how magnetic fields reorganize and exchange energy with matter," Luca Comisso, an astrophysicist at Columbia University and first author of the study, told Live Science via email. "Could something similar be true for gravity?"

"Gravity and magnetism describe very different aspects of nature, so there's no obvious reason to expect them to behave alike," Comisso said. "But when we express Einstein's equations in a particular mathematical form, some of the same principles that govern magnetic fields also emerge in gravity. We wanted to understand whether those similarities extended to reconnection itself."

Comisso and study co-author Felipe Asenjo, a physicist at Adolfo Ibáñez University in Chile, used a mathematical framework known as the tetrad formulation. "Einstein's theory describes gravity through the geometry of space-time," Comisso explained. But in the tetrad formulation, "certain aspects of gravity can be expressed through quantities resembling electric and magnetic fields."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In a prior study published in the journal Physical Review Letters earlier this year, the researchers applied this framework to gravity. That study suggested that gravitational fields can form two-dimensional structures called gravitational field sheets. Of the sheets' two dimensions, one stretches through space and the other through time — so each sheet is the trail a line leaves as time passes. A snapshot at any instant therefore catches each sheet as a line, akin to the field lines drawn around a magnet. And, like magnetic field lines frozen into a plasma, "under certain conditions, these sheets evolve without breaking or changing how they are connected," Comisso said.

An illustration depicting the sun’s magnetic field lines over an image taken by NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory. When magnetic loops get stretched to their limit, they snap and reconnect, triggering solar flares.

In the new study, published Oct. 28 in the journal Physical Review D, the researchers found that this is not always the case. "Gravitational field sheets can break and reconnect in a different arrangement, much like magnetic field lines do in plasmas," Comisso said.

The researchers showed that breaking the frozen-in rule doesn't, by itself, guarantee reconnection. Sometimes, the sheets merely slip relative to the flow that carries them, staying intact because they remain frozen into a different flow. Genuine reconnection happens only when no such alternative flow exists.

"We also derived equations describing how quickly this reconnection can occur and how it can affect the transfer of energy and momentum," Comisso said. In general relativity, gravity and matter can trade energy and momentum, with only their combined total conserved. The study shows that reconnection changes the local rate of that exchange.

Reconnection also alters gravitational helicity, the gravitational counterpart of a quantity that measures how twisted and interlinked magnetic field lines are. Frozen-in sheets keep their helicity fixed, but reconnection can create or destroy it.

The findings don't require new physics. "Everything follows from Einstein's general relativity," Comisso said.

"Einstein developed his theory more than a century ago, and it has passed an extraordinary number of experimental tests," he added. "Yet even after more than a century, there are still new insights to be gained from those same equations."

What could trigger gravitational reconnection in nature remains an open question. Among the candidates the researchers suggested are the singularities thought to lurk at the hearts of black holes and the combined effect of gravitational ripples that are too small to track individually. Quantum effects linked to Hawking radiation ‪—‬ the faint glow that black holes are predicted to emit ‪—‬ could also play a part.

"We're still at the beginning, but one of the most interesting possibilities is that gravitational reconnection could play a role in extreme events, such as the merger of two black holes or the collision of neutron stars," Comisso said. "These are environments where gravity is extremely strong and the geometry of spacetime changes dramatically."

Such collisions send out ripples in space-time called gravitational waves, which detectors such as LIGO (the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) have been recording since 2015. "We'd like to understand whether gravitational reconnection could contribute to transferring energy, and whether it might leave a recognizable signature in gravitational waves," Comisso added. "We don't know the answers yet, but these are questions that we can now begin to investigate."

Comisso, L., & Asenjo, F. A. (2026). Reconnection of gravitational fields. Physical Review. D., 114(8). https://doi.org/10.1103/lmqy-pf9k

Andrey got his B.Sc. and M.Sc. degrees in elementary particle physics from Novosibirsk State University in Russia, and a Ph.D. in string theory from the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel. He works as a science writer, specializing in physics, space, and technology. His articles have been published in AdvancedScienceNews, PhysicsWorld, Science, and other outlets.

#6412. A Tiny Region Deep Inside Your Brain Helps Decide What You Remember

Scientists have discovered that a small brain region best known for processing emotions plays a surprisingly broad role in determining which experiences become lasting memories.

The brain records countless sights and experiences every day, yet only a fraction become lasting memories. Scientists have now identified a pattern of neural activity that helps predict what will be remembered, pointing to a much broader role for a brain region traditionally associated with emotions and fear.

The discovery, made by researchers at Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University and published in Nature Neuroscience, centers on the amygdala, a walnut-sized structure deep within the temporal lobe. The findings suggest that specialized neurons in this region help determine which new experiences are selected for long-term memory storage.

The amygdala has long been known for its involvement in emotional and social behavior, particularly the processing of fear. Its contribution to memory was generally thought to center on emotionally significant experiences. The new research indicates that its influence extends to more ordinary visual experiences, even those without an obvious emotional component.

Researchers identified neurons that respond preferentially to certain types of images, including faces, animals, and landscapes. When these neurons reacted more strongly to an image from their preferred category, participants were more likely to remember that image later. This suggests that the strength of these specialized neural responses helps predict which experiences will remain accessible in memory.

“Our results demonstrate that the activity of specific kinds of neurons in the amygdala predicts, while the person sees an image for the first time, whether that image will later be remembered,” said Ueli Rutishauser, PhD,>

To investigate how the brain selects information for storage, scientists analyzed recordings from 112 patients who had electrodes implanted in their brains to monitor epileptic seizures. These electrodes allowed researchers to measure the electrical activity of individual neurons while participants viewed unfamiliar images.

Later that same day, participants were asked to recall the pictures they had seen. By comparing their memory performance with the earlier neural recordings, investigators could identify patterns of amygdala activity associated with successful recall. The findings were replicated in two separate datasets, strengthening the evidence for the relationship between these neurons and memory formation.

The unusually large collection of single-neuron recordings was assembled through a multi-institutional research consortium led by Cedars-Sinai and supported by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) Brain Research Through Advancing Innovative Neurotechnologies (BRAIN) initiative. Jiayang Xiao, PhD, led the research as the study’s first author.

“This is an impactful study that provides mechanistic insight into the role of the human amygdala—a region commonly associated with emotional responses—in determining which experiences and stimuli become lasting episodic memories. This rigorous human neuroscience study, which uses next-generation tools, has high potential to move discovery toward measurable health impacts,” said Mauricio Rangel-Gomez, PhD, program officer at NIH.

The results raise the possibility that disruptions to amygdala activity contribute to memory difficulties associated with neurological conditions. Although the recordings establish a relationship between neuronal responses and later recall, further research is needed to determine whether modifying these responses could improve memory.

“Our findings have important clinical implications, as the memory impairments seen in disorders such as Alzheimer’s disease and temporal lobe epilepsy might be partly due to disrupted processes within the amygdala,” said Rutishauser, also a professor of Neurosurgery. “The amygdala might therefore be a suitable new target for treating these disorders using neuromodulation and/or cellular therapies.”

An additional question is whether the same memory selection process operates across different senses. The current experiments focused on visual information, and Rutishauser said future studies could examine whether the amygdala also helps determine which sounds and smells become lasting memories.

“This study’s insights are the latest in a long line of research led by Cedars-Sinai and collaborators dedicated to revealing how human memory functions,” said Adam Mamelak, MD,> Reference: “Stimulus-specific recruitment of human amygdala neurons predicts episodic memory encoding success” by Jiayang Xiao, Jonathan Daume, Yousef Salimpour, Natalia Kurilenko, Clayton Mosher, William S. Anderson, Taufik A. Valiante, Adam N. Mamelak and Ueli Rutishauser, 27 October 2026, Nature Neuroscience. DOI: 10.1038/s41593-026-02493-9

This work was supported by the BRAIN Initiative through the National Institutes of Health (grant no. U01NS117839 to U.R.) and a Center for Neural Science and Medicine Postdoctoral Fellowship by Cedars-Sinai (to J.X.)

#6411. Everything You Need to Set Up a 3D Printer Lab at Home

It’s surprisingly simple to achieve better 3D prints in a dedicated print space.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

There is something deeply satisfying about building your own 3D printer lab. It streamlines your process, sure, making projects easier. But it also makes the act of using a 3D printer feel a bit like being a mad scientist, bringing wild creations to life. It doesn’t need to be sophisticated or expensive, either: Simply having a small, dedicated space for your printer goes a long way toward helping you use it safely and efficiently.

Here’s the good news: Converting a basement corner, garage, or spare bedroom into a printer lab doesn’t take a lot of work. With a little planning and a few simple tools, you can set up a space that allows you to make projects with long print times, and where the tools you need are close at hand (not buried under that stack of other projects you don’t have space for). I started working with 3D printers in my basement workshop about five years ago, and have been tinkering with my setup ever since.

If you’re new to 3D printing or want to get your maker space in order, I’ve learned a lot about how to make a neat, efficient space that lets you focus on your printing projects, rather than the logistics around them. We’ll walk through how to prep a space for printers, and all the gear you’ll want to have on hand when you print regularly. If you have the maker bug, the right space will unlock more options for creating anything your imagination can dream up.

Ready to design the printer lab of your dreams? Begin by assessing the space you have and considering what your printer (or potential printer) needs to operate safely and efficiently. Once you understand those two factors, you can let them guide your decisions about layout, environmental controls, and equipment.

Before we start moving furniture around, measuring spaces, and buying equipment, the first thing you need to look at is your 3D printer (or printers). The two most common consumer-grade printer types, fused deposition modeling (FDM) and resin printers, both have their own safety requirements, so having one or the other (or both) will impact your plans.

FDM printers need space to store filament spools, as well as tools and a working area to remove supports and (if needed) to assemble parts into a larger, finished piece. The biggest challenge for an FDM printer lab is controlling humidity, which means that a damp basement printer lab will need a dehumidifier.

Resin printers need space to wash away excess resin and cure the models after printing. The biggest challenge for a resin printer lab is fume extraction. Look for a space with good ventilation, such as windows, as long as there won’t be direct sunlight on the printer.

Now that we’ve reviewed the impact of the printers, let’s talk about what kind of space makes for a good printer lab. Like most design challenges, some elements are essential (like ventilation), while others are open to negotiation. And, obviously, we are all often limited by what kind(s) of spaces we may have available. With that in mind, these are the basics I’d look for:

Space No consumer-grade 3D printer takes up a ton of room, so you don’t need a giant workshop. More often than not, a corner of your basement or utility room will work well enough. As long as you have a space about the size of a card table (room for a printer and a small work surface) in a well-ventilated area, you can have a successful printer lab.

Don't set up your printers in an area that gets a lot of foot traffic, like a living room, or where you eat or sleep. These printers generate a lot of noise and, often, fumes. Escaping those side effects is a big part of why you want a “lab” in the first place.

Lighting From a practical standpoint, your printer lab should be well-lit, but it doesn’t need to be anything fancy: Some simple overhead lighting is all you need. I also like to have a swing-arm task light so I can put new prints under a spotlight while I remove supports or process resin.

Also, keep in mind that you should never place a resin printer in direct sunlight: The sun will cure the resin in your vat, ruining your prints and turning the material in your vat into an expensive plastic brick.

Storage The more you print, the more stuff you’re going to accumulate. If nothing else, you’ll need storage for your materials—resin or filament. If you’re just getting started, don’t be intimidated. All you need is a small shelf or storage bin that’s not in direct sunlight.

Ventilation 3D printing creates fumes. FDM fumes tend to be moderate, but the fumes from resin printers (and the post-print cleaning process) are serious stuff. This means proper ventilation is a critical safety feature for any 3D printer lab. You need a room with at least a window or two, and preferably some equipment to keep air moving. (See the Fumes section later for more suggestions.)

Humidity Control If there’s too much moisture in the air, your FDM printer will struggle. Filament absorbs moisture, leading to warped layers and wrapping your print in threads of over-extruded filament.

With the location selected and the type of printer picked out, we can begin stocking your printer lab with tools and accessories that make your workflow smoother and ensure that your prints come out right. Start by addressing humidity (if you have an FDM printer) or fume extraction (if you have a resin printer).

Humidity control is a major concern for FDM printers. In my printer lab, I use a dehumidifier to bring the overall humidity down to about 45 percent, then use filament dryers and desiccant bags to store filament at 20 to 30 percent relative humidity.

If you’re setting up in a basement (or live in a very humid area), you need a dehumidifier to pull water out of the air. Luckily, we have a whole guide devoted to helping you find the best one for your space.

To minimize the impact of humidity on your filaments, you should put them in containers that you can monitor and control. I use these affordable kitchen-grade plastic bins, which are the perfect size to hold a standard roll of filament.

Hygrometers are small, affordable humidity sensors that are great for tracking humidity in your lab or even in specific containers. I slip one into each individual filament storage bin, so I’m positive that all of my materials are being stored in a dry environment—I keep them below 30 percent relative humidity.

Desiccant bags, small bags of moisture-absorbing pellets that draw moisture from the air just like a sponge, are a very affordable way to minimize moisture inside storage containers and filament dryers. You can always purchase fresh silicone desiccant, but the ones that come with printer filament and printer tools (or any electronics) are easy to reuse.

Desiccant adds a little bit of maintenance to your setup: Just like you need to wring out a sponge, you’ll need to either replace or “recharge” your desiccant to make sure it keeps working. To “recharge” it, you’ll need to heat the bags and allow them to release their moisture. (I do it in the toaster oven: 150 to 200 degrees Fahrenheit for two to three hours.)

The most expensive, task-oriented option is a dedicated filament dryer, which heats your print materials to minimize condensation, then vents moisture-laden air. Many of them also have an outlet, so you can use them on the filament that’s currently feeding the print without removing it from humidity control.

Some manufacturers make multi-filament boxes that double as drying units. The Bambu AMS PRO 2, for example, can dry up to four spools of filament at once—though it only works when connected to a Bambu printer. I’ve also tested and really liked the Elegoo H1 HT, which is a universal option that pairs with any printer and has electronic controls to adjust settings and monitor humidity.

When printing with resin, you need to vent your fumes outdoors; an air purifier will help, but it’s not enough to get the job done completely. Even when venting fumes outdoors, be sure to use a respirator and gloves while working directly with the resin. Here’s what you need:

Dorundea Multifunctional 3D Printer Enclosure Ventilation

The best way to avoid fumes is to vent them out of your home quickly and efficiently. A full printer enclosure allows you to do that in one fell swoop. The enclosure surrounds the printer, minimizing contamination, and filters out the fumes via a tube that you feed outside a window or wall vent. It kind of looks like a miniature greenhouse kit.

Air purifiers capture odors and impurities in the air. They don’t replace good ventilation, but they improve air quality and make your space a much more pleasant place to be. Look for an air purifier that has at least one layer of activated charcoal filter to catch fumes from the resin printing process. For more info on picking out an air purifier, check out our Air Purifier Buying Guide.

You need a respirator to protect against the organic fumes associated with resin and some FDM filaments. These fumes will pass right through a mask designed to keep out particulates, like an N95 or dust mask. Make sure to buy cartridges designed to protect you from organic vapors. (These typically have a black or yellow color code on them.)

You are going to go through a lot of gloves with your resin printing hobby. Resin is harmful to your skin, and once it’s on your hands, it’s only a matter of time before it transfers to your face or anything else you touch. I recommend buying in bulk. A big box of 100 should last for a while.

Regular safety glasses protect your eyes against flying debris when removing supports from both resin and FDM prints. And UV glasses will keep your eyes safe when using a UV flashlight to touch up your resin prints. Even if you don’t have a resin printer now, it’s not a bad idea to pick up a pair of UV glasses and use them as a catchall.

Beyond the printer itself, every lab needs a workspace with a small set of tools to work with your prints post-production. These are the essentials that I break out after most of my prints, and I expect that you’ll find yourself reaching for them over and over, too.

A scraper is an essential tool for any maker. Sometimes the print sticks to the build plate when you’re taking it out. A plastic or steel scraper makes removing it much easier. Of course, you can always print a scraper and plastic blade yourself, too.

3D printers build a support structure to help the printed materials take shape. More often than not, that means you’re going to need to do some post-print cleanup work on whatever you make. A small pair of snippers is the best tool for this job.

Look for “flush-cut” snippers, which are flat on one side, allowing the cutting blades to get as close to the surface as possible. When in doubt, smaller is usually better in this case. Depending on the print, you may need to reach into very tight spots to remove supports.

And you need a clean workspace to do all that snipping. A large silicone mat gives you a safe workspace for post-print cleanup work, which is especially important if you’re working with resin. Resin can be difficult to clean off most surfaces, but easily comes off of silicone. Look for a mat with a slightly raised lip to prevent liquids or small pieces from getting loose.

If you're swapping out the resin in your printer’s vat (or just putting it away), you'll need to get the vat resin back into the original bottle. This stainless steel funnel is tailor-made for the job. It has a mesh filter, which prevents cured resin or other small items from contaminating the rest of your resin.

Run a UV flashlight beam over your resin-soaked paper towels, and they will instantly cure and be safe to dispose of. Or use it to touch up or repair resin prints; spread a few drops of resin along a crack, and hit it with the UV light to seal it together.

One of the most enjoyable parts of having a 3D printer lab is making it your very own. My workspaces are filled with failed prints, weird art, alien heads, masks, and a whole range of things that are unique to me. Once you start 3D printing, you’ll have your own collection of items in no time.

No matter how you design your space, you’ll find that there are unique issues in your setup not covered in this article. Lean on the 3D community to find solutions. Look at the public boards on Makerworld, Printables, or other manufacturer sites, along with Reddit and similar online communities. Chances are good that someone else out there has run into something similar. And if not, you’ll get to come up with your own unique solution. Which is good news, because there’s nothing in this world that’s better than having your own unique mad scientist laboratory.

A former residential remodeler and maintenance manager, Dan Stout has worked in nearly every part of the construction and DIY industry, from project planning and permitting to plumbing, drywall, carpentry, and more. He loves to write about the weird history of everyday objects, and to help readers make informed decisions about their homes.
