#6410. Scientists Trap a Single Antimatter Particle for Months in Quest To Solve the Universe’s Biggest Mystery

A single particle of antimatter, suspended for months in a laboratory trap, could help physicists unravel why matter survived to build the universe around us.

Northwestern University physicists have brought a positron, the electron’s antimatter counterpart, into a precisely controlled quantum state for the first time. After capturing the energetic particle from radioactive decay, they cooled it to nearly absolute zero and suspended it in a near-perfect vacuum.

Their achievement, described in Physical Review Letters, creates a “one-positron quantum cyclotron.” Like an artificial atom, the trapped positron has distinct quantum energy levels that researchers can manipulate and observe.

That control opens a path toward an exceptionally precise comparison of matter and antimatter. By measuring the positron’s magnetic properties and comparing them with an electron’s, the team hopes to test a fundamental prediction of particle physics and search for signs that current theory is missing something.

The Standard Model describes fundamental particles and three of nature’s four fundamental forces (electromagnetic, strong nuclear, and weak nuclear forces). Although experiments have repeatedly confirmed its predictions with extraordinary precision, it cannot explain why the observable universe contains overwhelmingly more matter than antimatter.

“Antimatter gets its popular charm from science fiction,” said study leader Gerald Gabrielse. “If you take an electron and an anti-electron (or positron) and collide them together, they both disappear. We describe that as annihilation, a concept that fuels science fiction writers’ imaginations. The big mystery of the universe is the Big Bang should have created equal amounts of matter and antimatter. But, if that were true, it would annihilate, and we’d be left with nothing. There’s clearly something wrong with that theory, and that’s what we’re trying to figure out.”

The unresolved question is how matter escaped annihilation to build stars, planets, and people.

“We know the Standard Model has to be wrong somewhere—or at least incomplete,” Gabrielse said. “For example, it cannot predict why the universe exists, so that’s a pretty big loophole. We’re very precisely examining the most fundamental and simple systems to find where the theory breaks down. We hope to find an unambiguous answer.”

Nearly everything on Earth consists of electrons, protons, and neutrons. An antimatter world could instead contain positrons, antiprotons, and antineutrons. Gabrielse says that if everything here were made of antimatter, the difference would be extraordinarily difficult to recognize. The trouble begins when matter and antimatter meet, which makes an ordinary container unsuitable for holding a positron.

“If we want to study antimatter, we must handle it carefully,” Gabrielse said. “To be clear, it’s not dangerous. We don’t have enough antimatter to make an explosion.”

The Northwestern team used specialized electric and magnetic fields to suspend the particle away from the walls of an advanced trap. A near-perfect vacuum minimizes encounters with ordinary matter, allowing the positron to remain confined for months.

Capturing it required first overcoming its enormous initial energy. The researchers obtained positrons from the radioactive decay of sodium-22, a rare isotope of sodium, then slowed a particle dramatically and guided it into the trap.

Inside the trap, the temperature is about 300 millikelvins, just 0.3 degrees Celsius (0.54 degrees Fahrenheit) above absolute zero. Cooling allows the researchers to bring the positron’s cyclotron motion, its circling movement in the magnetic field, into its lowest quantum energy state.

“We cool it down so much that it’s in its quantum ground state,” Gabrielse said. “We actually coaxed this very fast positron to sit there and behave for months at a time.”

The team then used carefully tuned microwaves to deliver tiny amounts of energy and detected the positron’s transitions between individual quantum states. Being able to both trigger and observe those changes provides the control needed for a highly precise magnetic measurement.

The experiment combines two strands of Gabrielse’s career. His group previously developed techniques to isolate electrons and measure their magnetic properties, while his pioneering work on slowing, capturing, and cooling antiprotons helped establish low-energy antimatter research. The new study extends the quantum control achieved with electrons to a single antimatter particle.

In earlier work, Gabrielse’s team used a one-electron quantum cyclotron to measure the electron’s magnetic moment to about one part in 10 trillion, among the most precise measurements ever made of an elementary particle. The magnetic moment describes how strongly a particle interacts with a magnetic field.

The next goal is to make a comparable measurement of the positron. Electrons and positrons have opposite electric charges, and theory predicts magnetic moments equal in magnitude but opposite in direction. An unexpected mismatch would challenge the Standard Model and could offer clues to the universe’s imbalance between matter and antimatter.

“Current theories suggest that there will be no difference in the two measurements,” Gabrielse said. “If it turns out they are not equal, that would be the biggest discovery in physics in the last century.”

Reference: “One-Positron Quantum Cyclotron” by T. G. Myers, L. Soucy, B. A. D. Sukra, B. Sinha and G. Gabrielse, August 20, 2026, arXiv. DOI: 10.1103/gbkc-6nlj

This study was funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation.

Scientists Trap a Single Antimatter Particle for Months in Quest To Solve the Universe’s Biggest Mystery. VERY GOOD.

Scientists are invited to reflect deeply: how do you interpret so-called antimatter?

This headline is essentially accurate at the level of experimental reporting, but at the conceptual level it perpetuates the matter/antimatter dichotomy, which the Topological Vortex Theory (TVT) holds should be abandoned. According to TVT, once a topological vortex and its antivortex are formed, they possess the same material attributes; “anti-” merely describes their relative relation at the moment of emergence—opposite directions of motion and opposite vortex chirality. Thereafter, the two evolve independently as material entities, and no persistent ontological distinction between “matter” and “antimatter” remains.

Thus, “antimatter” is more appropriately understood as another form of matter with an opposite mode of motion, rather than as a special entity opposed to matter. The fact that a positron can be confined for extended periods and measured with high precision precisely indicates that it is a stable material entity, just like the electron, differing only in the sign of its charge or in its mode of motion. The experimental data themselves are neutral; what matters is the interpretive framework. Mainstream physics regards the matter–antimatter asymmetry as “the universe’s greatest mystery” because it presupposes that the early universe should have produced equal amounts of matter and antimatter, which would then have almost completely annihilated. TVT rejects this presupposition: once the two vortex forms have emerged, both are independent material entities, and there is no necessary premise that they “should have annihilated entirely.” Hence, this “mystery” does not arise within the TVT framework.

#6409. Most Space Heaters Oscillate Side-to-Side. This Dreo Moves Air Upward for Better Coverage.

The powerful fan and rotating body poured out warmth in every direction.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

It’s been a bit chilly as the cold weather has begun to set in. In that chilliness, I’ve broken out the cable-knit sweaters and undershirts, but I can’t very well type in gloves. In order to beat the freeze in the cavernously large bullpen with high ceilings and large windows that is our office, I needed a space heater built for the moment. That space heater is the Dreo Whole Room.

The Dreo Whole Room space heater oscillates both horizontally and vertically to cover larger areas of space and better distribute heat throughout a room. At the same time, the device is also extremely powerful, blasting heat at three different temperature levels and fan speeds. Particularly for drafty rooms or larger spaces, this is a space heater that not only got my attention but helped get my blood flowing.

I loved the Dreo both for quick, on-demand heat as well as for more sustained use over several hours throughout the day. Even in the drafty office, there was a notable difference in temperature almost immediately, and it spread well beyond just my desk when oscillating.

The most notable feature on the Dreo Whole Room Heater is the dual oscillation. With both horizontal and vertical oscillation, the space heater is capable of spreading heat in more directions and bringing the temperature of a space up more holistically. This design choice prevents cold spots in a room and provides a more overall warmth so you don’t have to be in direct line of the heater in order to feel its effects.

In my own use, the feeling is noticeable. When left on and oscillating for a few minutes in a side room in our office, I walked back into a noticeable shift in temperature. The room was nearly as warm in the far corners of the space as it was within a three-foot radius around the heater.

While the oscillation is great for heating up full rooms, there’s still a lot of additional customization available to tinker with. The space heater comes with three different heat levels as well as three fan speeds so you can choose the intensity and strength of the air. While this is great for short bursts of time, I preferred using the temperature setting.

This setting allowed me to choose a specific temperature, and the Dreo would automatically run, slowing down as it neared it, and occasionally turning back on to maintain it. If you expect to use the space heater for extended periods of time, this mode makes it easier to both not overheat and save a bit of energy. That said, the Eco mode is your best bet for cutting down on energy costs.

Once I know that the heating power is powerful enough to be worth the money, the next concern is always safety (despite it probably deserving to be first). On this front, the Dreo Whole Room Heater is a solid choice.

The space heater not only has tip-over protection and a safety plug but also automatically shuts off if overheated and has a three-second child lock to prevent them from accidentally switching settings inadvertently. My only real issue with the child lock is that the three-second time might not be enough time to prevent a kid from unlocking the features and making changes.

As far as a space heater goes, I really only want to make sure it heats well and is safe to use. On those fronts, the Dreo Whole Room Space Heater gets the job done.

However, the Dreo goes far beyond what’s expected. The dual oscillation helps warm up larger spaces with greater speed and efficiency, and the safety features make me feel comfortable leaving it on when I’m out of the room for periods of time.

If you have larger rooms you want to warm up without turning on your central heating, or simply want to get a fuller warmth as opposed to an incredibly localized one, the Dreo Whole Room is a good horse to back.

The new Peerium architecture aims to power hyper-efficient computers capable of training AI models with up to 40 trillion parameters.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Engineers in China have built a new computer architecture they say can one day make up to a million artificial intelligence (AI) chips work as one. For comparison, Elon Musk's AI company, SpaceXAI (soon to be SpaceXSI), describes its Colossus cluster as the world's most powerful AI training system, comprising 200,000 interconnected chips.

Traditionally, the AI chips used to train foundation models are housed in separate servers and communicate over a network to share data and divide workloads. But the new architecture, Peerium, uses a high-speed interconnect system designed to maintain efficient communication between chips across multiple racks, even as the number of chips scales into the hundreds of thousands.

Huawei unveiled the new architecture Sept. 17 at the company's annual CONNECT conference.

Representatives from Huawei said in a statement that computers powered by Peerium could train models with up to 40 trillion parameters. For comparison, competing hardware, like GB200 NVL72 from NVIDIA and CS-3 from Cerebras, have reported training at the trillion-parameter scale, rather than the tens-of-trillions.

"Over the next two years, there will be roughly 6 or 7 frontier AI labs in China, and all will aim at training foundation language models of sizes ranging from 10 to 40 trillion parameters," Liao Heng, chief scientist for Huawei's chip design arm HiSilicon, told the Associated Press. "So you need such a scale of infrastructure to train these models."

Peerium's performance relies on three elements: nested parallelism, unified memory addressing, and peer-to-peer interconnects, Huawei representatives said in the statement.

Nested parallelism allows workloads to be broken into smaller tasks and organized across hierarchical groups of chips that work in parallel. It's similar to how a company breaks down work into departments and then smaller teams, all of which coordinate their efforts toward a common goal. Unified memory addressing allows processors to access memory across other servers, as opposed to only that attached to the processor's own server. Peer-to-peer interconnects allow components to communicate more directly with one another, rather than relying on an intermediary.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

All three principles are designed to make more efficient use of computing resources so that a single system can coordinate larger numbers of chips to handle demanding AI workloads.

According to Huawei, existing interconnect technologies — which link processors and servers to enable them to communicate — cannot support the Peerium architecture at the scale it envisages. For instance, NVIDIA uses NVLink for communication within racks and InfiniBand for communication between racks. The inter-rack communication bandwidth in this setup is 200GB per second, Eric Xu, Huawei's rotating chairman, told the AP.

"With such a low inter-rack communications bandwidth, there is no way you can make one million processors work as one computer," he said.

Huawei instead developed its own interconnect technology, UnifiedBus, which the company says delivers inter-rack communications bandwidth of up to 800GB per second.

"When one million processors work as one computer, this lays the foundation for better and more efficient AI training and inference," Xu added. "Therefore, I see UnifiedBus as the path for the future AI era. I believe, in the years to come, other players would certainly follow suit."

Alongside Peerium, Huawei also announced the Atlas 950 SuperPoD, a computing system built on Peerium and powered by more than 8,000 Huawei Ascend 950DT AI accelerator chips.

Xu said testing for AI training is underway on these SuperPoDs and that results show that they use their available computing power for AI training more efficiently than AI computing clusters that aren’t based on Peerium and UnifiedBus.

Huawei expects to begin supplying the SuperPoDs by early next year, at the latest, before its SuperClusters, which link multiple SuperPoDs to form a larger AI computing system, based on Peerium, eventually come online. Representatives said that one SuperCluster with 256,000 computing cards — hardware modules that add processing capacity — is currently being deployed and tested.

Models with large numbers of parameters demand greater computing resources and infrastructure, which isn't always desirable as it increases costs. In the summer, researchers used an IBM quantum computer to reduce the perplexity of Meta's Llama 3.1 8B language model — a measure of how well it predicts the next word or token — while keeping the number of parameters almost unchanged.

#6407. This may be the best evidence yet that dinosaur blood can fossilize

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Minerals may have preserved remnants of ancient blood in a dinosaur bone, but some are skeptical

Using a technique called scanning electron microscopy to peer inside an 115 million-year-old dinosaur limb bone, researchers captured images of tiny ellipsoid structures, about 20 micrometers in diameter, that may be fossilized red blood cells. Molecular analyses found preserved heme — the oxygen-carrying component of hemoglobin — in the bone.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The life and times of a dinosaur may be written in its blood — if blood can be preserved in bone.

Tiny microstructures found in the limb bones of a fossilized 115-million-year-old specimen are the remnants of red blood cells, researchers report November 2 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The team says these are both the oldest red blood cell structures yet identified and the first to be chemically proven. But not everyone is as sanguine about that conclusion.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The ability to identify such structures could offer a powerful molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals, including their metabolism and even activity levels, says paleontologist Kliti Grice of Curtin University in Bentley, Australia.

The bone, from a fossil-rich site in northeastern Brazil called Mina Pedra Branca, belonged to the dinosaur Aratasaurus museunacionali. Grice and her colleagues used a variety of chemical and imaging analyses to study the Cretaceous Period specimen.

Maurilio Oliveira/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

The team prepared thin cross-sectional slices of bone and imaged details of the limb bone’s internal structure with focused electron beams. That revealed ellipse-shaped microstructures within the limb’s fossilized network of blood vessels.

A map of the ellipsoids’ chemical element composition revealed that they were full of iron, carbon and nitrogen, all components of a biomolecule called heme. Heme is an iron-bearing, ring-shaped molecule found in hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout the body.

Then, the researchers used a technique that identifies molecules by how they scatter laser light. Those analyses suggested the presence of porphyrins, ringlike organic compounds found in blood — and the precursors of heme. Finally, they ruled out contamination from other porphyrins, such as the pigment chlorophyll, by separating and identifying the molecular contents of a bone extract. That experiment also suggested heme.

Taken together, these findings point unequivocally to the preservation of molecular traces of ancient blood, the team says. They also offer a clue to a novel pathway that might preserve those traces for so many millions of years.

Blood cells decompose within days of the death of an organism. Only unusual and fast-acting environmental and biochemical conditions could have stopped decay and held those tissues in place as the organism fossilizes.

In this fossil, the secret ingredient was a manganese oxide mineral called hausmannite, the researchers say. The team’s analyses had found the mineral within the ellipsoid structures. That mineral, they propose, may have acted as a time capsule, preserving the cellular structures and protecting the molecules within, including collagen amino acids.

Distinguishing fossilized blood cells from nonorganic minerals that formed within a fossil after the organism’s death is a tricky task. During fossilization, mineral-rich fluids seep in and around the bones, and the minerals that form within the fossil can bear a strong resemblance to bodily structures.

In a 1997 study, two paleontologists analyzed tiny spheres found inside the limb of a fossil, possibly a pterosaur. The spheres were once thought to be the fossilized remnants of ancient blood cells, but the duo determined that the spheres were instead pyrite, an iron mineral that had been deposited in the bones after death.

Those paleontologists suggested that, going forward, several criteria should be met before proposing a blood cell origin for fossilized structures, including comparing the shape of the structures with that of living related organisms and identifying certain biomarkers in the structures. One of those biomarkers is heme compounds.

Grice and her colleagues say that their study meets these criteria. Unlike the pyrite, hausmannite was crucial to preservation, “rather than simply a mineral that replaced biological material after it had disappeared,” she says. The close spatial relationship between the hausmannite, the blood cell-like structures and the chemical signatures of heme “raises the possibility that mineralization helped stabilize, entomb and protect components of the original biological material during fossilization.”

But Mary Schweitzer, a paleontologist at North Carolina State University in Raleigh who was not involved in the new study, says she doesn’t think these findings do fully meet those criteria.

The heme biomarkers, for example, don’t appear to be localized to the round structures alone, as would be expected in fossilized blood cells, but come from analysis of the entire bone. The proposed red blood cells also differ in size and shape compared with red blood cells from living birds and reptiles, she says.

Schweitzer is no stranger to skepticism over the discovery of ephemeral tissues in fossils. In 2005, she and her colleagues reported the first recovery of flexible, soft-tissue blood vessels from the 68-million-year-old fossilized leg bone of a Tyrannosaurus rex. It was a landmark study that sparked debate, including over how it would even be possible to preserve such tissues through deep time, as well as the most surefire way to detect them in the present.

“I am not convinced” that the research team has definitively identified heme compounds, Schweitzer says. “I do applaud them for bringing a plethora of methods to the study. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and that does require state-of-the-art technology.”

No one really knows what a dinosaur’s red blood cell shape would be, let alone how the process of fossilization might distort the original shape of the structures, or allow heme-related molecules to escape their cellular confines over time, Grice says.

And, she says, her team’s interpretation of the evidence doesn’t just rely on the observations of those structures. “[It] rests on the convergence of anatomy, morphology, mineralogy, elemental analysis and molecular chemistry,” she says. “That combination is critical.”

As for whether other fossils might have molecular traces that have been preserved by hausmannite, “we simply don’t know yet,” Grice says. “But this type of preservation may not be quite as rare as we currently think.”

D.M. Martill and D.M. Unwin. Small spheres in fossil bones: Blood corpuscles or diagenetic products? Palaeontology. 1997.

Carolyn Gramling is the earth & climate writer. She has bachelor’s degrees in geology and European history and a Ph.D. in marine geochemistry from MIT and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution.

#6406. The 6 Best Electric Snowblowers Are Plenty Powerful—and Quieter Alternatives to Gas Models

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Two more reasons to go green: Battery-powered outdoor equipment is also easier to operate and store.

If you’re looking for the quickest, least labor-intensive way to dig out after a big snowstorm this winter, a snowblower is it. While it’s only fall, it’s not too early to think about getting a snow blower if you found yourself wanting one during last year’s winter storms but struggled to find a retailer that wasn’t already out of stock. Getting ahead of the game is a good idea.

Electric models are more capable than ever, and in some cases meet or exceed their gas-powered brethren in some respects. Cordless, battery-electric blowers can clear a path up to roughly 2 feet wide through as much as 20 inches of snow. They start with the push of a button, require less maintenance than gas machines, and run relatively quietly. They’re also easier to store than their gas-powered counterparts.

Ahead, we review both two-stage snow blowers and single-stage snow throwers and recommend models from Toro, Ego, Milwaukee, and more.

Our selections for this list are based on our years of testing snow blowers of all varieties. Most of these examples we’ve tested in the last few years, and others are updated versions of models we’ve tested. We are also planning for a substantial update to this guide in the coming weeks with new models.

Tony Carrick, the original author of this article, is a regular PopMech contributor and writes about everything from landscaping to home improvement. He grew up in rural Pennsylvania, where he became well-acquainted with blizzards and the backbreaking labor of digging out after them. His recommendations are based on his personal experience testing snow blowers at home, along with plenty of research to inform the picks. He compared specs for a variety of corded and cordless models, while also plowing through recommendations and feedback from dozens of customer reviews.

Electric snow blowers may not be able to match the power of their gas-powered counterparts, but this self-propelled two-stage model from Ryobi comes close. It sports four rechargeable 40-volt 6-Ah batteries, which Ryobi claims can power the snow blower for up to 45 minutes, and move the same amount of snow as a 252-cc gas-powered two-stage snow blower. It has the power to scoop up a path that’s 24 inches wide and 21 inches deep, then chuck it up to 55 feet away.

We’re also impressed with the cockpit, which allows you to control the speed of the drive wheels and the auger, change the direction of the chute, and toggle the LED headlights without missing a beat. The handlebar even heats up so your hands don’t get numb as you're working.

Our only concern is with the charger. While we like the fact that this Ryobi supports rapid charging, the charger only has two slots, which means you’ll have to go through two rounds of recharging before you’re back to full power.

If you don’t relish the idea of pushing heavy machinery through heavy snow, Snow Joe makes a lightweight single-stage snow blower that’s fairly easy to push around. At less than 38 pounds with batteries installed, the Snow Joe 24V-X2-SB18 is easy to roll out of storage, push down the driveway, and maneuver through turns.

The scraper bar clears snow right down to the pavement, and it can launch snow up to 20 feet away. On top of that, it’s very cheap—one of the most affordable cordless snow blowers we’ve found.

Unsurprisingly, that light weight and low price come with some compromises. The 18-inch-wide chute cuts a narrow path, so you’ll need to take a few extra passes to get the job done right compared to a wider machine. Meanwhile, its two 24-volt batteries offer a modest 40-minute run time.

Combine those two things, and the 24V-X2-SB18 is best reserved for smaller jobs like clearing decks, walkways, and compact driveways. If that’s what you need, though, it makes snow removal cheap and easy.

We like Ego’s battery-powered outdoor equipment because it’s among the best when it comes to power and run time—and this two-stage snow blower is no exception. With its two 56-volt, 7.5-Ah batteries and 24-inch-wide intake, the Power+ SNT2405 can clear an 8-inch layer of snow from an 18-car driveway on a single charge.

We also like the cockpit on this self-propelled machine. You can change speeds while in forward or reverse, adjust the auger speed, and change the chute direction all without having to leave the controls. It also comes equipped with four bright LED headlights, useful in the event your snow clearing efforts take you past sundown.

We also like the fact that Ego uses mostly steel construction with this machine, so you can expect it to hold up for many a winter.

Ego claims its 21-inch Power+ snow blower can throw snow up to 40 feet with a 180-degree, adjustable chute, which is pretty far for a cordless machine. In the wet sawdust test, we were able to throw 24 feet with the heavier, denser material—longer distances are certainly achievable with lighter, drier snow. It took the Power+ 4 minutes 16 seconds to clear the sawdust down to pavement in our area test.

Like most single-stage blowers, the Power+ is not self-propelled, so we needed to push it into the snow. In our dense, heavy sawdust, that took some effort to make forward progress. It’s not a bad thing, though, as it makes it easier to prevent the machine from digging in too deep and bogging down. In very wet or ice-packed snow, we expect you’ll have to put in a similar effort.

The Power+ has a variable-speed auger, so we were able to adjust speed for the conditions and conserve battery when less power was needed. There isn’t too much to worry about in the battery department, since it comes with two 5-Ah batteries, enough to clear 8 inches of snow on a 12-car driveway—that’s six cars long by two cars wide.

The Power+ comes with a dual-port charger, so the two batteries can be charged simultaneously to get you ready for the next round faster. Ego rounds things out with front-mounted LEDs for low-light and dark conditions, plus an easy-folding handle for stowing the unit when not in use.

The 60-volt 26-inch Power Max e26 is one of the models we tested in November 2025, and it’s among the burliest two-stage cordless snow blowers we’ve used. It is built virtually the same as a gas model, except with an electric motor and two batteries. That includes the frame, drive system, auger, and auger housing.

Since it’s built the same, we can confirm it performs the same—so it could easily replace a similar gas model. No caveats here; the Power Max e26 isn’t a compromise in any significant way that we could determine. It comes with two batteries and a (claimed) runtime up to 70 minutes—enough to clear a driveway 30 car spaces long.

Operating the Power Max e26 was a pleasant experience, if you can call snow blowing pleasant. It has effective heated hand grips, and an axle with a differential that allows you to turn quickly, on a dime—no having to muscle it around.

The e26 easily handled our testing with wet sawdust, throwing it far enough to cross an average driveway—even when making a full 26-inch-wide pass. If you’ve questioned whether a cordless snow blower could ever be as good as a gas machine, the e26 answers that affirmatively.

Milwaukee’s M18 single-stage snow blower is the second machine we tested in November 2025, and it also impressed us. It's noticeably heavier than many other similar cordless models, which seems to be due to its metal frame. At 90 pounds, it isn’t heavy, at least in comparison to two-stage machines, but the weight is an advantage, helping prevent the blower from bouncing around or riding up when encountering denser, crusty snow.

We tested this snow blower with wet sawdust, which always presents a little bit of a challenge with single-stage snow blowers, as they have to lift the snow and eject it in one operation. Milwaukee’s M18 blower did this well enough in testing—and if it can throw wet sawdust, it will really throw the snow.

To facilitate ejecting snow, the M18’s chute is wider than that of most other models. This eliminates potential bottlenecks and ultimately clogs, where the snow passes from the blower body into the chute. Milwaukee's single auger is edged with a rubber paddle that both sweeps the pavement clean and pulls the machine forward. It does this well enough that, in some instances, we had to hold it back a little in testing.

The chute has a remote adjustment—you can crank a knob just below the handlebar to change the direction of the chute, allowing you to put snow where it needs to go. However, ejection elevation is manually adjusted at the top of the chute—but this isn't something you typically need to adjust as often.

Milwaukee claims the M18 blower can clear up to 11 parking places, or 500 feet of sidewalk on the two included 12.0-Ah batteries. But with two extra battery ports, you can double the runtime by adding another pair of batteries. We’ll be testing this more as we have snow available.

There are two types of snow blowers for homeowners, based on the number of “stages” in the mechanical process they use to collect and distribute snow.

Single-stage snow blowers have an auger that pulls the snow into a large intake at the front of the snow blower, and propels it out of a chute mounted to the top of the machine. Single-stage blowers, also frequently referred to as “snow throwers,” are small, lightweight and easy to maneuver, making them ideal for clearing light snowfall and smaller driveways and walks.

Dual-stage snow blowers, as the name suggests, have a two-stage process for collecting and expelling snow. Like single-stage models, they have an auger that pulls snow into the intake. The dual-stage snow blower follows up by pushing the snow into an impeller that ejects it out through the chute.

The one-two punch of auger and impeller allows a two-stage snow blower to remove more snow quicker, and throw it a longer distance. That makes them perfect for large driveways. That said, they are larger and heavier than single-stage machines, so they may not be able to maneuver around narrow walking paths as easily.

The width and depth of a snow blower’s intake determine how much snow it can move with each pass, and thus, how long it takes you to get the job done. Most single-stage electric snow blowers have a clearing width of around 20 inches and a clearing depth of around 8 inches. That’s good for carving out walks and medium-sized areas. Some heavy-duty two-stage electric snow blowers can remove a 24-inch-wide and 20-inch-deep swath of snow, which will make quick work of a large driveway.

Throwing distance refers to how far a snow blower can launch snow out of the chute. This gives you a sense of how to plan when and how you’ll dispose of the snow in your path. The average single-stage snow blower typically has a short throwing distance—around 25 feet. Unsurprisingly, a two-stage snow blower can send its snow as far as 50 feet.

Snow blowers typically have a throttle that allows you to change their mechanical speed, which will adjust how far it throws your snow. There are also controls that allow you to rotate the chute to change the direction of the flow of snow. If you can map out your snow-blowing route, check and make sure your snow blower throws the snow far enough to keep it out of your way until it melts.

Most electric snow blowers receive power from multiple large rechargeable batteries, which allow them to produce nearly as much power as a gas snow blower. No battery supplies uninterrupted power for as long as a tank of gas, though: On average, you should expect a battery-powered snow blower to run for about 30 to 45 minutes on a single charge. You can extend that time if you have multiple batteries, but the low run time still caps how much ground they can cover.

Though we largely consider them to be obsolete, some manufacturers also still produce corded electric snow blowers, which plug into a standard electrical outlet. They’re often cheaper than battery-powered models and run as long as you need them to. However, having a power cord substantially reduces their range: You will likely need to purchase an extension cord to extend its reach slightly beyond the length of the area you need to clear. No matter how much slack you have, though, the cable makes the whole process a little more awkward.

“Cordless snow blowers are easier, better, and safer to use,” says Popular Mechanics Test Editor Brad Ford. “Corded is old, out-of-date tech in most cases.”

They’re also limited to smaller, 15-amp motors that run on the power an outlet can provide. That usually translates to narrower clearing widths, shallower clearing depths, and shorter throw distances. Unless you have a very tight budget, we highly recommend going with a battery-powered electric snow blower rather than a corded one.

The most important thing you can do to keep your electric snow blower running season after season is to simply make sure that you store your charger and batteries indoors when you aren’t charging or using them. Lithium cells aren't able to hold the same amount of charge when the temperature drops below freezing. By storing and charging those batteries indoors, you’ll get the most run time out of them.

If you use a corded snow blower, you shouldn’t plug it into any old extension cord. These machines draw a lot of power, and not every cord can handle it. Using the wrong one can create a fire hazard or damage your snow blower. Make sure to check your snow blower’s specs before buying an extension cord to pair with it, so you can be sure it can handle its amperage.

Most corded electric snow blowers have a 12-amp rating, in which case you’ll want a 12-gauge extension cord that can provide at least 12 amps of power. You’ll also want to make sure it’s long enough for you to reach the far end of whatever walkway or road you plan to clear, preferably with some slack to spare for maneuverability. We recommend starting with 100 feet and scaling up based on your property.

Regardless, it would be wise to buy an extension cord to match the specs you need for your snow blower, rather than using one that you happen to have lying around.

With advancements in battery technology, there are now powerful two-stage cordless snow blowers capable of clearing deeper, heavier snow.

That said, the most powerful electric snow blowers still don’t match the snow-moving capabilities of the largest gas-powered snow blowers on the market. The most powerful electric snow blowers work best at maximum depths of about a foot, while some gas-powered models can clear snow up to 2 feet deep.

#6405. Can more snow save Antarctica’s ice? A new study weighs the odds

Antarctica is likely to lose ice through 2100 even with sharp emissions cuts, as extra snowfall struggles to offset losses driven by warmer seas.

Predicting how much ice Antarctica will lose means weighing two competing effects. Warmer air can bring more snow, adding ice to the continent, while warmer seawater speeds ice loss along its edges.

A new study suggests Antarctica is very likely to lose ice overall by 2100, even if emissions fall sharply.

Extra snowfall is very unlikely to make up for the ice that the ocean removes, and the researchers found that very high emissions would probably lead to greater losses.

The author leading the work is Yucheng Lin, an assistant professor at City University of Hong Kong, who worked with colleagues in Australia, New Zealand, the United States and the United Kingdom.

Their study used a machine-learning program to examine existing computer simulations of the Antarctic Ice Sheet and check them against the satellite record.

The Antarctic Ice Sheet contains enough ice to raise global sea level by about 190 feet (57.9 meters), and its losses accounted for roughly 10% of global sea-level rise between 2006 and 2018.

How much emissions will alter the losses during this century has been a source of disagreement, something the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change drew attention to in its 2021 assessment.

One large international comparison included some simulations in which Antarctica lowered sea level by more than 2.8 inches (seven centimeters) by 2100 and others in which it raised sea level by more than 15.7 inches (40 centimeters).

All of these simulations assumed very high emissions.

Making these models involves deciding how easily ice slides over the bedrock beneath it and how quickly seawater melts floating ice from below. It also requires choosing a climate model to provide the warming projections.

Different research groups make different choices about each of these things.

Counting each model equally also gives more influence to choices that appear in more models, Lin’s team wrote, and those common choices may not be the ones that best fit observations.

Their approach was to compare the choices with Antarctica’s recent behavior.

The team used 340 simulations produced by 16 research groups. They recorded the modeling choices behind each simulation, then trained a machine-learning program to predict how those choices affected the results.

Running a full ice-sheet simulation takes a lot of computing power, but the trained program could turn out about 30,000 projections a second on a laptop, so the team could try 100,000 combinations.

To judge them, the researchers used the GRACE satellite record, which showed an average loss of about 174 billion tons (158 billion metric tons) of ice a year from 2002 to 2021.

They gave greater importance to combinations that produced losses close to what the satellites measured, reducing the range of projected sea-level rise by 30% to 42% depending on the emissions scenario.

The middle estimate moved up by 15% to 25% as a result.

With the satellite record helping to decide how much importance each combination received, the estimated chance of Antarctica losing ice overall by 2100 went from 80% to 92% in the lowest-emissions case.

For very high emissions, the researchers put the chance of an overall loss at no less than 95%.

The middle estimate for Antarctica’s contribution to sea-level rise by 2100 was 1.3 inches (3.4 centimeters) under the lowest emissions and 2.4 inches (6.1 centimeters) under very high emissions.

There was an 89% chance of very high emissions producing more sea-level rise from Antarctica than the lowest-emissions scenario, the team calculated.

“We have to transform our energy system to cut every emission we can, and we must do it quickly,” Lin said.

One set of simulations showed how much the extra snow could matter, with a net gain of ice in Antarctica even though the climate model they used produced the most warming this century out of the five models in the study.

More snowfall, together with only modest warming of the surrounding ocean, accounted for the gain. But it did not last in simulations that continued beyond 2100, when losses to the ocean overtook the added snow.

For people planning infrastructure that has to last a long time, including nuclear power stations, the team also examined the outcomes with the most sea-level rise.

These were the top 1% under very high emissions, and all still matched the satellite record.

In this selected group the middle estimate for Antarctica’s contribution by 2100 was 6.2 inches (15.7 centimeters), with one in 20 outcomes exceeding 10 inches (25.4 centimeters).

The sea was the starting point in these simulations, with strong warming melting the floating ice shelves quickly from below.

Ice on land then moved into the sea faster as the shelves thinned or collapsed and lost their ability to hold it back, particularly where the ice could slide easily over bedrock.

For these highest losses the team was looking at the very high emissions case, which the authors described as increasingly implausible given current climate policies.

Researchers cannot use this program to learn what happens in a process that the original simulations never included.

Among the processes that most simulations leave out are flows of water beneath the ice sheet and a still-debated way in which ice shelves might rapidly collapse, both of which could speed up ice loss, the authors wrote.

The satellite record covers only about 20 years, offering limited insight into processes that have caused little ice loss so far but could become important later.

The researchers stopped their projections at 2100 because the available simulations for the following century are too few to capture the sharper changes that begin then.

Of all the choices researchers make when building these models, the authors identified three that need stronger evidence.

These are how ice slides over bedrock, how ice shelves melt and which climate model is used.

Lin pointed out that researchers have limited resources, so they need to work out which details of an ice model matter most.

The authors suggested collecting new field observations and studying records of past climates to help narrow these choices.

Future simulations that include the missing processes could also provide new data to train the program.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Geoscience.

#6404. Why some city blocks stay cooler may come down to their neighbors

A study of 101 cities links larger clusters of buildings with similar uses to cooler surfaces, revealing an overlooked factor in urban heat.

Cities run hotter than the countryside around them, and the usual suspects are pavement, missing trees and the heat given off by buildings and their air conditioners.

Another factor may be how buildings are grouped by use.

Across 101 cities, larger clusters of homes, factories or other buildings serving the same purpose were associated with cooler ground surfaces during both day and night.

Researchers at Sun Yat-sen University in Guangzhou and Ghent University in Belgium studied 101 cities, from New York and London to Doha, Shanghai, and Libreville.

Locations 330 feet (100 meters) farther inside a same-use cluster had daytime surface temperatures about 0.28°F (0.156°C) lower, roughly 4.5% of a typical urban heat island.

At night, the figure was 0.15°F (0.085°C).

The effect is modest per block, and it is an association rather than a proven cause. But it held after the team accounted for building height, tree cover, pavement, wind and a dozen other factors.

The authors argue it gives planners a lever they haven’t been using.

First author Xucai Zhang, who is also at Imperial College London, and colleagues started with building footprints and heights from OpenStreetMap, Microsoft, Google and two research datasets.

To each building they added the businesses and services mapped at that address.

A computer model then sorted every building into one of seven types: residential, commercial, industrial, medical, education, administration and other public services. It got the type right about 87% of the time.

From there, the team drew the city at a resolution of 33 feet (10 meters) and merged touching cells of the same type into clusters.

Their measure, which they call the urban homogeneous scale, is simply how far a spot is from the edge of its cluster.

A house deep inside a large housing estate scores high. A shop wedged between a hospital and a warehouse scores low.

Surface temperatures came from a NASA satellite for the summer of 2023, or the 2023-24 summer south of the equator.

The team measured each block’s heat island by comparing its surface temperature with the median surface temperature of the surrounding countryside.

Each block measured 1,640 feet (500 meters) across. That gave 233,844 blocks to compare.

On every continent, residential areas formed the largest same-use clusters, with industrial zones second.

Commercial, medical, education and government buildings sat in smaller, more broken-up patches.

Libreville in Gabon stood out for its wide stretches of informal housing, and Shanghai for its industrial belts. South American cities had the smallest clusters of all.

The measure is not density or greenery under another name.

Across the 101 cities, cluster size showed no consistent relationship with pavement, population density, road density, building density or tree cover.

Among the factors the team tested, wind did the most to lower daytime surface heat, and the share of paved ground did the most to raise it.

Cluster size ranked seventh by day and fourth by night, behind pavement, surface brightness and tree cover.

The relationship between cluster size and surface temperature was not linear.

Below about 360 feet (110 meters) from a cluster edge, the surface temperature barely changed. Past that, it fell steeply, and the decline kept going out to about 870 feet (265 meters).

At night, the benefit arrived at smaller cluster sizes and flattened sooner.

Inland cities gained slightly more by day than coastal ones, and coastal cities gained about twice as much at night.

The authors tie that to the sea breeze, which mixes the air by day and fades after dark. Humid cities also gained more than dry ones, which matters because the body struggles most to cool itself in humid heat.

Middle-income cities saw the biggest daytime benefit: surface temperatures were about 0.30°F (0.168°C) lower for every additional 330 feet (100 meters) from a cluster’s edge toward its interior.

At night the benefit rose with income, from 0.09°F (0.051°C) in low-income regions to 0.19°F (0.107°C) in high-income ones.

In low-income cities, bigger and bulkier buildings weakened the cooling more than anywhere else.

The authors point to the larger share of industrial land there, where clustering concentrates waste heat.

Low-income cities also have shorter buildings, less building volume and more tree cover, which may leave less room for additional cooling from clustering.

Tree cover worked in the opposite direction. In low- and middle-income regions, more trees strengthened the daytime cooling of large clusters, with the biggest gain in low-income cities.

The authors wrote that development adding building density in low-income regions should be tied to compensating tree planting.

The temperatures here are those of roofs, roads and ground as seen from orbit, not the air a person breathes at street level.

The researchers noted that the daytime pattern in particular should not be extended to air temperature without new measurements.

The data also cover one summer, and the study can show that bigger clusters and cooler surfaces go together, not that one causes the other.

The authors offer a few reasons why they might go together.

Buildings of the same type may share heights and shapes that allow wind to move through more smoothly.

Similar operating schedules could also create quieter periods with less waste heat, while mixed-use blocks may release heat over more hours of the day.

Satellite data cannot reveal whether the air above large housing clusters is also cooler. Answering that question will require direct measurements of air temperature.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

In this excerpt from "This is Life: A Journey from Inside Your Body to Beyond Earth," author and physicist Christophe Galfard explores the way 19th century scientists were starting to use thermodynamics to understand just how old Earth is.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the 1950s, American geochemist Clair Patterson presented findings that showed Earth is around 4.55 billion years old. His evidence was based on lead isotopic analysis that he used to calculate the age of the Canyon Diablo meteorite, which was discovered in Arizona in 1891. That result is now widely accepted as the age of our planet, but the buildup to this discovery was a long time coming.

Earth's true age was a subject of much debate among scientists in the 19th century. And rather than geologists taking the helm, it was physicists who realized that this giant ball of rock we live on must be far older than the thousands of years that had been assumed in prior centuries. Their main reasoning was heat.

In this excerpt from "This Is Life: A Journey from Inside Your Body to Beyond Earth" (University of Chicago Press/Picador, 2026), author and physicist Christophe Galfard looks at the progression among scientists who were coming to realize that thermodynamics was an essential piece of this long-standing puzzle.

Some two and a half centuries ago, the foremost experts on scientific matters knew a thing or two about heat. They knew, for instance, how heat could be transferred from one place to another. A new science was about to emerge out of this knowledge, a science called thermodynamics, which means "movements of heat" in Greek.

Thermodynamics isn't a force. It is more like a guidebook, a set of rules that apply to large

numbers of particles when they come together. It gives us, humans, a way to understand how particles behave when there is a lot of them without needing to refer to each one of them individually. It shows us how properties that don't exist on their own arise when many particles are together. It deals with these things we call emergent phenomena, such as heat and pressure, and which [Philip] Anderson's "More Is Different" tried to make sense of.

Understanding the dynamics of heat meant a lot to nineteenth-century scientists — so much so that many saw in it the roots of a philosophy so universal and powerful that they thought it should guide us through all our lives. Some even went as far as believing that heat was the source of eternal life. A prominent scientist became so convinced that this was the case that he locked himself up in his house and overheated it, thus shielding himself from all mortal diseases (ageing and death included). The experience was a true torture for the occasional guests who came to visit him, not to mention his wife, who had to endure it day and night.

The scientist held fast to his belief, though, piling on layer after layer of clothing to keep himself ever warmer. Unfortunately, the bulk made it difficult to move, and he eventually missed a step on his own staircase and died from the fall.

As a scientific discipline, thermodynamics was born with a book written in 1824 by a 27-year-old French physicist named Nicolas Léonard Sadi Carnot, who, as he explained how heat could produce work, told everyone how the steam engine worked.

Lord Kelvin giving a lecture at Glasgow University in 1899.

With Carnot's vision, the way hot objects cool down began to be understood, raising hopes that the resolution of one particular problem might be imminent: the determination of the Earth's age. Were we to somehow guess how hot our planet was at birth, thermodynamics could then be used to tell us how much time had gone by for it to have cooled to its present temperature. Many scientists tried it, keen to be the first one to nail the true age of our world.

Considering our planet in all its complexity to be far too difficult, simplifications were in order, and British physicist William Thomson shot first by picturing our world as a ball. A very simple, rock-solid ball made of pretty much the same stuff throughout, from surface to core. No ocean, no mountain, just a smooth ball the size of the Earth. He then calculated how long it would take it to cool down from being red hot to its present temperature, and declared that the Earth was something between 40 and 400 million years old.

Refining his calculations, he then announced that the world was 100 million years old, before settling for 40 million again.

Thomson's result does not correspond to the true age of the Earth, but it was a start. It was the result of a model, an attempt at figuring out something about our world using still-to-be-refined laws, and mathematical sense. What was more problematic was that no one dared question his results. Even as it shifted from one paper to another, the age of the Earth given by Thomson was always greeted as the right one. A reason for this is that at the end of the nineteenth century Thomson had become Lord Kelvin.

The same Kelvin after whom the Kelvin unit of absolute temperature is named. A scientific superstar who had the power to undo, in a snap of fingers, the career of anyone who disagreed with him.

Lord Kelvin was a physicist, not a geologist, so geologists could have questioned his work, but they didn't. In fact, they weren't bothered. Many of them back then believed that being a geologist was all about intuition and proper English, a language they deemed far more efficient than mathematical gibberish.

That being said, and however wrong the results, Kelvin's calculations were beautiful, giving whoever wanted to think about the problem of the age of the Earth a way forward, which is exactly what one of his former students, Northern Irishman John Perry, did. He thought that Kelvin had overlooked something. As a man of science talking to his former mentor (and job provider), Perry explained his vision to Kelvin but was ignored.

John Perry, a student of Kelvin's, who realized Earth was billions of years old — and that its mantle was a liquid, not a solid.

Still, he published his thoughts in Nature. But again, the article was ignored. Not just by Kelvin, but by the scientific community at large, including geologists.

It would have saved us all quite a bit of time had this not been the case, because Perry not only found a much more correct way to picture the Earth and estimate its age than Kelvin had, but he also found the source of the power that makes our planet's continents drift.

In his model, Perry didn't picture the Earth to be uniformly the same from surface to core as Kelvin had. Instead, he modelled the Earth's interior as being divided into three regions: a metallic core at its centre, a solid crust at its surface, and a mantle that lay in between the two. Rather unexpectedly, Perry didn't envision the mantle as everyone else would have; he believed that it didn't behave like the solid rock it was, but as a liquid.

No wonder his former master didn't take him seriously. However, he pictured the mantle behaving like a liquid only when considered over long periods of time. Sandwiched between a hot core and a colder crust that very much looked like a lid, he believed the mantle had no choice but to behave just like water does in a heated pan, with the hottest parts at the bottom rising and cooling before diving back down and rising up again, in repeated loops, albeit in extremely slow motion. This type of movement is called convection, and it happens in solids, too.

If he was right, there would be two immediate consequences. The first one was that the time it would take for our planet's surface to cool down from red hot to its current temperature could now be far longer than Kelvin had estimated. The lid and the convection patterns prevented our planet from quickly radiating away all its energy into space, so we were now inhabiting an Earth that could be as old as 2 or 3 billion years. Maybe even more. Such timescales were unheard of in the scientific community. Back then, no one knew that the universe itself was 13.8 billion years old. They knew next to nothing.

The second consequence of Perry's model was that the mantle's circular movements underneath the crust could drag the crust itself via friction. The solid surface of our world would then move, and split into pieces that would drift, and collide, and plunge underneath — or slide above — one another. Where they collided, mountain ranges would rise, like the Alps, the Himalayas, the Rockies . . . Where they split apart, rifts would appear, probably in the middle of oceans, along ridges . . . just like [Marie] Tharp had found.

Nowadays, these broken pieces of our planet's surface have all been mapped. They are our world's plates and their movements through time are called plate tectonics. Today, most of us have heard about plate tectonics. Back then, however, no one had, and if very few people remember Perry today, it is because another scientific breakthrough made the estimation of the age of the Earth much easier and precise, showing us that our world isn't 2 or 3 billion years old, as Perry suggested, but precisely 4.567 billion, give or take a few million.

#6402. Ammonia pollution from farms reaches beyond the air we breathe

A new review examines ammonia pollution, its health risks, and the potential for bacteria to help remove excess ammonia.

Farming is the biggest source of ammonia pollution, mainly from animal waste and fertilizers.

Once released, ammonia mixes with other pollutants in the air, creating tiny particles that can harm our health. It can also seep into water sources and affect drinking water.

Researchers from four Chinese universities reviewed evidence on ammonia pollution, ammonia buildup inside the body, and bacteria that might help remove it.

By the authors’ estimate, agriculture is responsible for 80% to 90% of the ammonia released worldwide by human activity.

That share takes in livestock farming, fertilizer use and aquaculture, the farming of fish and shellfish.

Ammonia is given off by manure and urine as they decompose, the authors wrote, so a portion is lost wherever animal waste is stored and handled.

They identified fertilizer applied to crops as the other major source.

China, India, the United States and Europe were named as the main hotspots for these emissions. Chemical plants, fertilizer factories, drug makers and oil refineries contribute to the total as well.

In cities, the researchers attributed ammonia to sewage and garbage that are poorly managed.

They added that some diesel vehicles also emit the gas from their exhaust systems, especially where low-quality urea is used in them.

Those emissions feed air pollution well beyond the fields themselves.

People who live or work near a farm or factory may inhale ammonia directly.

The authors described the gas as an irritant to the eyes and airways, and wrote that long exposure can damage the tissue lining the nose and airways.

They cited animal experiments in which the bacteria living in the nose and gut changed after exposure to ammonia.

What those changes might mean for human health has not been established, they wrote.

The review also describes how ammonia reacts with sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, pollutants released when coal and fuel are burned.

That reaction yields ammonium salts, which are a component of the fine airborne particles known as PM2.5.

Such particles are no more than 2.5 micrometers across, roughly one-thirtieth the width of a human hair, and can reach deep into the lungs.

Fine-particle pollution has been found to aggravate asthma, chronic bronchitis and the lung disease known as COPD, and to raise rates of heart disease and death.

One analysis from 2015, cited by the authors, estimated that outdoor fine particles are responsible for more than 5% of premature deaths worldwide.

Nitrate, which is what soil microbes turn ammonium into, doesn’t stay put. The authors described it being carried down into groundwater by rain and irrigation, or washed off the land into streams and lakes.

The review also describes how plants take nitrate up from the soil while they are growing, and how lettuce and other leafy vegetables hold it in their leaves.

As a result, the authors wrote, people may be taking in nitrate with their food as well as with their drinking water.

A portion of the nitrate a person swallows is turned into nitrite in the body.

Nitrite changes hemoglobin, the protein red blood cells use to carry oxygen, so that the protein can no longer carry it.

Young infants are the ones most at risk, and severe cases of what is known as blue baby syndrome can prove fatal.

The danger to babies is one reason the World Health Organization set limits for nitrate in drinking water.

In the stomach, according to the authors, nitrate and nitrite can react with compounds from food to produce cancer-causing substances.

They linked long-term intake of the two to higher rates of stomach, esophageal and other digestive cancers.

Nitrate that is washed into rivers and lakes can fuel large blooms of algae and related organisms.

Some of those blooms give off toxins that contaminate the water or build up in fish and shellfish.

The toxins can then be swallowed in drinking water or food, and the authors wrote that some can damage the liver.

The nutrients help the bloom to grow, but the injury is caused by the toxin.

Environmental exposure is only part of the picture. The body also produces ammonia when it breaks down protein, and gut microbes generate some while processing food.

Normally the liver converts most of it into urea, which then leaves the body in urine.

The authors wrote that gut bacteria can use ammonia as they grow, or help supply substances the liver needs in order to process it. Several species with those abilities are described in the review.

Among them is Lactobacillus plantarum, which can incorporate ammonia into amino acids, the building blocks of proteins.

Experiments cited by the authors suggest it may help reduce ammonia in the brain.

That ability has yet to be shown safe in people with high ammonia levels, they added. A useful result in an experiment doesn’t amount to a treatment that doctors could offer.

A badly damaged liver may fail to remove enough ammonia from the blood.

Rising levels can then affect the brain, the authors wrote, and the result is confusion and problems with balance or movement.

The gut can add to the trouble in cirrhosis, the scarring caused by years of liver damage. They cited evidence that an enzyme which produces ammonia in the intestine becomes more active.

Studies in mice found that a long period of high blood ammonia changed the gut’s bacterial community as well.

Some bacterial groups became more common, according to the authors, and others declined, including beneficial ones.

Researchers are now trying to find out whether changing those bacteria might help patients.

Most of that research concerns ammonia made inside the body, the authors added, which leaves open questions about exposure through polluted air, water and food.

Lactulose and the antibiotic rifaximin are the drugs used to manage ammonia-related problems in people with liver disease.

Lactulose encourages a helpful species in the gut, the authors wrote, while rifaximin cuts back several harmful groups.

Both medicines can have side effects. Too much lactulose may result in dehydration and other complications, they wrote, and some patients develop severe diarrhea while taking rifaximin.

Dialysis may be used in some cases to take ammonia out of the blood.

For patients with severe liver disease, a transplant treats the underlying liver failure.

Sodium benzoate is used as a food preservative and in some ammonia-lowering treatments.

One experiment cited by the authors found little change in the gut microbiome even at ten times the accepted daily intake.

The effects of such drugs on gut bacteria have rarely been studied, they wrote.

Some bacteria studied in wastewater can convert ammonium directly into nitrogen gas, without producing nitrate or nitrite along the way.

One example given in the review is Zobellella taiwanensis, which uses acetone during the process.

Getting such bacteria to work in a person’s gut would present several problems, among them whether they could survive there at all.

The authors also wrote that some ammonia-processing bacteria take days or weeks to grow.

Four approaches are set out in the review. The first two are to start from a gut-adapted species instead of a laboratory strain, and to use dead bacteria that still carry working enzymes.

The third is to hold cells or enzymes in place so that they remove ammonia, in the gut or outside the body. The fourth is to edit the wider gut community instead of one strain at a time.

It has still to be established whether any of these proposed treatments safely lower ammonia in people, and which patients might benefit.

The review was published in the journal The Innovation Reviews.

#6401. A high-fiber diet may clear away plastic in the gut

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Mice that ate lots of fiber had far less particles accumulate in the body

A diet that includes high-fiber foods, like these vegetables, might come with a surprise benefit. Fiber could help carry nanoplastics out of the body, suggests a new study in mice.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Here’s a new reason to eat your beans and greens.

A high-fiber diet may help sweep plastic particles from the gut, researchers report October 15 in Nature Communications. In mice that ingested plastic, eating loads of fiber daily kept the particles from piling up in the intestines. The finding hints at fiber’s power to protect the body from environmental garbage, says Eddy Y. Zeng, an environmental scientist at South China University of Technology in Guangzhou.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have long known that fiber can improve our health, in part by lowering cholesterol, keeping blood sugar levels in check and easing food through the gut. But now, Zeng says, his team’s results suggest an additional benefit.

We live in a world littered with plastic, much of it too small to see. These micro and nanoplastics, shed by disposable water bottles, fast food containers and other worldly junk, can make their way into our bodies. It’s not completely clear what such shards do to our health, but we have some hints. Scientists have linked plastic particles in people’s arteries to increased risk of heart attack and stroke. And mice that ingest tiny bits of plastic can show signs of organ injury.

Zeng’s team thought dietary fiber might provide some defense. Fiber forms a complex network of polymers that could trap ingested plastics like flies in a spider web, he says.

The researchers put mice on low-, medium-, or high-fiber diets, then fed them plastic particles. Over the next 24 hours, the medium- and high-fiber groups of mice cleared more particles from their bodies than their low-fiber counterparts, the team discovered. That’s important, Zeng says, because these particles can do damage. After a week of daily plastic feedings, his team saw gut tissue damage — but only in the low-fiber group. Experiments in test tubes suggest that fiber physically wraps around and sticks to plastic particles.

It’s too soon to say if dietary fiber does the same in humans. Zeng’s study was performed in mice and not tethered to realistic fiber numbers. Though mice in the high-fiber group ate far more fiber than what what’s recommended for people, he thinks the findings are worth pursuing in follow-up studies.

And even if fiber doesn’t end up purging plastic from people’s guts, Zeng says, it probably wouldn’t hurt for us to add a little more to our diets.

#6400. Scotland’s waterlogged landscape hides thousands of years of carbon

A satellite image of Scotland’s Flow Country reveals a waterlogged landscape where peat bogs have stored carbon for thousands of years.

Today’s Image of the Day from NASA Earth Observatory features the Flow Country, a peatland landscape in the Scottish Highlands.

Landsat 8’s Operational Land Imager captured this view on March 4, 2024, recording a spring scene in one of Europe’s most important blanket bog regions.

Dark brown ground stretches between scattered lakes in northern Scotland, broken by green fields and sharply outlined blocks of trees.

From above, the contrast between bogs, farmland, and tree plantations becomes clear.

What the image cannot show is the deep store of ancient plant material beneath the bogs, where carbon has been accumulating for thousands of years.

The brown expanses mark boggy ground dotted with lakes.

Around Thurso, on the right side of the image, lighter green farmland contrasts with the darker green shapes of conifer plantations closer to the center.

Those geometric tree plantations stand out against the irregular outlines of water and peatland.

Together, the patterns show how farming and forestry occupy parts of a region whose distinctive character comes from persistent wetness.

At ground level, the bog’s surface has a texture that the satellite view cannot fully resolve.

Mossy hummocks rise above hollows, while pools interrupt the vegetation. Grasses and heathers grow across this uneven, largely treeless terrain.

“Blanket bog” describes how peat spreads over the landscape, covering slopes and hollows rather than remaining confined to a single basin.

Its formation requires conditions that keep the ground wet for long periods.

Northern Scotland has a useful combination of climate and terrain for building bogs.

Rain arrives frequently from the Atlantic, while rocks, soils, and landforms slow its escape.

Cool conditions also limit water loss through evaporation and plants.

Under these circumstances, water collects faster than the landscape can shed it. Bog plants grow, die, and leave their remains in saturated ground.

Usually, microbes break down dead vegetation, returning much of its carbon to the atmosphere.

Waterlogged soils restrict oxygen, slowing that process. Some plant material remains only partly decomposed and gradually becomes peat.

The growing peat then helps retain more water, sustaining conditions in which additional bog plants can flourish.

Over time, this relationship between vegetation and water builds a thick organic layer beneath the living surface.

Sphagnum mosses play a central role in that process. Their contribution is easy to overlook beside a forest’s towering trees, yet these small plants help create an ecosystem capable of preserving carbon far beyond a single growing season.

Parts of the Flow Country have been forming peat for around 9,000 years.

In places, deposits exceed eight meters in thickness, preserving the accumulated remains of countless generations of plants.

That depth also holds evidence of environmental change.

Pollen and plant fossils within the peat record earlier vegetation, offering researchers a way to investigate how the landscape developed and how people influenced it.

In 2024, the Flow Country joined UNESCO’s World Heritage List.

The designated property covers approximately 1,870 square kilometers across seven component areas, recognizing an exceptional example of an actively accumulating blanket bog.

Its value extends beyond what lies underground. The mixture of pools, ridges, wet hollows, and vegetation supports distinctive wildlife communities, including breeding birds.

More than 30 species of sphagnum moss occur here, adding variety to ground that can appear uniform from a distance.

The Flow Country illustrates a much larger global pattern.

Peatlands occupy only about 3% of Earth’s land surface, yet the United Nations Environment Programme reports that they store roughly twice as much carbon as all the world’s forests.

That comparison concerns carbon already stored, rather than the amount absorbed each year.

Much of a peatland’s importance comes from protecting material that accumulated long before modern climate records began.

Drainage can disrupt that protection. As peat dries and oxygen enters, decomposition accelerates, allowing stored carbon to escape as carbon dioxide. Burning can also release carbon accumulated over centuries.

UNESCO identifies historical drainage and woodland creation among the pressures that have affected parts of the Flow Country.

Restoration is therefore part of protecting the landscape’s future. Seen from orbit, the bogs offer few obvious clues to their age or depth.

The brown surface is simply the visible top of a much older system, still growing wherever water allows plant remains to accumulate.

Image Credit: Michala Garrison, NASA Earth Observatory, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey.
