#6399. Scientists Solved the Mystery of Why Some People Shiver in the Cold While Others Wear Shorts

Experiments in mice suggest that testosterone and a molecular cold sensor shape who reaches for the parka.

Shuffling outside in three layers and a parka to pick up mail or take out the trash on a winter afternoon, you notice your neighbor is running the same errand in a sweatshirt and shorts. Just the sight of this gives you the chills, as if you weren’t shivering already. Could there be some freakish biological reason that, unlike your neighbor, you can hardly even imagine yourself in something that isn’t heavyweight and lined with fleece when the sky is threatening snow?

Like with plenty of other quirks of our daily lived experiences, the answer to that question is yes.

Your tolerance of the heat or the cold may actually be determined at a molecular level. Researchers Peter McNaughton and Bruno Vilar of Wolfson Sensory, Pain and Regeneration Centre at King’s College London exposed mice to different temperatures and saw that female mice preferred higher temperatures than males. The mice were given a choice of two heated metal plates, and the females scurried to the warmer plate at 100.4°F (38°C) while males would crawl towards the cooler control plate kept at 91.4°F (33°C). It was only when the researchers began to alter certain genetic mechanisms that the mice changed their preferences.

“Human females have a lower surface temperature and a higher central temperature than males and prefer a higher ambient temperature,” McNaughton and Vilar said in a study recently published in The Journal of Physiology. “Although the comfort temperature varies significantly among species, a sex difference in thermal preference is consistent in most bird species and in mammals such as mice.”

The answer lies in ion channels, tiny pores in cell membranes that let electrically charged particles called ions flow in and out. Two of them, TRPM2 and TRPM8, work as temperature sensors. Among other functions, TRPM2 regulates adaptations related to heat, while TRPM8 is activated by cold. Mice were allowed to feel out the heated plates for half an hour and usually showed a final preference halfway through the time they were given. There was no significant difference between male and female mice when they had to choose between the control plate and one at a cooler temperature of either 82.4°F (28°C) or 73.4°F (23°C). Both the male and female mice preferred the control plate to anything cooler. But then things began to get heated.

Distinct preferences began to appear when the mice had the opportunity to decide between the control plate and a warmer alternative. Most females began shifting over to the warm plate and spent more time there, while males, whose preferred ambient temperature is known to be about the same as that of the control plate, apparently found that more tolerable. Upping the temperature of one plate to 109.4°F (43°C) had the same effect. The biological females preferred an average temperature of 96.8°F (36°C) while males’ average preferred temp was 89.42°F (31.9°C). Core body temperature doesn’t explain the difference. Male and female mice have the same core temperature, but the females still went looking for more heat.

Genetic experiments helped show what drives the difference. When researchers deleted TRPM2 in male mice, the males suddenly moved toward the warmer plate, just as the females did. Deleting TRPM2 in females barely changed anything. TRPM8 played a much more significant role. When it was blocked with an injection or deleted entirely, both female and male mice stopped avoiding the cold and readily moved onto the cooler plate. This shows that TRPM8 is essential for sensing cold. A third channel, TRPV1, turned out to matter only for detecting intense heat.

Hormones explain part of the difference, and testosterone seems to be the main one. Lowering testosterone in male mice shifted them toward the females’ preference for warmth, and giving females extra testosterone made them more averse to heat. Estradiol and progesterone, the main female sex hormones, had no effect. Even so, testosterone didn’t account for the whole gap between the sexes.

“The simplest explanation of these observations is that TRPM2 and TRPM8 are expressed in different peripheral thermally sensitive nerve terminals,” the researchers said, “where they drive the generation of action potentials that convey thermal sensation to the [central nervous system].”

#6398. Astronomers trace a black hole’s powerful jet to a surprising source

A fast-feeding black hole in the galaxy 3C 120 launches its jet from a hot gas cloud where its disk ends, a billion miles from the center.

Some of the fastest-feeding black holes in the universe launch jets of plasma at nearly the speed of light.

Those jets come from the region around the black hole, and standard models struggle to explain how they form when so much gas is pouring in.

Now astronomers have looked closely at one of them, and the disk of gas feeding it stops about a billion miles (1.6 billion kilometers) short of the black hole.

Inside that gap, the gas appears to form a hot, swollen cloud. The measurements suggest the jet originates within this hot region, matching the arrangement theory predicts for launching a jet.

Hirofumi Noda of Tohoku University and Kazuhiro Hada of Nagoya City University in Japan led the work with colleagues across East Asia.

The result rests on one galaxy observed over a few weeks in 2025, so whether every fast-feeding black hole with a jet works this way is still open.

“By looking at the same black hole with state-of-the-art X-ray and radio telescopes, we were able to see both the hot plasma surrounding the black hole and the jet emerging from it,” Noda said.

“This allows us to directly connect the extreme environment near the black hole with the formation of the jet.”

The leading explanation for a black hole jet is that magnetic fields threaded through the black hole tap its spin.

Gas near the black hole has to hold those fields in place, and only a hot, thick flow of gas can hold enough of them.

A black hole that feeds slowly, like the one in the galaxy M87, has that kind of flow and fires a famous jet.

Fast feeding is a different case, because in standard theory it builds a cold, thin disk that reaches almost to the black hole.

Computer models find such a disk can’t carry strong magnetic fields inward or squeeze a jet into a narrow beam.

The galaxy 3C 120, in the constellation Taurus, breaks that rule. Its black hole has the mass of about 63 million suns.

Its surroundings shine at roughly 10% to 20% of the brightest a black hole that size can get. It fires a powerful jet anyway.

The team pointed the Japanese X-ray satellite XRISM at 3C 120 for about 55 hours in March 2025.

XRISM measures the energy of each X-ray far more precisely than earlier satellites, and the team used it to read the X-rays given off by iron atoms in the disk.

Near a black hole, that iron signal gets smeared out. Motion in the disk shifts it both ways, and the black hole’s gravity drags the whole signal to lower energies.

How badly the signal is smeared tells astronomers how close the disk’s inner edge comes to the black hole.

Five weeks later, 18 radio dishes around the world observed the same galaxy for 20 hours as the Global Millimeter VLBI Array.

Linked across more than 5,900 miles (9,500 kilometers), they resolved details about 50 millionths of an arcsecond across.

The Very Long Baseline Array and the East Asian VLBI Network traced the jet farther out.

The iron signal showed the thin disk ending at about 17 times the black hole’s gravitational radius, give or take six.

For a black hole of 63 million suns, that is roughly a billion miles (1.6 billion kilometers) from the center, farther than Saturn orbits from the Sun.

Inside that edge, the gas has changed into a thick, hot flow that reaches hundreds of millions of degrees.

Earlier X-ray instruments had hinted at a gap like this but couldn’t pin it down.

The jet narrows as it approaches the black hole.

When the team traced that narrowing all the way in, the beam was no wider than about 7 gravitational radii at its base.

That places the inferred jet origin inside the hot zone, rather than in the cold disk.

The X-ray data gave one more number: the outer disk is tilted about 31 degrees to our line of sight, while the jet is tilted only about 19 degrees.

If the jet follows the black hole’s spin axis, the different viewing angles suggest the outer disk is tilted relative to that axis.

The hot inner flow may be tilted too, and a tilted inner flow should wobble slowly around the spin axis, like a top.

The team saw a possible flicker in the galaxy’s X-ray brightness repeating about once a day. Only four or five cycles were caught, though, and they call it marginal.

A wobble isn’t the only candidate, though. Magnetic fields packed tightly around a black hole can also erupt in bursts, and that could make the X-rays pulse on a similar schedule.

A hot inner flow appears necessary for a jet, but the team doesn’t think it’s sufficient.

Some galaxies with fast-feeding black holes show the same kind of truncated disk and launch no jet at all, which leaves black hole spin as the likely deciding factor.

This study couldn’t measure the spin of 3C 120, because the disk ends too far out for the X-rays to carry that information.

Whether the inner flow is as magnetically loaded as the theory needs is also unconfirmed. The once-a-day flicker would help settle that, but it needs a longer X-ray watch than 55 hours.

The team is now observing a heavier black hole the same way.

“Our next goal is to build a more complete picture of how matter, magnetic fields and black hole rotation interact in these extreme environments,” Noda said.

For now, 3C 120 offers a clearer view of how a rapidly feeding black hole can still launch a powerful jet.

The full study was published in the journal The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

A man's appendix had to be removed, but not for dangerous inflammation, as you might expect.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The symptoms: The man went to the emergency room because he had a sharp pain in his lower-right abdomen.

What happened next: When doctors examined the man, the type of pain and the location of his discomfort suggested that he might have appendicitis, or inflammation of the appendix.

Appendicitis can be dangerous because it can cause the appendix to burst and release bacteria from the bowels into the abdominal cavity, thereby infecting the cavity's lining. This infection, called peritonitis, can spread to the bloodstream and cause the life-threatening condition sepsis, which kicks the immune system into overdrive.

Even though the patient had acute pain in his lower-right abdomen, he did not show signs of peritonitis, such as fever, nausea, symptoms of dehydration and an elevated heart rate, according to a report of his case. His doctors then performed abdominal ultrasound scans and found that the man's abdominal organs, including the appendix, appeared normal, with no signs of inflammation.

The report's authors did not include details about the man's treatment after this examination. But eight months later, he was still in pain and returned to the hospital for further evaluation, they noted.

The diagnosis: This time, when medical personnel questioned the man, he recalled that approximately 15 years earlier, he had accidentally swallowed a piece of a long bone containing edible marrow. The report does not mention if the man sought treatment immediately after swallowing this bone.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

At this second visit, doctors performed an abdominal X-ray and found a round object near the upper right of the man's pelvis. It measured about an inch (2.5 centimeters) long and a little over an inch (3 cm) wide.

According to a subsequent CT scan, the object contained bone tissue and was near the appendix. When the doctors looked inside the patient's abdomen with a laparoscope — a long, flexible tool with a camera at one end — they saw that the appendix was enlarged.

The treatment: Surgeons performed a laparoscopic appendectomy, which uses small incisions in the abdomen to insert instruments for removing the appendix. Inside the appendix was a hardened mass of fecal matter, called a fecaloma, which surrounded a long bone.

The organ's muscular walls had been stretched out by the mass, but there were no signs of inflammation. No complications developed after the surgery, and the patient was discharged two days later. The report does not describe any follow-up visits or treatments.

The appendix (orange) is a small, thin pouch of tissue attached to the colon.

What makes the case unique: It's relatively uncommon for people to accidentally swallow something indigestible and then require a medical visit for it. In the United States annually, about 120,000 people — roughly 90% of whom are children — are treated for ingesting foreign objects, and most of the objects are swallowed accidentally. Most commonly, the adults requiring treatment have ingested jewelry, while children are more likely to swallow coins, toys and batteries.

Typically, small, swallowed items pass harmlessly through the intestines within 48 hours; less than 1% require surgical intervention. Some objects, however, need immediate attention. For example, sharp items can tear the esophagus or puncture digestive organs. Batteries are hazardous if swallowed, as they contain corrosive acid that can leak into the gut. And small magnets are a big risk, especially if two or more are involved, since they may stick together through intestinal walls, which can tear holes in tissues or cause blockages and contortions in the intestines.

Swallowed foreign bodies rarely affect the appendix. Whether they enter the organ depends on the size of the opening into the appendix where it connects to the colon (which can vary between individuals), the dimensions of the ingested object, and the appendix's position in the body at the time. These objects cause approximately 0.005% cases of appendicitis, according to the man's case report. Such items recovered by surgeons through appendectomies include pieces of coal, nails, bits of enamel and glass, shells, dental crowns and bullets.

When a foreign body migrates to the appendix, it typically generates appendicitis within a few months, at most. However, this is not always the case. One report described a man who had eaten pigeons as a child and discovered more than 30 years later that he had 27 lead shot pellets in his appendix. Despite containing these pellets from the birds' flesh, his appendix was not inflamed.

"It is therefore possible, although rare, that a foreign body in the appendix even after many years (in our case, 15 years) does not lead to an authentic appendicitis either histologically or clinically," the authors of the marrowbone case report wrote.

They added that their patient was the first record in the scientific literature of a sizable bone lingering inside an appendix for more than a decade without causing significant inflammation. His pain was likely caused by physical shifting of the hard mass. His experience presented "a unique clinical picture," the doctors wrote.

"This case could offer a possible diagnostic and therapeutic option for appropriately treating patients with foreign bodies within the appendix," they said.

For more intriguing medical cases, check out our Diagnostic Dilemma archives.

#6396. Fear actually makes it harder for your brain to tell if you are safe, which may help explain PTSD

Fear stores danger and safety as overlapping brain maps, and the researchers think that strategy may go into overdrive in PTSD.

After something frightening happens, the brain should be able to distinguish between the location where it actually occurred from every other place where it didn’t. However, a new study shows that fear tends to blur that line in the brain.

A memory center deep in the brain stored the dangerous place and the safe place as overlapping maps. The overlap seemed to help the animals recall the threat faster.

The researchers think that speed may be the point. They also think an exaggerated version of the same trade-off could help explain why a harmless situation can suddenly feel threatening to a person with PTSD.

Mark Brandon’s lab at the Douglas Research Centre, a mental health research center at McGill University, did the work with Robert Rozeske of the University of Toronto Scarborough.

It rests on 16 mice that learned to fear one room, and on recordings from the hippocampus, the brain structure that stores memories of places.

“Our findings suggest fear may blur the boundary between danger and safety rather than sharpen it,” said Brandon, an associate professor in McGill’s Department of Psychiatry. “This could reshape how scientists think about anxiety and PTSD.”

A mouse knows a room by its walls, its floor and its sounds, so the team built an arena where all three could change at once.

A mouse that never moved would find itself, as far as its senses could tell, somewhere else. One room had a light patterned wall, a dark floor and a hiss of white noise; the other had a gray wall, a light floor and a single high tone.

For two days, mice in the first room got six shocks to the feet each day, and the second room never came with a shock.

On the third and fourth days, the arena switched between the two rooms every two minutes. A tiny microscope fixed to each mouse’s head recorded large groups of neurons.

Shocked mice froze in fear far more often in the dangerous room than in the safe one, even though they hadn’t gone anywhere.

Mice that had never been shocked barely froze in either. Freezing is how mice show fear. The animals were telling the two rooms apart.

Robert Rozeske is an assistant professor of psychology at the University of Toronto Scarborough, and the study’s lead author.

“That gave us something conventional fear conditioning experiments cannot easily provide: a moment-by-moment view of the brain switching between competing maps of dangerous and safe memories,” he said.

The hippocampus builds a map of each place an animal knows out of cells that fire at particular spots. The team recorded two parts of it, in separate groups of eight shocked mice.

The dorsal hippocampus, toward the top of the structure, keeps the detailed spatial maps, and the ventral hippocampus, toward the bottom, is more closely connected to the brain’s emotion circuits.

The first shock changed the map of the dangerous room right away, in both parts. The change was bigger in the ventral hippocampus. There, the mice whose maps shifted the most were also the ones that froze the most.

Once the rooms started switching, the dorsal maps of the two rooms stayed distinct, and the fear training made the difference between them larger.

In the ventral hippocampus, the two maps grew more alike. Mice that had never been shocked kept two clearly separate ventral maps, so the fear itself was what blurred them.

The textbook account says the hippocampus keeps memories from interfering with each other by giving similar places different maps.

A shock in one room should then have made the two maps more different. However, the ventral maps moved the other way.

Overlap didn’t make the ventral hippocampus worse at telling the rooms apart. When the arena switched to the dangerous room, the ventral map of that room reached full strength sooner than the dorsal map did.

And the moments when one map was much stronger than the other were the moments that best predicted whether a mouse froze in fear.

Rozeske said the ventral hippocampus “may be part of a system that prioritizes a rapid ‘better safe than sorry’ response. In other words, the brain may sacrifice precision for speed when danger matters.”

The researchers suggest the ventral hippocampus keeps a rough, quick sketch of a place while the dorsal part keeps the detailed map. A sketch that overlaps with its neighbor is faster to switch into.

Over the third and fourth days, the dangerous room kept coming back without a shock, and the mice gradually froze less there. As the fear faded, the ventral maps separated again.

By the fourth day, the ventral maps looked like those of mice that had never been shocked. The ventral map of the dangerous room no longer arrived faster than the dorsal one, either.

The reversal is why the researchers think the blur is a strategy rather than damage. The overlap appeared with the fear, was larger in the mice that froze more, and was gone once the fear faded.

People with anxiety or PTSD can feel intense fear when a safe situation calls up a bad memory. Brain scientists call the system that keeps similar memories apart pattern separation.

“Our study suggests that’s not necessarily a broken pattern-separation system, but possibly an overactive version of a normal survival mechanism gone into overdrive,” Brandon said.

“That reframing could guide therapeutic approaches to address an overly fast transition to ‘danger mode,'” he added.

Everything here happened in mice. The two parts of the hippocampus were recorded in different animals, because no microscope can yet record both at once in one mouse.

The recording method was also too slow to show how the brain flips between the two maps, moment to moment.

Freezing also didn’t line up tightly with the strength of either map. So another region, such as the amygdala, probably reads the hippocampus’s maps and decides when the animal freezes.

The mice in this study stopped freezing as much after two days of safe visits. So the team can’t say what the ventral maps look like in an animal whose fear never fades, which is closer to PTSD.

The authors said future studies should take on how the quick sketch and the detailed map work together while a fear is learned and then lost.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Neuroscience.

#6395. Drugs like Ozempic may help reverse chronic kidney disease

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Semaglutide helped repair blood vessels and reduce inflammation in the kidneys, a study finds

A patient undergoes hemodialysis, a process that filters waste from blood when the kidneys can’t. A new study shows how the popular weight loss drug semaglutide can help repair damaged kidneys.

Maria Symchych-Navrotska/iStock/Getty Images Plus

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Ozempic’s key ingredient fixes faulty filters in the kidney.

The well-known weight loss drug repairs and restores blood vessels that power people’s waste disposal systems, researchers report October 1 in Nature Medicine. Those actions mean the ingredient, called semaglutide, can add another notch to its list of health benefits: treating chronic kidney disease.

In patients with the condition, semaglutide also increased blood flow and tamped down inflammation, the team found. The study reinforces the GLP-1 drug’s known anti-inflammatory effects, while also suggesting that it may play a direct role in protecting the kidney’s blood vessels, says Susan Quaggin, a nephrologist at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago who was not involved in the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Chronic kidney disease affects an estimated 674 million people worldwide, with some of the most common causes being diabetes and high blood pressure. As the disease progresses, the kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter out waste from blood and excrete it as urine. This causes other health complications, as well as a sharply increased risk of dying from a heart attack or stroke.

Patients with diabetic chronic kidney disease who took semaglutide were less likely to wind up in kidney failure, or die from a heart attack or stroke, than those taking a placebo, researchers reported in 2024 in the New England Journal of Medicine. That trial was stopped early, as the drug was so effective at preventing death that doctors no longer considered it ethical to keep giving participants the placebo.

For the new study, some of those same researchers then looked at a subset of 106 participants to find out how the drug worked. The team collected kidney tissue samples before and after the participants took semaglutide, and compared them with samples from participants given the placebo. Semaglutide use led to striking visible changes in the tissues, including increased blood flow, reduced scarring and reduced blood vessel stiffness, a measure of vessel health.

Increased blood flow is important because it increases filtration, which is the kidneys’ main job, says Peter Nguyen, a nephrologist at Houston Methodist Hospital who was not involved in the study.

Researchers also looked at levels of a protein, called albumin, in patients’ urine. High levels can be an early sign that the kidneys’ filters aren’t working well. While those levels didn’t change much in those on the placebo, they dropped in patients taking semaglutide ― a sign the filters weren’t quite as leaky any more.

The team then looked under the hood for genetic clues to how semaglutide appeared to heal the kidneys. Within the glomerulus, the tiny blood vessels responsible for the kidney’s filtering action, genes relating to metabolic stress were turned off, Katherine Tuttle, a nephrologist at the University of Washington’s Providence Medical Research Center in Spokane, and colleagues found. Within these same cells, inflammatory genes were also turned off, while repair genes were switched on.

The researchers also looked at a subset of genes responsible for cells “talking” to each other within the glomerulus. Before semaglutide, the blood vessels and immune cells were “chattering” with each other, sending lots of inflammatory signals, Tuttle says. After semaglutide, the immune cells went quiet, silencing the messages that ramp up harmful inflammation. These changes in gene activity point to a healthier kidney that’s less stressed and inflamed, and that has had repair processes flipped on.

With semaglutide treatment, Tuttle says, patients’ damaged kidneys showed clear signs of repair.

#6394. Official reports could be underestimating the amount of forever chemicals in drinking water by at least half

A model of 1.8 million EPA water tests estimates that reporting below-limit PFAS as "zero" misses over half the estimated PFAS in US drinking water.

Seeing “not detected” next to forever chemicals on a water report might seem like you have completely clean water. However, it actually means the lab just could not detect the chemicals below a specific cutoff point.

For the two most common forever chemicals, this cutoff point is exactly the same as the highest legal limit allowed.

Researchers have now modeled the EPA’s national test results with those below-limit values filled in. Counting them as zero, they estimate, captures less than half of the PFAS the model projects for community water systems.

The missing share is an estimate, not a measurement, and it doesn’t mean any one household’s tap holds twice as much PFAS.

PFAS, short for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, are the man-made forever chemicals that can persist in the environment for a long time.

Gehendra Kharel, an environmental scientist at Texas Christian University in Fort Worth, led the work with colleagues at TCU, the University of Florida and Oklahoma State University.

In an interview with Earth.com, Kharel said the size of the information gap stood out to him. “About 98 percent of the roughly 1.86 million individual PFAS results in the January 2026 dataset were below reporting limits,” he said.

“Those records still contain information: we know the concentrations were below specified thresholds, even though their exact values are unknown.”

The EPA requires public water systems to test for 29 PFAS. The January 2026 release held results from 10,297 systems, including a sample of small ones.

A reporting limit is the lowest concentration a lab can measure with confidence. Anything under it is logged as “less than” the limit, and when the EPA compares results with its health benchmarks, it counts those results as zero.

Counting them as zero makes sense for checking a benchmark. But the same rule, the team wrote, is the wrong tool for estimating how much PFAS is in the water overall, because it sets 98 percent of the results to zero.

For each PFAS detected at least once, the team fitted a statistical curve to all the results, measured and below-limit alike.

From that curve they drew 500 possible values for every below-limit record, averaged them, and added up all the chemicals for each water system.

Across 9,991 community water systems, weighted by the people each one serves, the zero rule gave an average of about 6.6 parts per trillion for the 25 PFAS combined.

The model’s estimate was about 15 parts per trillion. That difference is the whole finding.

A part per trillion is a nanogram in a liter of water, about one drop in 20 Olympic swimming pools. The standard way of adding up the results captured 44 percent of what the model estimated.

For the six PFAS that carry federal drinking water limits, the gap was narrower: about 2.6 parts per trillion under the zero rule, and an estimated 5.2 from the model.

Kharel told Earth.com that “more than half” describes the share of the model’s estimate that the zero rule leaves out.

“It is not a direct measurement of previously unreported contamination or a finding that every household’s water contains twice as much PFAS,” he said.

The gap was not the same everywhere. Among the 12 PFAS detected most often, the zero rule captured about 74 percent of the model estimate in systems that draw on groundwater.

In systems that use surface water or a mix of sources, it captured about 45 percent. Smaller systems showed a wider gap than larger ones.

Asked by Earth.com which systems most need more testing, Kharel said the study does not produce a priority list. The patterns suggest where more sensitive follow-up testing could be useful, he said, and they do not show that those systems have higher concentrations or greater health risks.

The EPA set a limit of 4 parts per trillion for PFOA and PFOS in April 2024. The monitoring program’s reporting limit for both chemicals is the same number.

Under the zero rule, 1,277 sampling locations were at or above the PFOA benchmark and 1,364 were at or above the PFOS benchmark.

The model added between 16 and 33 locations for PFOA and between 4 and 25 for PFOS, depending on which curve it used. No location where every result fell below the limit crossed the benchmark.

So a large gap in the national average barely changed which places are near the limit. “Better concentration estimates do not automatically mean more regulatory violations or greater health risk,” Kharel said.

The comparison is a screening exercise, and whether a system violates the rule is decided separately.

Lower reporting limits would close most of the gap. If labs reported PFOA and PFOS down to 1 part per trillion instead of the current 4, the zero rule would capture 84 to 92 percent of the model’s combined total.

Kharel’s advice for anyone holding a water report starts with the utility that issued it.

“Ask your utility what ‘not detected’ means in that report, which PFAS were tested, what reporting limits were used, and when samples were collected,” he said. “‘Not detected’ does not establish that the concentration is zero.”

Because the reporting limit for PFOA and PFOS equals the legal limit, a clean result says only that the water is somewhere below that number.

“A below-limit result does not tell us whether the concentration is close to that value or much lower,” Kharel said.

The size of the gap depends on the curve. The main model used the shape that fit the data best. Two other shapes gave smaller gaps.

For the 12 most-detected PFAS, they put the zero rule’s share at 65 percent and 76 percent, instead of 55 percent. The direction never changed; the size did.

The estimates cover only the systems in the EPA dataset, sampled where water enters the pipes. Private wells and the water at anyone’s tap are outside them, and the study does not estimate exposure or health risk.

What the water actually holds below 4 parts per trillion is still unmeasured. The records can say only that it is somewhere under the limit, and finding out means labs reporting lower numbers.

Until they do, the team has made its model available as a screening tool called PFAS-CAST. Utilities can run the same calculation on their own results and see where more sensitive testing would help.

The full study was published in the journal Cell Reports Sustainability.

#6393. A mother bat’s heart actually beats faster the second she hears her own baby calling in a crowded colony

Mother bats' heart rates rose only for their own pups' calls, and the strongest reaction came from calls the pups made after learning to fly.

A newborn bat’s distress call does the job of a human baby’s cry. The researchers who study these bats expected it to be the sound that a mother reacts to most. It isn’t.

When mother Japanese house bats heard recordings of their own pups, their hearts sped up, while recordings of other mothers’ pups barely changed their pulse.

And the biggest rise came from a sound that isn’t a cry at all. It was the echolocation calls their pups made at a month old, once the young bats could fly.

For a mother raising pups in a dark roost shared by many other families, that heartbeat is a sign of recognition that can’t be detected by watching her.

Japanese house bats raise their young in colonies of 50 to 200 animals, with many mothers and pups roosting together.

Each mother looks after her own, and a companion study from the same laboratory found that mothers retrieve their own pups and not the pups of other mothers.

Kazuki Yoshino-Hashizawa, the study’s lead author, works at Doshisha University in Kyoto and the Institute of Science Tokyo. He said the idea came from watching the laboratory colony.

“When a pup was separated from their roosting area, only the biological mother immediately rushed over to bring it back,” he said.

In an interview with Earth.com, he compared a mother bat’s heart rate reading to a lie detector, which catches reactions a person never shows.

“Just as with humans, overt behavior doesn’t always tell the whole story – we all experience internal emotional states that aren’t immediately visible outside,” he said.

In May 2022 the team caught four pregnant females from a colony roosting in bridge girders near the Doshisha campus in Kyotanabe. Between June 20 and 22, each gave birth to three pups. Two died soon after birth, which left ten.

A newborn weighed about 0.04 ounces (1.1 to 1.3 grams), roughly the weight of a paper clip. Every day for a month, the researchers separated each pup from its mother for three minutes and recorded its calls.

Until they were about 10 to 12 days old, the bat pups gave isolation calls, the long, low-pitched sounds a pup makes when it is away from its mother.

At around eight days, the first echolocation calls appeared. Those are the short, high-pitched pulses that bats use to find their way in the dark. By 30 days the pups’ calls matched an adult’s, and the young bats could fly.

The heart recordings were taken 38 to 45 days after the births. Younger pups can’t hold their body temperature for more than an hour, the authors wrote, so earlier testing would have put them at risk.

The team recorded each mother’s heartbeat through three small electrodes placed under her skin. In a soundproof booth, a speaker 6 inches (15 centimeters) away played her three-second clips of calls. A resting bat’s heart runs at 200 to 300 beats a minute.

Each mother heard five kinds of clip. Four were pup calls: her own pups’ isolation calls from day two, and echolocation calls from day 30. She also heard the same two call types from other mothers’ pups.

The fifth was the echolocation calls of an adult male she had never met.

Only male pups’ calls were used, because some litters had no females. One mother died before the second day of testing.

Her own pups’ isolation calls raised a mother bat’s heart rate by about 70 beats a minute. Other pups’ calls produced small increases that could have been due to chance. All four mothers reacted more to their own pups than to the others.

The researchers expected the newborn distress calls to matter most, since those calls exist to bring a mother to a lost pup.

Instead, the echolocation calls of her own month-old pups produced the largest rise, about 130 beats a minute at its peak. A mother’s response didn’t fade as her pups grew up and their voices changed.

“We were intrigued to find that physiological responsiveness is not just a simple, fixed reflex to infant distress, but something that adapts as calls develop,” Yoshino-Hashizawa told Earth.com.

He said it suggests mothers stay highly sensitive to their own pups’ voices as the pups move toward independence.

Because all the families shared one cage, the mothers had heard the other pups daily, so familiarity alone doesn’t explain why their own pups stood out. The team’s best guess for the month-old calls is memory.

Mother goats and sea lions appear to update their memory of their young’s calls as those calls change. By the time of the test, the day-two cries were more than a month old. The researchers can’t settle this yet, because the two call types also came from pups of different ages.

The team hadn’t planned for one result: the unfamiliar adult male’s calls also sent heart rates up. The mothers, about 40 days past giving birth and not in mating season, may have reacted defensively to a strange male’s voice, the authors suggest.

A faster heart rate shows a mother bat is aroused, not whether she is drawn to the sound or alarmed by it.

Asked how he would tell the two apart, Yoshino-Hashizawa pointed to heart rate variability, the small changes in timing from one beat to the next. It helps separate the two in people, but nobody knows what a normal reading looks like in a bat.

“Their heart rates fluctuate dramatically depending on their physiological state – ranging from deep torpor to intense flight,” he said. A version that fits bats is his group’s next goal.

All of this rests on four mothers and 135 usable heart recordings. Pregnant bats are hard to breed in captivity, the authors wrote, and larger groups are needed to generalize the pattern.

Until then, four mothers’ heartbeats say a bat knows her own pups’ voices long after they stop crying for her. Whether what she feels is care or alarm is still an open question.

The full study was published in the journal Frontiers in Ethology.

#6392. There’s One Thing That Separates Us From Self-Driving Cars. Scientists Are Fighting Over What It Is.

Many theories about consciousness ask how it works, but a new study tries to pin down an equally important question: Where is it located?

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Understanding the ins and outs of human consciousness is a devilishly difficult problem seen in the dozens (or in some estimates, hundreds) of hypotheses put forward to explain our lived experience. However, a majority of those ideas place the cerebral cortex at the center of the consciousness conundrum, and at first glance, the association makes sense. This outer layer of the brain contains more cortical neurons than any other mammalian species and handles all kinds of complex processing, but not everyone agrees.

“I’m absolutely confident that the fundamental form of consciousness is raw feeling, and it’s located in the upper brainstem,” University of Cape Town neuroscientist Mark Solms said on a podcast. “My major opponents are the corticocentrist theorists. That is the majority of neuroscientists by far…those who think it’s obvious that the cortex is the seat of consciousness.”

But Solms isn’t alone in his assertion. A new paper, published in the journal The Neuroscientist, takes a closer look at this idea by expanding two types of awareness: access consciousness and phenomenal consciousness. While access consciousness refers to things a person is aware of at any given time, phenomenal consciousness explains the raw sentience of existence, or what the paper describes as the “me inside.” As PsyPost notes, if you were to block your eyes, cover your ears, and sever yourself from any source of sensory information, there would still exist an experienced self within you.

The idea that consciousness resides somewhere other than the cortex isn’t a new one, and that’s partially due to some pretty compelling evidence that the cortex doesn’t run the entire show. For one thing, some humans are born with hydranencephaly where major parts of the cerebral cortex are missing, but they continue to show signs of consciousness. Studies of patients with extensive damage to the cerebral cortex likewise show signs of lasting consciousness, while damage to the brainstem can cause a loss of consciousness or even a coma.

“The leading theories of consciousness, all cortico-centric, have difficulty dealing with these facts and typically fall back on the thought that residual bits of cortex may be enough,” The Hebrew University of Jerusalem’s Marshall Devor and Harvard Medical School’s Mark Baron write in the study. “If so, even minor disruption of cortex, to say nothing of massive disruption, ought to distort or eliminate both raw consciousness and pain sensation.”

Redirecting the focus to the brainstem, Devor and Baron conclude that the experience of pain is a major clue that consciousness resides in this lower cerebral structure. Senses like vision and hearing each have a clear home in the cortex, but pain doesn’t. Even when scientists stimulate the cortical areas linked to pain, people don’t actually feel it. The brainstem is also an ancient part of the brain, and humans have it in common with many other animals, which feel pain as much as we do. Devor’s previous work also explored how tiny amounts of anesthetic injected into small pockets of the brainstem caused unconsciousness in rats.

“The brainstem computation that we envision is strictly biological and a relatively simple, ‘primitive’ one. What it provides is a kind of ‘flavor’ to the complex, nonconscious computations carried out mostly in the cerebral cortex,” Devor and Baron write. “Without this ‘flavor,’ cortical processing closely resembles computations executed in today’s self-driving cars and robots.”

The authors argue that the sensation of pain provided “Darwinian fitness benefits” retained by evolution that first evolved directly in the brainstem, without the need for cortical processing. As a more complex mammalian mind emerged from the mists of evolutionary biology, the brainstem worked with the cerebral cortex to provide sentient experience for a wider range of sensations.

“Damage restricted to the cortex may cause blindness or sensory neglect, but it does not cause unconsciousness,” the authors conclude. “Focal brainstem damage does.”

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

#6391. What keeps people recycling for decades? One town offers clues

A Japanese study found that stronger neighborhood ties and wider social connections were linked to higher recycling participation.

Most recycling programs demand the same daily effort for years to come. They need rules and bins to get off the ground, but the factors that keep people sorting after decades have received less attention.

Osaki, a town in southern Japan, offers a test case. Residents have sorted their trash for more than 20 years, and the town has one of the country’s highest recycling rates.

A new survey found that residents who reported closer ties with their neighbors also reported more waste sorting and more help for others at collection points.

They also reported more positive views of recycling as well as feeling that family and neighbors would expect them to recycle.

Naoko Kaida, a professor at the University of Tsukuba, led the study with colleagues.

The small town of Osaki was running low on landfill space by the late 1990s.

Businesses, residents, and the local government worked together to keep as much waste as possible out of the landfill.

Residents sort their waste into 28 categories including cans, plastic bottles, plastic packaging, cardboard, and even diapers. They separate other bottles by color.

Residents take their sorted waste to shared community recycling stations managed by local hygiene associations. In many communities, residents oversee the sorting themselves.

The effort has worked, sharply reducing the town’s reliance on landfills. Since 2006, over 80% of the waste generated in Osaki has gone to recycling.

Previous studies tried to clarify the relation between recycling and social ties.

Few studies, however, have examined these relationships in a place where waste sorting has become routine. Osaki began with 16 sorting categories in 2000 and later expanded to 28.

Kaida works at the Institute of Systems and Information Engineering, University of Tsukuba, and her team mailed the anonymous questionnaire to all 5,773 households in Osaki in late 2024. Any adult living in one of the households could fill out the questionnaire.

Of the 805 questionnaires returned over four weeks, 277 were complete enough to analyze.

A number of the questions focused on the residents’ perception of their neighbors in terms of the degree of trust they inspired, how well they knew them, and how sure the residents were that their neighbors would help in the case of a disaster.

The questions on social relationships other than those with close neighbors covered people with whom residents shared hobbies, friends with whom they kept in touch although they lived far away, and trusted contacts at the workplace or at school.

Social scientists call both kinds of relationship social capital.

On a six-point scale, residents rated their waste handling on average at 5.36 for following the rules and 4.11 for helping others at the waste sorting stations.

The first score covered all 28 sorting categories and labeling garbage bags, while the second covered unloading garbage and helping people unsure how to sort it.

The team refers to a model of behavior that psychologists frequently use.

According to this model, a person’s intention to behave in a certain way depends on their attitudes to the behavior, other people’s expectations, and their capacity to behave in the intended way.

First, residents who reported stronger neighborhood ties felt more positive about the sorting of waste, and felt more strongly that their family and their neighbors expected them to follow the rules and recycle.

These views in turn were associated with an intention to continue sorting waste, which Kaida and her team found to be the best predictor of the recycling behavior residents reported.

The relationship between neighborhood ties and sorting behavior was indirect, through attitudes and expectations, with no direct link between the two in the team’s model.

Of the three factors in the model, attitude had the strongest tie to intention, which the authors suggested could reflect decades of town policy promoting waste sorting and its benefits.

Social connections outside the neighborhood, such as friendships and hobby groups, were directly linked to recycling and helping others at the station.

This link was about as strong as the indirect link between neighborhood relationships and these behaviors.

The authors suggested, however, that outside contacts may be sources of information or even of resources which can help residents learn and keep up with a very complicated system such as that of waste sorting in Osaki.

In the model, these wider ties had no clear link to residents’ attitudes, their sense of others’ expectations or how capable they felt.

Both kinds of relationship were associated with higher levels of recycling behavior but only to a small degree.

Neither type of social connection was clearly linked to how confident residents felt about their ability to recycle.

The researchers suggested that this confidence may depend more on clear rules, available facilities, and years of recycling experience.

Osaki is an aging town with about 11,700 inhabitants and an average age of 53 in 2020, part of the wider pattern of shrinking, aging populations in rural Japan.

Older residents reported stronger neighborly ties and felt more expectation from others, but the relationship between social ties and recycling behavior remained after controlling for age.

This one-time survey can only report on correlation, meaning that it can show a link between close neighbors and recycling but cannot tell us whether one causes the other.

One point for future studies is to measure social ties and recycling attitudes over time to see how they change together.

The 277 respondents were an older group. About half of them were in their 60s or 70s, and only five respondents were in their 20s.

As mentioned earlier, the same residents rated their recycling behavior, and the researchers did not watch them sort.

Osaki’s established sorting system and neighborhood involvement may limit how well the findings apply elsewhere.

The authors suggested that the same type of relationships may exist in other localities where residents of the neighborhoods help manage waste collection.

In contrast to the rural settings of many Japanese towns, however, community ties in the cities are generally looser, and the link may be weaker.

Very close ties to neighbors, however, carry risks too, the authors wrote, as residents can perceive pressure to conform or find themselves excluded when neighbors monitor one another.

The researchers suggested that towns should do more than share information and enforce recycling rules to keep recycling rates high.

They should also organize regular activities that bring neighbors together and encourage younger generations to recycle.

How much these ties matter likely depends on how a town organizes its waste collection, which future studies comparing towns with different waste sorting systems could clarify.

The full study was published in the Journal of Material Cycles and Waste Management.

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope could capture images 30% sharper than — and remain operational for twice as long as — initially expected. Researchers say these "remarkable" developments could greatly enhance the volume and quality of the data they will analyze.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is nearing its final destination more than 1 million miles (1.6 million kilometers) from Earth, where it will soon scour the universe for a host of cosmological treasures, including an estimated 100,000 new alien worlds.

But even before its mission truly begins, recent developments suggest the state-of-the-art spacecraft could take better images than — and remain operational for more than twice as long as — initially expected, further delighting already-excited astronomers.

"It is fantastic to learn that Roman is not just reaching its design goals but exceeding them," Eamonn Kerins, an astronomer at the University of Manchester in the U.K. who will help lead one of Roman's major surveys, told Live Science.

Roman is NASA's latest flagship space telescope, following in the footsteps of iconic observatories like the Hubble Space Telescope and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The $4 billion machine ‪—‬ which is over 42 feet (12.7 meters) long and weighs around the same as a fully grown Tyrannosaurus rex ‪—‬ successfully launched into space on Aug. 30, more than a decade after scientists started building it.

The telescope is now en route to Lagrange point 2 (L2), a fixed point relative to our planet where Earth's gravity and the sun's gravity cancel each other out. There, Roman will join several other important spacecraft, including JWST and the European Space Agency's Euclid telescope.

Roman was launched into space on board one of SpaceX's Falcon heavy rockets. It lifted off Aug. 30 from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

During Roman's journey to L2, which is currently around 85% complete, mission scientists have remotely switched on the telescope's various instruments to test whether they function as expected. So far, this "commissioning process" has gone off without a hitch, and by the time Roman arrives in less than two weeks, it should be ready to snap its first in-depth images of the cosmos.

Researchers were already pumped to see what Roman will be able to do once it is in place and fully switched on. However, that excitement has further intensified in recent weeks, thanks to two postlaunch developments.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

First, a series of near-perfect rocket burns, executed during and shortly after launch, saved more than a decade's worth of fuel that can now be used to extend Roman's mission. Second, after remotely adjusting the telescope's mirror, researchers discovered it should be capable of snapping images with around 30% greater detail than engineers predicted.

The team that designed, launched and remotely commissioned the orbital observatory has "done an amazing job" and "their work has ensured that Roman is more than up to the task," Kerins said.

Shortly after Roman arrived in space on board a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket that lifted off from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, mission scientists conducted two major burns, or engine firings, which gave the spacecraft enough momentum to escape Earth's orbit and make the journey to L2.

Roman is around the same size as a small truck and was packed into the nose cone of the Falcon Heavy rocket prior to launch.

Thanks to a combination of "exquisite planning by our orbital dynamics team" and "brilliant execution by the operations team," these burns were so precise that each one saved up to four years' worth of fuel, Jamie Dunn, director of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, said in a Sept. 14 statement.

On top of this, Roman ended up being much lighter than initially planned, which allowed engineers to pack another four years' worth of fuel into the spacecraft before launch. "Since Roman's [weight] was lower than we budgeted for, we were able to fill the propellant tanks to their capacity rather than only filling them as much as we needed," Alison Rao, the Roman propulsion lead at NASA Goddard, said in the statement.

In total, these savings could give Roman an additional 12 years of fuel, which could more than double the mission's planned 10-year lifespan. That means Roman could still be capturing images of the cosmos in 2048.

Given that Roman can collect data up to 1,000 times faster than Hubble, this extended lifespan will greatly enhance the amount of data the new space telescope will be able to capture. "With a 20-year Roman lifetime, we could, in theory, do over 20,000 years of Hubble survey work," Kerins said. "That's a lot of science!"

Roman is now on its way to L2, where the gravity of Earth and the sun cancel out, allowing it to remain in one place without expending much fuel.

This prolonged lifespan will let astronomers compare images of specific objects decades apart — such as expanding nebulas or colliding galaxies — allowing them to detect changes they otherwise might have missed.

It may also let them study objects or phenomena that we haven't even discovered yet, which is particularly exciting, Kerins noted. "The real show-stopper results will be new things we just aren't even thinking about right now," he said. "The possibilities are truly breathtaking."

There is also the chance that Roman's mission could be extended even further, because engineers often find clever ways of making active spacecraft last longer. For example, Hubble is more than two decades past its initial mission parameters, and the recently deceased Swift Observatory lasted 10 times longer than initially predicted before falling back to Earth last week.

Roman's secret weapon is arguably its Wide Field Instrument (WFI), made up of a 288-megapixel camera attached to a 7.9-foot (2.4 m) mirror, which will capture ultra-detailed images with a field of view roughly 100 times larger than Hubble's.

Roman's WFI consists of a 288-megapixel camera attached to a 7.9-foot (2.4 m) mirror. It will be capable of capturing images with a field of view 100 times greater than Hubble.

We have already seen the first WFI images — a series of blurry, green dots captured during a test of the instrument's 18 different light detectors ( see below). However, those photos were nothing like what WFI will capture in the future; those images will be so detailed that you would need dozens of high-definition TVs to properly display a single snap in full resolution, Kerins said.

After Roman completes the initial WFI commissioning phase, those images will be around 30% sharper than designers predicted. "All of the images from Roman's cosmic surveys will be even sharper than we expected," Alden Jurling, a senior optical engineer who works on Roman at NASA Goddard, said in an Oct. 14 statement. "It's a great outcome."

The improvements were first noticed after the WFI's car-sized mirror was realigned by just one-sixteenth the diameter of a human hair, demonstrating just how intricate the commissioning process has been. "Calibrating an instrument is like tuning a piano or guitar before a concert," Maxime Rizzo, a WFI systems engineer at NASA Goddard, said in the statement. "You adjust everything until it's just how you want it and then leave the settings alone so it performs consistently while you use it."

NASA released Roman's first photos on Sept. 15. Each small square represents one of the telescope's light detectors, and each blurry green spot is a distant star. (This is just a test image and does not represent how the telescope's proper photos will look.)

The improved image quality could really come to the fore during Roman's hunt for potentially habitable exoplanets, which is what Live Science's readers are most excited about for this mission.

Kerins, who is leading the Exoplanet Demographics Working Group for the Transits in the Roman Exoplanets Survey, is particularly excited about this development, but he said it does not necessarily guarantee that Roman will find more exoplanets than initially predicted.

The rest of Roman's commissioning phase is also proceeding as planned.

Roman's coronagraph instrument, which will block out the light from distant stars to allow WFI to spot alien worlds, has passed its main commissioning phase and is working as intended, according to a NASA blog post.

Roman has completed around 85% of its journey to L2 and should arrive at its final destination in the next few weeks. (The timeline in this image is a screenshot from Roman's commissioning process website, captured on Nov. 11.)

Meanwhile, a global network of ground stations, which will receive up to 1.4 terabytes of data from Roman every day, has established contact with the spacecraft and is receiving signals as expected, another blog post revealed.

All of these early wins raise hopes that Roman can have a long and successful career, and are a testament to the years of work that went into designing the spacecraft and planning the mission.

"What we're seeing now with the actual optical performance and estimated lifetime of Roman is just how good that design process has been," Kerins said. "It's a remarkable achievement. I can't wait to see what Roman is going to give us."

#6389. Early humans may have kept souvenirs half a million years ago

Early humans may have collected keepsakes 500,000 years ago, a habit researchers suggest could have helped shape memory and a sense of self.

Somewhere in your house there’s a stone from a beach. A shell from a holiday. A pinecone your kid picked up on a walk three years ago that you can’t bring yourself to throw away.

It does nothing but it means everything. And according to a new study, you’re not the first human to feel that way. Not by about half a million years.

The study was led by Ran Barkai and Yoav Ram at Tel Aviv University.

The team argues that early humans in the Levant were already picking up colorful pebbles, fossil-studded rocks, and old weathered tools and carrying them home for reasons that may have gone beyond practical use.

According to the scientists, the habit of anchoring memories to objects didn’t just reflect the human mind. It may have helped build it.

The most striking evidence comes from the Sakhnin Valley in Lower Galilee.

Out of more than 200 surveyed handaxes at this Acheulean landscape, roughly ten were shaped around fossil imprints or unusual geological formations embedded in flint nodules.

Those nodules were harder to knap. Toolmakers normally avoided them.

But someone chose them anyway, then went out of their way to position the fossil or geological oddity at the center of the tool’s face.

The researchers argue that these choices were deliberate.

At Qesem Cave, small round colorful pebbles showed up starting around 400,000 years ago and kept showing up for the next 200,000 years. Their practical purpose remains unclear.

Then there’s something stranger. At Revadim, Jaljulia, and Qesem Cave, people picked up old flint tools that had been lying in the landscape long enough to develop a visible patina.

They resharpened the cutting edges, but they kept the old surfaces: the scars, the color changes, the story written into the stone.

Under magnification, wear traces show these recycled tools were barely used in their second life.

The fresh edges made them functional; preserving the patina may have held personal meaning.

The researchers call them “memory objects.”

Most discussions of weird prehistoric objects land on the same explanations. Art. Ritual. Status symbols. Shared cultural meaning.

This study does something different. It argues these objects worked at the personal level first.

No audience was required and no shared convention needed. Just one person who remembers what the stone means.

The authors lay out four things that separate a souvenir from a decoration: it’s tied to a specific episode in someone’s life, it helps verify a real experience against an imagined one, keeping it takes deliberate effort, and its meaning is private.

That last part matters. A keepsake points to something that happened to you, and only you need to know its meaning.

So how does holding a rock help you remember? The mechanism the authors point to is source monitoring. That refers to the brain’s way of sorting real experiences from dreams, hearsay, and imagination.

The hippocampus reconstructs episodes from partial cues. The perirhinal cortex handles familiarity, and the parahippocampal cortex fills in contextual detail.

The authors propose that a keepsake’s physical features could engage these memory systems together.

That matters more than it sounds. In small societies built on reciprocity, people who could reliably distinguish real experiences from imagined ones may have had an advantage.

Over enough generations, routine souvenir-keeping may have created a “souvenir niche” that favored brains better wired for autobiographical memory and sense of self.

“The disappearance of large animals, particularly elephants, required early humans to develop new hunting methods and become familiar with hunting grounds inhabited by animals such as fallow deer and wild cattle,” Barkai said.

“Objects taken from these places may have helped them maintain a personal connection with the places that would henceforth provide their livelihood.”

The elephant vanished from the Levant around 400,000 years ago. So did Homo erectus and  the Acheulean tool tradition.

Everything shifted. Smaller, faster prey meant learning new territories from scratch.

Familiar landscapes couldn’t be taken for granted anymore. Portable pieces of those places became worth carrying home.

The authors are clear this isn’t proof. Not every odd stone was a keepsake.

But the pattern is there. Objects with no clear practical role were carried far from their source, curated over long use-lives, and found near hearths and living areas rather than tool-making debris.

Aesthetics and raw material shortage don’t explain it cleanly.

“When early humans brought a colorful stone or an old tool they had found in the landscape back to their cave, that object may have helped them remember a significant event or encounter for the rest of their lives,” Ram said.

“In this way, keepsakes may have become a kind of ‘external memory device,’ supporting the evolution of brain mechanisms responsible for autobiographical memory, which is so characteristic of us as humans and so important in shaping our identity.”

The study is published in the journal Evolutionary Anthropology.

#6388. Fossil fuel emissions are down in 2026. Green energy isn’t the reason

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The decrease is probably temporary and a result of high gas prices from the Iran war

The disruption of oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Iran has raised oil and gas prices around the world. According to new projections, those higher fuel prices will decrease global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuel burning in 2026 by about 0.16 gigatons from 2025.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Scientists project that global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels will decrease by 0.4 percent this year, after having grown by 0.8 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025.

But the dip may not last. The lower emissions are probably driven by high oil prices stemming from the Iran war, researchers report November 9 in Nature Climate Change.

Global emissions probably would have grown again this year without the energy shock of the Iran war, says Glen Peters, a climate scientist at the Center for International Climate Research in Oslo, Norway. “So the energy transition that’s happening … it’s not quite big enough to get emissions heading downward yet.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

For the study, Peters and his colleagues used data on countries’ electric vehicle stocks and wind and solar energy generation to project those technologies impacts on global fossil CO2 emissions through 2028. The team used the generative AI model Claude to source data and write code for analysis.

By year’s end, global emissions will reach 38.24 gigatons, the researchers found, which is about 0.16 gigatons less than were emitted in 2025. For comparison, annual global emissions fell by nearly two gigatons in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic and by about 0.5 gigatons in 2009 because of the global financial crisis.

If electric vehicle sales and solar and wind capacity continue growing at the rates they did in 2026, those technologies should counteract about 63 percent of the growth in emissions from 2025 to 2028 — or help avoid about 1.64 gigatons of added emissions.

The results indicate that the energy transition needs to accelerate if humankind is to realize consistently declining emissions, though EVs, solar and wind are already having a large impact. Without the offset in emissions provided by those technologies, global emissions would have risen by 1.9 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025, the researchers note.

It’s very hard to say exactly how long it will take for humanity to reach peak emissions, Peters says. However, he notes, “the fact that we’re talking about this means that we’re close to that point.”

#6387. There May Be a Point in Life When Stress Ages You Fastest. The Pandemic Just Helped Us Find It.

Epigenetic clocks suggest puberty is a pivotal window when stress leaves a deeper mark on our DNA.

On New Year’s Eve 2019, health officials in Wuhan, China, reported a mysterious cluster of pneumonia cases. It was the first sign of what would become the years-long Covid-19 pandemic. Across the world, every facet of life was interrupted, and many societies, including a growing anti-vaccine movement in the U.S., continue to grapple with the pandemic’s legacy, not to mention the millions of loved ones lost to the virus.

However, a new study led by researchers at the Max Planck Institute in Germany suggests that the pandemic didn’t impact every age cohort equally—at least, according to four separate epigenetic clocks that measure age-related changes in DNA methylation patterns. This chemical process changes predictably as we age and is a standard measurement for gauging someone’s genetic age. The team got lucky with its timing. Just before the pandemic took hold in March 2020, a project called the TwinLife Epigenetic Change Satellite had collected DNA samples from children, adolescents, and young adults in Germany. It sampled them again through spring 2022.

Senior author Elisabeth Binder studies how genes and the environment shape psychiatric disorders. She and her colleagues tracked how each age group’s epigenetic clocks changed over time. They also looked at data on socioeconomic background and physical health to see how pandemic stress affected each group. At first glance, the data showed some expected correlations between certain groups and health outcomes.

“Across all age groups, stress was most significantly felt by those who were already at risk before the pandemic, whether due to poorer physical health, lower subjective well-being or lower socio-economic background” Binder said in a press statement.

Because stress is a well-known driver of aging and key driver of inflammation, it wasn’t surprising that all age groups showed accelerated aging during one of the most stressful global eras in recent memory. But when the researchers dug deeper, they found something surprising. Adolescents showed more stress-related epigenetic aging than either children or young adults. According to the study, this suggests that mid-to-late puberty may be a pivotal window for “subjective stress-related alterations.”

“This suggests that adolescence may be a time period that is especially sensitive to the effects of stress—this could be due to the changes happening in the body during puberty, or because lockdown measures, like restrictions on seeing peers, had a particularly strong impact on this age group,” Alicia Schowe, a post-doctoral researcher and lead author of the study, said in a press statement.

The authors say lifestyle changes during lockdowns, such as less physical activity and weight gain, may also have played a role. But those factors alone can’t explain why adolescents showed more epigenetic aging than the other age groups.

The findings are a reminder that human aging is complex—our biological age isn’t set by our genes alone. Events far beyond our control, like a global pandemic, can leave their mark too. As these young people grow further from the pandemic, researchers will keep following them to find out whether the years the virus added to their epigenetic clocks will fade or stay with them for life.

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

#6386. Laser scanner that maps the chemistry inside tissue samples has been miniaturized into a handheld portable device

A handheld probe maps tissue chemistry without stains, and in lab tests its images closely matched those from a full-size instrument.

Machines that can map the chemistry inside a slice of tissue, showing where proteins and fats sit without using dye, have been too big to leave the lab bench.

A research team has now modified the imaging head of one to fit a probe that is 8 inches (20 centimeters) long. In side-by-side tests, its pictures closely matched those from a full-size lab instrument.

That matters because full-size machines can’t be carried to where patients are. A probe this size could someday work in the room where a tumor is removed.

So far, though, it has only tested the chemistry in thin slices of preserved tissue and plastics.

The work was done in Rohith Reddy’s lab at the University of Houston, and a pathologist at MD Anderson Cancer Center supplied bone marrow samples. Reddy already has a use in mind.

“Ultimately, this technology could make it possible to assess tissue during cancer surgery,” said Reddy, who leads the team. “After removing a suspected tumor, a surgeon could scan the freshly excised tissue.”

This would “help determine whether it is malignant or whether cancer cells remain at the surgical margin. This complementary information would be available while the patient is still in the operating room instead of having to wait for results from laboratory testing,” Reddy explained.

The instrument works with mid-infrared light. Like all infrared light, it’s invisible, and its waves are longer than the ones a TV remote sends. Molecules absorb this light at wavelengths set by the bonds holding their atoms together. That gives proteins, fats and DNA each a pattern of their own.

The system uses two lasers aimed at the same tiny spot. One sends mid-infrared light in bursts, 1,000 times a second. Where molecules in the spot absorb it, the spot warms very slightly. A second laser, a red one, picks up the small changes that the warming causes.

Sweep that spot across a sample, point by point, and the result is a map of where a chosen chemical sits. Because visible red light does the detecting, the map shows tissue chemistry detail finer than a single cell.

No stain is needed. Pathology labs normally dye tissue before anyone looks at it, and dyes are often impractical outside the lab because of toxicity, regulation and cost, the team wrote.

Shrinking the machine meant solving one stubborn problem. The red light and the mid-infrared light have to land on exactly the same point. However, lens materials that work well for one tend to work badly for the other.

Materials that pass red light often absorb mid-infrared, while ones built for mid-infrared can bend different colors by different amounts and blur the signal.

Reddy’s team sent the infrared light through a special glass fiber made for those wavelengths, which did away with bulky open-air optics.

They also swapped lenses for mirrors, since a mirror reflects both kinds of light. A curved mirror at the tip focuses both beams onto one spot.

“Careful optical design and alignment helped to minimize the image distortions that mirrors can cause. We also designed the handheld scanner to connect to the light source through a fiber-optic cable, allowing it to be maneuvered easily around a sample,” Reddy said.

The lasers and electronics sit in a base unit of less than 1.5 square feet (0.14 square meters). Commercial instruments of this kind take up more than 9 square feet (0.84 square meters) of optical table, more than a card table’s top.

The team first scanned a test chart patterned onto a crystal slide. The handheld system picked out details about 0.00008 inches (2 micrometers) across. Its images of the chart closely matched a commercial benchtop instrument’s.

Next came human tissue: thin slices of cervical cancer from two patients and ovarian cancer from two others.

Images from the handheld probe and the benchtop machine correlated at 0.90, compared at a coarse level of detail, on a scale where 1 would be a perfect match.

In ovarian cancer tissue, the tissue chemistry patterns it recorded agreed with a standard lab infrared measurement at 0.935 on a similar scale.

In plain terms, the small probe recorded close to what the big machines did. Its scans also lined up with dyed slices of the same tissue, the kind that pathologists read every day. Connective tissue that the dye highlighted showed up strongly in the undyed chemical image.

A bone marrow biopsy from a patient gave a harder test. Doctors check marrow for a buildup of collagen, a kind of scarring linked to the marrow making fewer blood cells. They usually spot it with a stain that turns collagen blue.

Without any stain, the chemical scan picked out the dense framework of bone in the sample. It also showed the collagen wrapped around a blood vessel, matching the blue in a stained slice next to it.

The team tried a second scanning style on mouse kidney tissue, with the mirror at the tip both turning and moving. That scan showed a glomerulus, one of the kidney’s tiny filters, along with chemical detail that a plain image from the red laser alone didn’t have.

Every sample was a thin, preserved slice on a slide. The team hasn’t imaged living tissue, and none of the samples was fresh from surgery, which is the setting Reddy described.

“Although the current platform is still a research prototype, it establishes a technical foundation for field-deployable, label-free chemical imaging,” Reddy said.

The probe also used only part of the range its laser can reach. That laser is built from four chips that point in slightly different directions, so crossing from one chip to the next meant realigning the light into the fiber by hand.

In these tests, a moving mirror inside the probe or a stage that shifted the sample did the scanning.

The team hasn’t yet tested whether these scans can help a doctor tell cancer from healthy tissue. The researchers plan to widen the range of infrared light the probe uses and to speed up scanning, which would make holding it freehand more practical.

Before any clinical use, its repeatability, safety and diagnostic performance still have to be tested under realistic clinical conditions.

The full study was published in the journal Optica.
