A new study supports a more nuanced approach to obesity diagnosis. Here's what to know.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Obesity is linked to a range of health problems ‪—‬ including heart disease, diabetes and early death ‪—‬ but it can be hard to know who is most at risk for these outcomes. Doctors and researchers often use body mass index (BMI) as a convenient tool to assess patients, but this metric does not account for individual differences in body composition, scientists have long argued.

"BMI misses a lot of information," Dr. Francesco Rubino, a professor of bariatric and metabolic surgery at King's College London, told Live Science.

Rubino recently chaired a team of 56 experts that was assembled to better define obesity and develop new diagnostic criteria for the condition. First proposed in January 2025, their new framework includes more body measurements beyond BMI and distinguishes between "preclinical" and "clinical" obesity.

Now, a new study published Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Nature confirms that these new criteria could detect obesity with greater precision than BMI alone. In other words, with the new approach, more people would be accurately diagnosed with obesity and fewer people would be misdiagnosed than are with BMI alone.

Live Science spoke with Rubino and other experts to break down the new findings and learn what they mean for patients.

At the simplest level, obesity is excess body fat. There are special scans and exams that send weak electrical signals through the body to measure a person's body fat percentage directly, but criteria based on body measurements are more accessible across clinical settings.

BMI is the most common of these measurements, as it simply involves dividing a person's weight by their height squared. However, it does not account for individual differences in lean muscle mass or bone density.

BMI doesn't capture nuances and variation between patients, experts argue, and it limits what doctors can say about a given person's health risk.

Additionally, the different BMI categories — such as "overweight" and "obese" — don't carry the same risks for all patients. Certain racial and ethnic groups tend to experience health consequences, such as higher mortality rates, at different BMI levels than others do.

For a given patient being assessed for obesity, the proposed guidelines would suggest using at least one additional body measurement alongside BMI and having their doctor review their medical history for other signs of bodily or organ dysfunction.

The proposed body measurements are less influenced by a person's muscle mass or bone structure than BMI is. They include waist circumference, waist-to-hip ratio and waist-to-height ratio. Notably, because different ethnicities are associated with different fat distribution patterns in the body, the latest Nature study incorporated different waist circumference cutoffs based that varied by ethnicity.

In addition to these body measurements, the proposed criteria look at 18 conditions and signs of bodily or organ dysfunction that are related to obesity, such as cardiovascular diseases, joint pain and sleep apnea. (All 18 factors can be found detailed in this chart.)

Rubino and his colleagues — which together made up what's known as a Lancet Commission — defined "clinical obesity" as a disease state involving at least one of 18 forms of bodily dysfunction caused by excess fat tissue. Preclinical obesity, by contrast, is when a person is at risk of this disease state and may need interventions to avoid obesity-related dysfunction.

That means that two people with the same BMI, waist circumference and waist-to-height ratio may be classified differently, depending on whether they have other conditions. In the new study, between 77% and 91% of individuals with preclinical obesity did not progress to clinical obesity within 10 years, depending on the cohort analyzed.

This distinction can be complicated, though, as the diagnostic metrics for each form of dysfunction contain their own ambiguities.

"There needs to be more consensus on what's actually defining clinical obesity," said Dr. Aayush Visaria, an internal medicine instructor at Rutgers Robert Wood Johnson Medical School in New Jersey. Visaira was not involved in writing the new criteria but authored an analysis of the proposed measures.

The Lancet Commission argues that the categories of preclinical and clinical obesity could help doctors identify the people with the greatest need for treatment. The researchers tracked health outcomes using electronic health records from China, the United Kingdom, the United States and Spain, and they determined that their clinical obesity classification was better at flagging people's risk of death than BMI alone.

Changing the diagnostic criteria for obesity could, in turn, change who is recommended to receive weight-control medications.

They found no clear association between BMI and mortality risk, but clinical obesity was linked to a 69% greater risk of all-cause mortality, compared to no obesity.

The Lancet Commission's approach could drive a small net uptick in individuals diagnosed with obesity, according to the new study.

Under the current framework, "we are definitely missing some people who actually need obesity treatment but just did not meet the BMI criteria," said Dr. Jennifer Hwang, an instructor of medicine at the University of Chicago who has published her own analysis of the new criteria.

With the BMI-only approach, people with BMIs of 30 or higher are categorized as obese. With the new definition, some people with BMIs under 30 would be newly categorized as clinically obese, while a smaller group of people with high BMIs would suddenly not count as clinically obese, the Nature study predicted.

For instance, the former group might include people who have "overweight" BMIs but also have obesity-related dysfunction, while the latter group might include people with "obese" BMIs but without any dysfunction.

Overall, the new criteria would increase obesity prevalence by about 3.3% to 7.4%, the team predicted. The percentage varied depending on the group analyzed.

More research is needed to prove that the Lancet Commission's criteria would improve patient care and be practical to use in a clinical setting, Hwang said. She noted potential challenges in implementing both new aspects of the new framework. While the body measurements sound simple enough to use, clinicians would need training to perform them accurately.

Providers also may struggle with the new distinction between preclinical and clinical obesity. A 2025 analysis of the Lancet Commission framework noted that some patients who qualify for obesity medications under the Food and Drug Administration's guidelines may be recharacterized as having preclinical obesity and no longer receive a prescription.

Rubino and the rest of the Lancet Commission plan to continue validating their framework to see how it could best support personalized obesity treatment. For instance, they want to determine which forms of organ dysfunction are of greatest concern and develop a way of scoring each patient's level of risk.

#6384. Flowers with clear petal ‘windows’ carry fewer microbes, which influences pollinators

Clear petal windows let infrared heat into two Florida shrubs' blooms, and warmth, not ultraviolet, thins out the flower microbes inside.

Some flowers have tiny, clear windows built right into their petals. While they might just look like a pretty design, researchers at Florida Atlantic University (FAU) have discovered that these see-through spots actually control the temperature inside the flower, changing the nectar and affecting how insects pollinate them.

Ultraviolet is the part of sunlight known for killing microbes, so the windows looked like a way of letting the sun scrub a flower clean.

Instead, the heat-carrying infrared coming through them is what mattered: warmer flowers held fewer microbes, and the ultraviolet didn’t explain the difference.

Jessica Williams, a Ph.D. student at Florida Atlantic University, did the work with four colleagues. They focused on shrubs named Lyonia lucida (also called fetterbush), and Lyonia fruticosa.

They are close relatives in the heath family that also includes blueberries. Both grow in the sandy, sun-baked scrub of south-central Florida and bloom together in late spring.

Each flower is a narrow urn with its petals fused into a chamber, and near the base of that urn a patch of petal has almost no pigment in it.

Other members of the family have the same windows, blueberries among them, and Williams’ team asked what they do to the light and heat inside.

Fetterbush flowers are visited mostly by moths at night, while L. fruticosa gets bees and wasps. Those visitors are probably how most microbes reach a flower.

Over three days in May 2025 at Archbold Biological Station, the team took seven flowers from each of nine plants per species, 126 in all.

For every flower, a thin temperature probe went in through the opening to the base of the chamber while a second probe hung just outside the petals.

Then the flower was clipped off with sterile scissors, dropped into a tube and kept on ice. Within five hours it was rinsed with a few drops of sterile water, pumped in and out five times.

That rinse went onto growth plates for two days at 81°F (27°C), and the team counted the colonies of yeast, mold and bacteria that grew.

Across the 108 flowers with a full set of measurements, the warmer a flower was inside, the fewer microbes grew from its rinse. Yeasts were the most common, then molds, then bacteria, and in both species the warmer flowers had fewer yeasts.

The two shrubs didn’t respond the same way. In L. fruticosa, warmer flowers had fewer bacteria, while in fetterbush the temperature made little difference to the bacteria. Fetterbush also carried more mold.

A fetterbush flower warmed by a bit more than half a degree for every degree the air around it warmed. An L. fruticosa flower barely moved, staying warmer than the air when the air was cool and cooler than the air when it was hot.

So a microbe’s experience of a hot May day depends on which shrub it landed in.

Heat was already known to matter to these microbes. A 2022 study in Frontiers in Microbiology found that heat can change which bacteria live in a flower’s nectar.

The windows let through more light than the pigmented petal, both ultraviolet and infrared. So the team tested the obvious idea, that ultraviolet was sterilizing the flower.

A germicidal ultraviolet lamp did kill. After 30 seconds under it, the share of L. fruticosa rinses with any yeast fell from 90 to 60 percent.

But microbes from flowers whose windows let through more ultraviolet were no better at surviving the lamp than microbes from flowers that let through less. The lamp was probably harsher than the ultraviolet a flower typically sees inside, Williams’ team wrote.

Infrared was a different story. In May 2026 the team chilled cut flowers in a refrigerator, then set them under a 500-watt halogen work light behind a filter.

One filter passed only deep red and infrared, and the other blocked infrared and passed only visible light. A probe inside each flower logged its temperature for 10 minutes.

Fetterbush flowers under infrared alone warmed about 5.8°F (3.21°C) more than flowers with the infrared blocked. After 10 minutes, they were 12.9°F (7.18°C) above where they started.

L. fruticosa flowers warmed about the same amount under either filter. Infrared, in other words, does warm a fetterbush flower.

Williams’ team doesn’t claim the windows evolved to keep microbes out. The chain they describe runs the other way. The windows let infrared in and, in fetterbush at least, the infrared warms the flower.

The warmth then probably makes the flower a harder place for microbes to persist. Microbes were still present in warm flowers, only fewer of them.

The windows may be doing several other jobs at once, the team wrote. Those could run from helping pollen develop to changing how bright the inside of the flower looks to a visiting insect. Fewer microbes would then be a side effect of those jobs.

“One of the exciting things about this work is that a seemingly small floral trait can change the physical environment inside a flower in ways that affect its microbial community,” Williams said.

“Because floral microbes can influence nectar traits and plant-pollinator interactions, these results suggest that flower structure may have ecological consequences that extend beyond the flower itself.”

Nectar and pollinators were not measured here. The field sampling covered 18 plants at one station over three days, and growth plates count only the microbes that will grow in a lab dish.

The team measured heat, not who delivered the microbes. Moths and bees bring different passengers, and which ones arrive first and how they compete inside the flower also shape which microbes settle in.

How those arrivals interact with the heat is, in the team’s words, an open question.

A warmer flower may also keep a different set of microbes rather than simply fewer, a subset that can take the heat. The study didn’t test that.

Finding out would mean identifying which microbes each kind of visitor drops off and which of them survive a warm afternoon inside a fetterbush flower.

The full study was published in the journal New Phytologist.

#6383. Glue used in batteries makes recycling hard, so engineers designed one that comes off in water

Battery recycling is harder because of the fluorine glue in each cell. A citric acid version dissolves in water and lasted longer in tests.

The glue inside a lithium-ion battery is a tiny share of its weight, yet it shapes how the battery gets built and how hard it is to take it apart for recycling.

In most batteries that glue contains fluorine, and removing it at the end of a battery’s life takes high heat or corrosive chemicals.

However, the new glue is made from two common materials and citric acid, the acid in citrus fruit, and it comes off in plain water.

Test batteries built with it held their charge as well as standard ones, and in extended runs they held it longer. If that holds up at factory scale, the glue would take a toxic solvent out of battery making and simplify recycling.

Engineers at the University of California San Diego developed the glue in Zheng Chen’s Sustainable Materials and Energy Lab. They worked with John Muldoon of Toyota Research Institute of North America and colleagues at Arizona State University.

Every test ran in small lab cells, from watch-battery size up to flat pouches about 1.3 inches (3.3 centimeters) across. Those are far smaller than the packs in electric cars.

Inside a battery, the glue binds a powder that stores charge to a thin metal foil. The standard glue is a fluorine-containing plastic, and it has to be dissolved in a toxic solvent before it can be mixed with that powder.

Once the mix is spread on the foil, big ovens dry the solvent off, and it has to be captured and cleaned for reuse.

Standard-glue electrodes dried off under vacuum at 248°F (120°C) for 12 hours. New-glue electrodes dried in an ordinary oven at 140°F (60°C) for four hours.

“Those extra steps significantly increase the cost and energy use – as well as the environmental impact – of battery manufacturing,” said Jiao Lin, a postdoctoral researcher in Chen’s lab and the study’s first author.

The fluorine glue is also very stable. That helps a battery last, but it means the glue leaves residue that only high heat or harsh chemicals will strip from the material before recycling.

“But that same stability also makes batteries much harder to recycle,” Chen said.

Water-based glues already exist. Carboxymethyl cellulose, a plant-derived thickener found in foods and paper products, holds together the graphite side of some commercial batteries.

On their own, though, glues like this tend to crack as they dry, which leaves the coating brittle. Chen’s team mixed that thickener with polyacrylic acid, a plastic that spreads evenly and bends.

Then they added citric acid, which bonds to both and links them into a single network. Lithium hydroxide kept the mix only mildly acidic, so it wouldn’t corrode the aluminum foil.

The glue made up just 2 percent of each electrode’s weight. Electrodes made with either ingredient alone, or with the two mixed without citric acid, cracked or pulled away from the foil as they dried. The citric acid version dried smooth.

When the team stuck tape on the coating and peeled it off, almost nothing came away. Standard-glue electrodes lost material after only a few peels. The new coating also stayed on when the foil was twisted.

Most test cells used lithium iron phosphate, a battery material that standard recycling methods earn little or no money from. At the start, cells with either glue stored nearly the same charge per gram.

After 1,000 rounds of charging and draining, cells with the new glue had 75.7 percent of their starting capacity. Cells with the standard glue lost capacity faster, especially after about 400 rounds.

So the water-soluble glue didn’t shorten the battery’s working life. In these tests, it added some.

A pouch cell built like a commercial battery, with graphite on the opposite side, kept 76.4 percent of its capacity after 1,600 rounds.

A stack of several layers did a little worse than a single layer, 74.5 percent to 83.5 percent after 700 rounds, which the authors traced to uneven conditions inside the stack.

The glue also worked with other electrode materials, including a nickel-rich one and silicon.

After 100 rounds of use, the team took cells apart. For the standard-glue electrodes, the team used the toxic solvent to lift the coating off.

New-glue electrodes soaked in purified water until the glue dissolved and the coating came cleanly off the foil.

Recovered material from the standard-glue cells still carried fluorine on its surface, left over from the liquid inside the battery. Material from the new-glue cells showed no detectable fluorine.

The team then restored the recovered lithium iron phosphate in a way that keeps it intact instead of breaking it down to raw metals.

Cells built from it kept more of their capacity, and handled fast charging better, than cells built from material recycled out of standard-glue batteries.

Graphite that was recovered in the same way worked again in new cells through 420 rounds.

The team also estimated the environmental cost of a battery cell. By that estimate, building one with the new glue would produce 6.9 percent less greenhouse gas and use 9.3 percent less energy than building one with the fluorine glue.

Recycling it would use 10 percent less energy and release 7.2 percent less greenhouse gas.

The authors call those figures a comparison of scenarios, not measurements from a working plant. The numbers would shift with how much solvent a factory recovers and how it captures fluorine, though the authors say the new glue would still come out ahead.

The new glue doesn’t remove all the fluorine from a battery. The salt in the battery’s liquid contains fluorine too, so the team calculates that the new glue cuts a cell’s total fluorine by about 30 percent.

Lin and Chen are inventors on a patent application for the glue, and Chen’s team plans to commercialize it with industry partners.

Whether the glue works as well when made by the ton and built into full-size batteries is an open question. Scaling up production is the team’s next step, along with adjusting the recipe for other battery types.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

#6382. Toxic secrets are hiding in Arctic ice

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A century-old pollution trail leads scientists back to Montana mining

At the turn of the twentieth century, the Anaconda Smelter in Montana spewed arsenic into the air — those heavy metal particles that are now trapped in Arctic ice cores.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Ice cores record Earth’s secrets, even the dirty ones.

Some of the cylindrical sections of ice extracted from the Arctic contain elevated levels of arsenic, lead and other heavy metals that circulated in our planet’s atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Those pollutants, which have been tied to declines in IQ and higher rates of certain cancers, were probably emitted by a mining and smelting company in Montana whose grounds are now designated as multiple Superfund sites, the researchers report November 3 in Nature Sustainability.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The ice cores contain tiny particles that were once airborne — including pollutants, volcanic ash and salt from ocean spray — and fell to our planet’s surface within a few days or weeks. In polar regions, that fallout combines with snow and is preserved as ice.

Joseph McConnell, an environmental scientist at the Desert Research Institute, and his collaborators recently analyzed 10 ice cores collected across Canada, Greenland and Russia. The cores contained material that had fallen to Earth as early as 210 BCE, but the interval spanning the Industrial Revolution in the United States — from roughly 1870 to 1914 — was what caught the team’s collective eye.

In the ice layers from that period, arsenic concentrations in some of the ice cores were up to 15 times higher than pre-Industrial Revolution levels. Because the heavy metal exposure has been tied to upticks in the rates of certain cancers, McConnell and his team set out to determine the most likely source of all that pollution.

The largest increases in arsenic existed in the ice cores from Greenland. That finding was a big hint, McConnell says, because atmospheric circulation patterns tend to move material from west to east. “The only way you can explain that pattern of deposition is if the emissions are coming from North America,” McConnell says. “Had it been from Europe, we would have seen much larger increases in the Russian Arctic.”

The most likely source, the team concluded, was a massive copper mining and smelting operation in southwestern Montana operated by the Anaconda Copper Mining Company. It was one of the largest in North America during the Industrial Revolution and, unlike other copper mining operations in the area, it worked with copper ore that contained heavy metals like arsenic and lead. It was no secret that those toxic metals were entering the atmosphere, says Fred Quivik, a historian and the author of Smoke and Tailings, a book about the environmental history of copper smelting in Montana. “Ranchers and farmers started seeing their livestock die from arsenic poisoning.”

Based on the concentrations of arsenic in the ice cores and models of how material disperses in the atmosphere, McConnell and his colleagues estimated that the Anaconda Copper Mining Company was emitting roughly 30 tons of arsenic per day into the atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. By comparison, Chile, currently the world’s largest producer of copper and home to more than 20 mining operations, collectively emits roughly one quarter as much arsenic today.

Beginning in 1919, the Anaconda Copper Mining Company installed devices near its smokestacks and other facilities to capture arsenic and prevent its release into the atmosphere. Arsenic emissions dropped by about 60 percent as a result, the ice core data showed, but by then hundreds of thousands of nearby residents had already been exposed for decades. That exposure could have been lessened, McConnell says, if the Anaconda Copper Mining Company hadn’t waited so long to install the pollution-abatement technology. “They delayed installation for about a decade.”

These new findings should be combined with census records to trace the effects of this pollution on human health in the 19th and 20th centuries, McConnell and his team suggest. “We hope that epidemiologists will take this information and really investigate potential impacts on human populations.”

#6381. A tiny remote controlled beetle robot named BeetleBot uses artificial muscles to explore narrow spaces and grab hidden objects

Printed muscles that shrink when heated let this beetle-sized soft robot walk, grip an object and send back what it feels.

Shrink a walking robot and its motors and gears get harder to fit, not easier. Insect-scale machines have mostly solved this problem with tiny, rigid parts. BeetleBot has neither.

Its legs move because strips of printed plastic shrink when an electric current warms them, the way a muscle shortens when it fires.

The robot is about the size of a real beetle, and a person wearing a sensor patch on one finger steers it by bending that finger.

A camera on its head and a pressure sensor in its jaws send back what it sees and what it is touching. The operator can decide the next move without seeing the robot at all.

Inho Kim built it as a postdoctoral researcher at Caltech and is now an assistant professor of chemistry at Sungkyunkwan University. Sang Ouk Kim of KAIST and Wei Gao of Caltech led the work with a group at NTU Singapore.

The artificial muscles are made of a liquid crystal elastomer, a rubbery plastic with molecules that line up in one direction.

Heat it past a certain point and that alignment breaks down so the material contracts along the line of the molecules and pulls. Let it cool and it stretches back.

The team printed each muscle as a stack of layers with a laser-cut metal heating wire sandwiched inside. Running current through the wire warms the plastic.

At 3 volts, a free-standing muscle shortened by about 45 percent but returned to its full length once the power stopped.

Pulling force matters as much as travel. At their strongest these muscles pulled with 0.18 megapascals of stress. This is within the 0.1 to 0.35 range of a mammal’s skeletal muscle.

That’s why a sheet of printed plastic can carry a robot with a camera and a gripper bolted to it.

The placement of those muscles came from the insect. The team dissected and filmed Mecynorrhina torquata, a large flower beetle, and measured how its leg joints swung when its muscles were stimulated.

That relationship set where the artificial muscles went on the beetle robot’s own six legs.

Insects work their legs with muscles arranged in opposing pairs. One pulls a joint one way and the other pulling it back. BeetleBot copies the arrangement.

Its front legs lift and lower the body, bending about 20 degrees, while the back legs swing forward and back, bending about 12 degrees.

Walking consists of those two groups firing in turn. The front muscles lift the front of the body, which tips the rear legs onto the ground. The back muscles then fold and push the beetle robot forward. Heat one side only and the robot turns.

For the head, the researchers copied the mandibles a beetle uses to hold its prey. Two curved flaps close when their muscles contract, a simpler arrangement than the spring-and-air hand built for the same job. A capacitive pressure sensor sits on the gripping surface.

The sensor is two thin, metal-coated sheets with an air gap between them. Squeeze them closer and the electrical charge they hold changes. This is what the beetle robot reports as contact.

It registered a touch in 0.127 seconds, and its reading rose almost in step with pressure up to 50 kilopascals.

The gripper can also tell shapes apart. Gripping a small sphere, a large sphere and a cube produced three different signal traces. This means the operator learns something about the object without ever seeing it close up.

A perching drone reads a branch the same way, by touch, where a camera stops helping.

The control patch is a printed strip of rubbery polymer loaded with carbon nanotubes, tiny conductive threads that form a network through the material.

Bending the finger stretches the strip, breaks some of those connections, and raises its electrical resistance.

Four finger movements produced four clearly separated signals, which the system reads as forward, left, right and grip, then sends to the robot over a short-range, wireless link. The patch held its signal through 1,000 bending cycles.

“A key feature of this work is the bidirectional feedback, which links the information detected by the robot to the user’s next action,” said Inho Kim, the paper’s first author.

Information running both ways is what separates this beetle robot from a remote-control toy. Other soft machines go further still, thinking without electricity by building the logic into the material itself.

The person sends a gesture, the robot sends back a camera frame and a pressure reading, and the next gesture depends on what came back.

To test all of it together, the team set a target object behind an obstacle and had an operator drive the robot there using the camera feed alone.

It took eight separate movements, turns and forward runs in sequence, to get around the obstacle, reach the object, close the gripper on it and carry it.

The pressure signal jumped at the moment of contact, which is how the operator knew to grip. That is the whole loop in one run: a finger moves, legs move, a sensor answers, and the finger moves again.

“This study expands the potential uses of soft robots by connecting the movement of artificial muscles, sensing, and user control in a single system,” said Sang Ouk Kim.

The muscles only work hot. Full contraction needs the plastic above roughly 230°F (110°C), and surfaces on the robot climbed past 212°F (100°C) during walking.

A thermal camera showed that heat staying local to the working muscle rather than spreading through the frame.

Heat is also what sets the pace. Each step waits for the plastic to cool, so the walking cycle runs slower than the muscle’s own limit. Adding payload slowed it further.

Two other limits stand in the way of sending one of these somewhere real. The finger patch’s signals pass through a wired front end before they go wireless, and the course the robot crossed was a small, built setup, not rubble or a pipe.

KAIST said the actuation speed, the energy efficiency and the power supply all need work before soft robots like this one inspect industrial equipment or explore the environment.

Nobody has driven one of these through a space that a person could not enter. Inho Kim said he plans to make the muscles faster and more efficient, and to improve the control methods that use the robot’s own sensing.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

Scientists have discovered that a known mushroom, Galerina indica, contains both psychedelic chemicals and deadly toxins.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A tiny brown mushroom found in Florida's swamps is the first known fungus to contain both psilocybin, the chemical compound in psychedelic mushrooms; and amatoxin, the poisonous substance in the world's deadliest mushrooms.

The species, Galerina indica, has been nicknamed the "dark magic mushroom" and was characterized in a study published Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Current Biology.

"There is no species of mushroom anywhere, in any group, that has been known to produce both at the same time," study first author Andrew Kunik, a fungal biology researcher at the University of Florida, told Live Science. "So it's quite remarkable."

Exactly why the dark magic mushroom has evolved to contain these two compounds is unclear, but the authors told Live Science that they may give the fungus a powerful defense against being eaten.

The ability to produce either psychedelic or toxic chemicals has evolved multiple times across fungal lineages. A process called horizontal gene transfer, which is widespread among fungi, has played a part in that process.

In horizontal gene transfer an organism passes new genetic material to another, as opposed to vertical gene transfer, in which a parent passes genetic material to offspring. It can lead to unexpected genetic combinations and, in bacteria, plays a key role in the development of antibiotic resistance.

The tiny mushrooms seem to have acquired both psychedelic and toxic compounds via horizontal gene transfer.

Some of the world's deadliest mushrooms, from the Amanita genus, stop cells from producing proteins and can cause death through liver failure. Past work has shown these mushrooms shared the ability to produce their poisonous amatoxins via horizontal gene transfer with mushrooms from the unrelated genera Galerina and Lepiota. Some mushrooms have acquired the ability to produce psilocybin via horizontal gene transfer as well.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

But Kunik and colleagues weren't looking for specific chemicals when they began hunting for Galerina mushrooms in the swamps of Florida; they just wanted to learn more about the mushrooms' chemical makeup, as not all Florida Galerina mushrooms had been characterized before.

To find them both together in one mushroom, I never expected to find that.

They collected five specimens from Galerina, a genus that contains over 300 species worldwide, many of which are poisonous. Among the samples they collected were small G. indica specimens that grew on moss-covered palm trunks. The largest mushrooms were only about 0.2 inches (0.5 centimeters) tall, with caps up to about 0.1 inches (0.25 cm) wide.

Chemical analyses revealed that the dark magic mushroom contained both psilocybin and amatoxins, including one amatoxin that had never been documented in mushrooms. The new amatoxin wasn't wholly unexpected, given that other species of Galerina produce closely related amatoxins, Kunik said.

The production of psilocybin alongside the amatoxins was more of a surprise for the research team.

"To find them both together in one mushroom, I never expected to find that," study co-author Matthew E. Smith, a plant pathologist at the University of Florida, told Live Science. "We were shocked."

To understand how the tiny, deadly mushroom acquired its mind-altering, liver-poisoning abilities, the team compared the genes of G. indica with those of other psilocybin-producing mushrooms, finding the genes shared a common evolutionary origin — even though the mushrooms themselves are distantly related.

Scanning electron microscopy image of the spores from the “dark magic mushroom”.

The researchers also found G. indica’s psilocybin-producing genes are arranged in a different order than in other psilocybin-producing fungi, which suggests the gene cluster was rearranged during its evolutionary history, a clue that horizontal gene transfer happened.

G. indica seems to have acquired the ability to produce psilocybin via horizontal gene transfer from unrelated fungi about 15.5 million years ago, based on reconstructions of Galerina’s evolutionary history from DNA analysis, Smith said. However, it’s possible that psilocybin-producing genes entered the lineage through two separate horizontal gene transfer events, possibly as recently as 6 million years ago, Kunik noted. Collecting and sequencing more Galerina specimens could help untangle their evolutionary history.

The findings are surprising, said Hannah Reynolds, a fungal ecologist at Western Connecticut State University who was not involved with the new research. "What was exciting about this paper was seeing both of these [compounds] present, seeing that this gene cluster jumped in, got rearranged, maybe came in twice — it's very cool," Reynolds told Live Science.

The ability to produce two types of incapacitating chemicals could form a powerful defense against being eaten, because organisms that would normally eat them would have difficulty evolving defenses against both, Kunik speculated.

But the idea that this duo of compounds prevents the mushroom from being eaten is just a hypothesis. To buttress that idea, further research might tweak the genes of the dark magic mushroom to observe how removing one compound affects the species' role in the food web, Kunik suggested.

Tropical and subtropical mushrooms are historically understudied, so there is likely much more incredible fungal diversity right under our feet, Smith said.

Kunik et al. (2026). "The 'dark magic mushroom' co-produces amatoxins and psilocybin." Current Biology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2026.10.041

#6379. Scientists found a hidden ‘aging clock’ in human blood that can predict future diseases and early death

Scientists have figured out a new way to measure how fast your body is actually aging on the inside, rather than just counting the years you have been alive.

Two people born the same year can have bodies that age at different speeds. A routine blood draw may now be enough to tell which is which.

In a study of 18,476 people aged 1 to 96, some had blood chemistry that read older than their birth certificate. Those people went on to develop fatty liver disease, high blood pressure and diabetes more often.

More of them died over the following years, too.

The older readings lined up with everyday habits. Smokers’ blood read about 1.2 years older than nonsmokers’, and people who exercised read about half a year younger.

Linlin Cao, Kun Qian, Jun Pu and Wei Xu of Renji Hospital at Shanghai Jiao Tong University led the study, with participants from six clinical centers in China. It’s observational, so it shows patterns, not causes.

Blood plasma carries thousands of small molecules left over from the body’s chemistry. The field that measures them is called metabolomics.

The team measured 232 of these molecules, in each person, with a laser-based instrument that needs a droplet of plasma and about 30 seconds per sample.

From those, 56 molecules changed most reliably with age. Some rose steadily, such as creatinine, a waste product of muscle.

Others fell early in life and stayed low, such as a building block of collagen that was highest in childhood and dropped fast before age 20.

A set of 12 machine learning models, stacked together, used the 56 molecules to guess each person’s age. The guesses were close.

In 5,252 healthy people used for training, the guess landed within about two years on average. In 5,456 healthy people held back as a test, it landed within about 4.5 years.

The difference between that guess and a person’s real age is the number that matters. The team called it metabolomic age acceleration, and a positive value means the blood reads older than the calendar.

Everyone gave blood in 2019. The healthy participants answered a questionnaire on diet, sleep, smoking, exercise and family history, and 3,745 of them returned for a health check in 2023. Deaths were tracked through January 2025.

The team compared the quarter of healthy people with the most accelerated blood chemistry against the quarter with the slowest.

The accelerated quarter had more new cases of fatty liver disease, high blood pressure and diabetes, and the same held for coronary heart disease and stroke.

The accelerated quarter also died at a higher rate. There were 291 deaths among the 6,169 people with death records, and the accelerated quarter accounted for a larger share of them.

For predicting death, the blood clock edged out two standard yardsticks, a frailty index and the American Heart Association’s Life’s Essential 8 score. It also added information when combined with them.

People of the same age can follow different aging paths, and this is one way to see it.

Several habits lined up with the clock. Current smoking was associated with blood chemistry about 1.2 years older, secondhand smoke with about 0.6 years, shift work with about 0.9 years, and hair dye with about a year.

Sugar, fried food, processed meat and organ meat were also associated with an older reading. Exercise was associated with a reading about half a year younger, and mixed grains with about a third of a year younger.

In 1,500 people who gave blood again in 2023, the clock moved with their habits. Those who became more active or ate less fried food saw their blood chemistry read younger by two to three years.

People newly exposed to secondhand smoke, eating more preserved food, or crossing into overweight saw it read older. The authors wrote that these habit links are observational and shouldn’t be read as causes.

Other studies have tied biological aging to teenage body weight, early menopause and even the time between pregnancies. Air pollution also leaves a chemical trail in the blood.

In 7,768 people who already had a chronic disease, the age guess worked less well, so the team built a different measure.

Using the same 56 molecules, they modeled each person’s risk of death and then asked how far it sat above or below what their age would predict.

They called that age deviation. Eight molecules carried the death signal, and the strongest was 3-methylindole, made by gut microbes from the amino acid tryptophan. The collagen building block, 4-hydroxyproline, pointed the other way, toward lower risk.

Higher age deviation went with worse kidney numbers, more organ systems affected and more conditions at once. Chronic kidney disease had the largest link.

People with high blood pressure who got it under control by 2023 saw their age deviation improve more than those who didn’t.

Nearly everyone in the study was Chinese, so the clock needs testing in other populations before it travels. Most people gave blood only once, and the authors wrote that more frequent sampling and longer follow-up are needed.

The identities of some of the 56 molecules are confident matches rather than certainties.

The open question is whether changing a habit to move the clock changes what happens to a person afterward. The authors wrote that intervention studies would be needed to find this out.

The age-prediction tool, called MetS-Age, is public for researchers to run on their own data.

The full study was published in the journal Science Translational Medicine.

#6378. The 7 Best Portable Jump Starters to Bring Your Vehicle Back to Life

The days of needing jumper cables and another motorist to revive your vehicle are over.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If you’ve got a dead car battery, you’ll want the option to revive it without waiting for help. According to AAA’s most recent report, of the 27 million calls received across the country for roadside assistance, 7 million of those vehicles had battery trouble. The causes may include anything from neglecting to turn off your car’s ignition or headlights, residing in an extremely cold climate, or even a slowly deteriorating alternator.

A portable jump starter, which is a compact and powerful battery consisting of lightweight lithium-ion, is a handy device that’s faster, safer, and more convenient than jumper cables because you don’t need to find another car with a willing driver.

Like all batteries, lithium-ion cells have different power ratings and can become depleted from repeated use or by sitting idle over time. That’s why before purchasing a portable jump starter, consider these two specs: peak amperage (amps) which conveys how much power a device can deliver, and capacity (rated in milliampere-hours, mAh), indicating how long a device can hold a charge when stored and still have enough power to provide a jump. It’s also important to monitor the charge level on your portable jump starter from time to time. I do this regularly while waiting to fill my gas tank.

There are other convenience features these devices offer, like USB ports to recharge portable electronics and lights for illumination when it’s dark. Many portable jump starters have what’s called a boost button, which I recommend having, as it supplies extra momentary power for severely drained batteries. After several rounds of testing, research, and evaluation, these are the top portable jump starters to buy now.

I’ve owned close to a dozen vehicles during my 30-year-plus career writing about cars and have had plenty of dead batteries. I keep jumper cables in each of my three current vehicles, and now I also have a portable jump starter on board along with a portable tire inflator, dash cam, and Cobra RAD 700i radar detector, which I move between vehicles depending on which I decide to drive.

In short, each device in this roundup can quickly start a vehicle with a depleted battery. While testing each product, I also evaluated its peak instantaneous power measured in amps, power capacity measured in milliampere-hours, the quantity and variety of output ports to charge portable electronics, and extras such as lights and a boost button.

My recommendations are based on a product’s price, capability, and capacity to fit a wide array of vehicles and budgets. I took into account my own experiences with portable jump starters, each brand’s reputation, and for further background, I spoke with fellow car enthusiasts and auto journalists to get their impressions.

With 6,000-amp peak current to jump-start a vehicle with up to a 12.0-liter diesel engine coupled with 27,000 mAh of power capacity, the Gooloo GT6000 is the most powerful device in our guide. The GT6000 offers up to 24 months of standby time—and with that, you get incredible peace of mind. This device can sit unused for long stretches and still be counted on to crank your car when needed. If its battery is depleted, the GT6000 is ready to jump-start a vehicle after just 7 minutes of recharging and is fully recharged in 1.4 hours via its 100-watt USB-C in/out port.

This device also stands out for its generous quantity and variety of charging ports. In addition to a 100-watt USB-C in/out port, it also has a 12-volt/cigarette-lighter cord to recharge its battery in a pinch. A 15 volt/10-amp DC port can be used to power assorted car accessories like portable air pumps and power inverters. There are two USB-A power ports, one rated at 5-volts/2.4-amps and another rated for 5/9/12-volts

The GT6000 is one of only two devices here with an LCD screen, which makes checking battery level, charging output, temperature, and jump-start status quick and easy. There are 10 safety features, in addition to a built-in LED flashlight with three lighting modes (flashlight, strobe, and SOS) that provides illumination when using the device in low-light situations—important so other motorists can see you if you’re stuck on the side of the road.

While the GT6000 admittedly provides more power than most motorists will likely need, and it’s one of the heaviest of our picks, it is without question the best overall jump starter for maximum instantaneous power, long standby time, quick recharging, and plenty of output ports.

The AstroAI S8 isn’t the most powerful jump-starter recommended but it’s one of the lowest-priced and is user friendly and small enough to fit in your car’s glove box or map pocket. Although it taps out on vehicles with anything larger than a 6.0-liter gas or 3.0-liter diesel engine, it’s fine for most vehicles. I’ve kept this in one of my vehicles for months and used it several times to provide jump-starts to others without an issue.

Protection against reverse polarity, overcurrent, overvoltage, overload, overcharge, over discharge, and short circuiting are built in. The AstroAI S8 has two 5-volt/2.4-amp USB-A output ports to charge portable devices and an LED flashlight with normal, strobe, and SOS modes. It is supplied with a USB A to USB C charging cable to recharge the device.

The interface is one of the most barebones of all the units tested—just a power button and four blue LEDs to indicate power level. It does have a boost button but is the only unit of our selections without a shut-off switch; instead it automatically powers off after 30 seconds.Full AstroAI S8 Portable Jump Starter Review

This is the smallest device I tested (only slightly larger than most smartphones) and the lightest at 1.2 pounds. With 2,000 amps of peak power, the Gooloo GP2000 can jump-start vehicles with up to 8.0-liter gas or 6.0-liter diesel engines and its 12,000 mAh of capacity is impressive for its size and price.

It has 10 safety protection features including short circuit and reverse polarity, and a 400-lumen LED flashlight with normal, strobe, and SOS modes to provide light in dark environments and during emergency roadside stops. It comes with two USB-A outputs—one 5/9/12-volt and one 5-volt/2.4-amp—for charging portable devices, a USB-C charging cable, and a storage case instead of a bag like many portable jump starters at this price.

Like the AstroAI S8, it has only an on-off button. It’s easy to use and has a boost button. I recommend this option for anyone looking for a small, inexpensive, and hassle-free portable jump starter.

With an IP65 water-resistance rating and rubberized casing, the Noco Boost Plus is the portable jump starter I turn to during the rainy season in Oregon—which means anytime other than summer. I go for this one because it has spark-proof and reverse polarity protection for safe use in wet or dry conditions.

Its 1,000-amp peak power rating can start vehicles with up to 6.0-liter gas and 3.0-liter diesel engines. However, its 2,150 mAh capacity is the lowest of any product here, so it may not hold a charge as long as jump starters with a higher capacity. While this is adequate, I don’t recommend a mAh rating any lower.

The Noco GB40’s 100-lumen flashlight is dimmer than that of some of the other units in this roundup but it has the most modes, six total, which include 100-, 50-, and 10 percent; blink, SOS, and strobe. It also comes with a 1-foot USB-C charging cable, but it has only one 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-A output port for charging your portable electronics.

If you own a large vehicle, the Noco Boost X GBX155 cranks out 4,250 amps to boost batteries instantaneously for vehicles with up to 10.0-liter gas and 8.0-liter diesel engines, and has an impressive 26,750 mAh capacity, just shy of the Gooloo GT6000’s 27,000-mAh spec. A 60-watt USB-C input/output allows recharging from 0-to-100 percent capacity in 2.7 hours to ensure it’s ready to jump-start a vehicle after charging only 5 minutes (slightly faster than the Gooloo GT6000’s 7 minutes.)

I found the Noco Boost X GBX155 more complicated to operate than the other portable jump starters I tested. For example, it doesn’t have a boost button like other units but rather a manual override feature that’s used to jump start severely depleted batteries if the device detects the battery is below 3 volts. Aactivating the feature requires holding the Manual Override button for 3 seconds, which can send the GBX155’s maximum output of 4,250 amps to jump start a vehicle. This Manual Override shuts off the Noco’s automatic spark-proof and reverse-polarity protection so users need to be extra careful to attach the jumper cables correctly (red to positive, black to negative) to avoid damaging the car’s electrical system, and not touch the clamps together, which can create dangerous sparking.

The Noco is heavy, too, at 5.8 pounds. In addition to its 60-watt USB-C input/output, it has only one 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-A port whereas other lower-priced devices have at least two. But you won’t be working in the dark if you are trying to start your battery at night. This device has a 500-lumen LED flashlight that’s the brightest of the portable jump starters in our roundup. Another perk: it’s got an IP65 waterproof rating (with its input/output ports covered) that only the Gooloo GT6000 and Noco GB40 also have.

For motorheads with multiple vehicles and a garage or shop to keep them, the Clore Automotive Jump-N-Carry JNC660 is a worthy device to have on hand. Its 120-volt male receptacle connects to an extension cord so that it can be powered by a regular wall outlet and is always charged and ready.

This device uses a lead-acid battery instead of a lithium-ion one. This makes the battery replaceable, so this device is not ultimately disposable like portable jump starters with a lithium-ion battery. At 18 pounds, it’s by far the heaviest here, but also has the longest (46 inches) and thickest (2-gauge) jumper cables.

With 1,700 peak amps, it’s not the most powerful portable jump starter included but makes up for that with a 22,000 mAh rating which means its internal battery holds a charge longer. A built-in digital voltmeter shows the battery’s state of charge before and after a jump start and it has a DC outlet to power 12-volt accessories such as a tire inflator or power inverter. A notable drawback: It doesn’t have USB output ports.

For years, I relied on a Battery Tender trickle charger to supply a slow, steady current to keep the battery in my classic Chevy Impala SS charged. If you also have a vehicle that sits idle for months on end, check out the Battery Tender Charge N Start 4120. It does double duty as a trickle charger and a jump starter. However, combining two devices in one comes with compromises such as not having output ports to charge portable devices, or a boost button.

With 1,200 amps of instantaneous current, this device can jump start cars with up to 6.0-liter gas or 4.0-liter diesel engines and proficiently cranked the engine on several large and small vehicles during my testing. Its basic push-button interface makes the Charge N Start a breeze to operate. Safety features include spark-proof connection, reverse-polarity protection, and more.

This portable jump starter sends a small amount of current to traditional lead-acid as well as lithium batteries at 4 amps, and an onboard microprocessor maintains the optimal voltage to keep a battery at 100-percent capacity without overcharging during long-term storage. It also includes temperature compensation to handle a range of climates.

Something you may need to think about is its size. Its larger than other trickle chargers I’ve used, which affects placement. Ideally, a trickle charger should be located close to the battery under a car’s hood. The Charge N Start may be too large to tuck away under the closed hood of certain vehicles, but a supplied 6-foot extension cable that attaches to low-profile battery-charging clamps allows locating the device away from the engine on, say, a shelf next to a wall outlet.

The Noco AX65 is another portable jump starter we’ve tested and recommend, but we moved it out of our guide because it’s not singularly a portable jump starter like the others. This is a combo device with a portable air compressor so you can start dead batteries and inflate flat tires. What I like is that the unit doesn’t skimp on either function. The jump starter has an impressive 16,000 mAh capacity and delivers 2,000 amps of peak power while the tire inflator pumps out 67 liters per minute of airflow, which converts to 2.3 cubic feet per minute (cfm)—well above average for the portable tire inflators I’ve tested.

The portable jump starter can crank a dead battery on vehicles with gas engines as large as 8.0 liters and diesel engines up to 6.0 liters. It can be used for SUVs, boats, and snowmobiles. The not-so-good news: It’s short on output ports compared to the other portable jump starters here, and heavy at more than 9 pounds.

Portable jump starters are essentially heavy-duty batteries that come with jumper cables, controls, and accessories like lights, charging ports, and air pumps. Here’s what to look for when shopping for a portable jump starter that fits your vehicle, needs, and budget.

The two most important specs to look for when comparing portable jump starters are peak amperes (amps) and milliampere-hours (mAh). Peak amps indicate the maximum short-term current a device can deliver, while mAh measures how much electrical charge a battery can store.

Bigger is better for both specs, although mAh isn’t always as prominent or even stated with portable jump starters compared to peak amps. About 400 to 600 peak amps is sufficient to jump-start vehicles like cars and crossovers, although large SUVs, trucks, RVs, and commercial vehicles may require up to 1,500 or 2,000 amps. Some portable jump starters come with a boost button that provides roughly 10 additional amps and is helpful when reviving a very dead battery that needs an extra jolt of juice. At least 10,000 mAh of capacity means the battery in a portable jump starter will hold enough charge for 3 to 6 months to deliver 5 to 10 jump-starts.

Portable jump starters are a much safer alternative to using jumper cables to revive a dead battery because connecting jumper cables to a battery’s terminals can cause sparks that can sometimes ignite gas produced by the battery and cause an explosion. Also, if you connect the cables incorrectly, called reverse polarity, it can severely damage a car’s electrical system. Unlike jumper cables, portable jump starters have built-in protection against issues like sparking and reverse polarity in addition to other safety features and are much less risky and easier to use.

Most portable jump starters also come in handy for recharging phones, tablets, and other portable devices. USB output ports are the most common, but a few devices also provide a 12-volt outlet. While USB ports typically charge at 2.5 to 5 volts, a 12-volt outlet can not only charge a device faster but can also be used to power devices such as portable air pumps and coolers.

If you need to jump-start a vehicle at night, you’ll be thankful your portable jump starter has an LED flashlight. Typically a portable jump starter’s lighting feature also provides strobe or SOS patterns to warn other motorists on the road of your presence.

Look for a portable jump starter with a boost button to give an extra jolt of juice to a very depleted battery when the device’s standard output can’t crank the engine. This surge of power gives you about 15 to 30 seconds to start the car once the boost button is pressed.

A portable jump starter rated for 400 to 600 amps is sufficient to jump-start most passenger vehicles such as cars, crossovers, and smaller SUVs. But for larger SUVs, trucks, RVs, and commercial vehicles you want to look for a device with at least 1,500 to 2,000 amps. Weather also affects a car battery and engine, so if you live in a very cold climate more power may be needed to jump-start a low or dead battery.

Yes and no since it depends on the wide range of passenger vehicles available. A portable jump starter with a lower amp rating can jump-start smaller vehicles such as most cars, crossovers, and small SUVs. But a large SUV or truck with a large engine will require a portable jump starter with a higher amp rating.

Peak power rating (measured in amps) to ensure a portable jump starter has enough juice to crank your vehicle and capacity (measured in milliamp hours) that indicates how long it can potentially hold a charge are the most two important. Other features to look for include the number and types of output charging ports, whether it has a 12-volt output and charging input, a boost button, and a flashlight.

Definitely. Make sure to first read the owner’s manual to understand how your portable jump starter works before connecting it to a car’s battery. When using it, take off any jewelry and wear safety glasses and gloves anytime you work on a vehicle and especially around a battery. Most portable jump starters come with built-in safety features that will issue a warning if they are connected incorrectly. But it’s up to you to double-check that the jump starter’s red/positive and black/negative clamps are connected to the (typically) red positive and black negative terminals of the car battery.

Yes, a portable jump starter is a much safer alternative to using traditional jumper cables to start a vehicle with a dead battery. Connecting jumper cables to a battery’s terminals can cause sparks that have the potential to ignite gas produced by a battery which in some instances can lead to an explosion. And if you connect the cables incorrectly (in reverse polarity) it can severely damage a car’s electrical system. Unlike jumper cables, most portable jump starters come with built-in protection against issues like sparking and reverse polarity and are much less risky and easier to use. Plus, with a portable jump starter you don’t have to find another car—and a driver—like you do with jump cables. That said, I carry a set of jumper cables as a backup.

#6377. Researchers proved that tiny lab-grown brains can process information and read Braille just like a real computer

Three brain organoids read Braille letters far better than one, and the living tissue held up even when researchers damaged the data.

Could a computer one day run on living brain cells instead of silicon? A small experiment has just given that question a plain, partial answer.

Specks of human brain tissue, known as organoids, were grown in a dish in a lab. They received the shapes of Braille letters as electrical pulses, and a program read the letters back from how the cells fired.

One speck got the letter right about 61 percent of the time. Three specks, with their signals combined, got it right 83 percent of the time.

Tianyi Liu, a doctoral student at the University of Bristol, led the work with Hemma Philamore and Benjamin Ward-Cherrier in the University’s School of Engineering Mathematics and Technology.

The brain organoids are clumps of human neurons and support cells grown in a lab. Each is about a fiftieth of an inch (half a millimeter) across, the width of a mechanical pencil’s lead.

Nothing in this experiment learned anything, and that matters for how far the result reaches.

“We can take information from a real tactile sensor, turn it into a form that a living neural network can receive, and then recover meaningful information from the organoid response,” said Liu.

“That gives us a practical way to connect artificial sensors with biological neural systems, which are a very interesting possible route towards more energy-efficient computing,” she added.

The attraction is power. A human brain runs on roughly 20 watts. Silicon brain-inspired chips scaled up to the size of a cortex would need kilowatts to megawatts, the team wrote.

Other labs have already had lab-grown brain cells tell Japanese vowels apart and play a simple video game.

The brain organoids never touched a Braille dot. A touch sensor did that for them. The team mounted a sensor with a soft silicone pad, a kind of electronic skin, on a small robot arm.

The arm slid the pad across each of the 26 letters on a 3D-printed Braille board about 9 inches by 5.5 inches (23 by 14 centimeters).

A camera inside the pad recorded tiny shifts in a grid of markers as the dots pressed into the gel, the way a robot fingertip gets its sense of touch. Each letter was scanned 10 times at each of five pressing depths, 1,300 recordings in all.

The team split each recording into eight regions, one for each electrode under an organoid. The touch in each region then became a train of electric pulses.

More contact in a region meant more pulses, between four and ten, and a longer contact meant longer pulses.

The organoids live on electrode arrays run by a company called FinalSpark, and the team reached them over the internet. Kept under a steady flow of nutrient liquid, an organoid can stay electrically active for up to about 100 days.

For each letter, the team counted the cells’ firing on each of the eight electrodes for half a second after the pulses arrived. A standard pattern-sorting program then learned which firing patterns went with which letter.

With a single organoid, the program named the right letter about 61 percent of the time, where guessing would get just under 4 percent right.

Three organoids on the same array, each read on its own, scored 59, 62 and 67 percent. Combined into one pattern, the three organoids’ signals lifted the score to 83 percent.

So the gain didn’t come from one unusually good organoid. It came from combining them.

Why that works isn’t settled. The team’s best guess is that the three organoids differ slightly, so each one transforms the same input a little differently. The program then gets three partly different views of one letter.

“Different organoids may have slightly different network connections, developmental states, and ongoing activity, so the same input can produce similar but not identical responses,” Liu said.

“Combining those responses may give us complementary information that we would not get from a single organoid. At the same time, if every organoid behaves differently, it obviously makes it harder to build a predictable and standardized system,” she added.

There was an obvious objection. The pulse patterns were designed to preserve each letter’s shape, so maybe the program was reading the team’s own encoding and the tissue was only passing it along.

The team tested that directly. Given the pulse patterns with no organoid in between, the same program scored 82 percent, almost exactly the three-organoid result. On a clean signal, the organoids made almost no difference.

Then the team corrupted half of the channels in four ways: two kinds of random noise, some entries set to zero, and some values tripled. Reading straight from the pulses, the program fell to between 55 and 67 percent.

Reading from the three organoids, it held at 83 and 82 percent under random noise, and fell to 72 and 68 percent when entries went missing or were tripled.

In every one of the four tests, the organoids came out ahead. That, more than the headline score, is the contribution the team claims for the living tissue. Ward-Cherrier, the senior author, summed up the two results.

“After processing by the organoids, the tactile data still contains enough information to classify Braille letters with good accuracy. Combining outputs from several organoids also showed an improvement in performance.”

The signal in this experiment ran one way. Pulses went in, firing came out, and nothing went back to the tissue to say whether it had been right. No organoid got feedback, so none could get better with practice.

“We showed that tactile information could be encoded, processed through the organoids, and decoded, but we did not demonstrate learning or long-term changes in the organoids,” Liu said.

“We also tested one tactile task using a fixed encoding scheme and a relatively simple measure of neural activity.”

Eight electrodes per organoid is also a coarse view of a clump of cells, too coarse to see fine patterns in the firing.

And the team hasn’t measured how alike the three organoids’ responses are, which would show whether they carry different information or three copies of it. Whether a fourth organoid would help is also untested.

In 2024, a robot with a camera in its fingertip read Braille faster than a person can, and nothing here beats that.

The question this study asks is different: whether living tissue can hold a job inside a machine, and do it on a fraction of the power.

In the next experiments, the team plans to give the organoids textures and edges to feel, and then feedback on what they do with them.

Only then can anyone ask whether this tissue can learn.

The full study was published in the journal Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence.
