#6312. Where to Find 15 of Philly's Best Cheesesteaks, According to a Longtime Local

The City of Brotherly Love is filled with meat-and-cheese sandwich lovers. Philadelphia is defined by the big three: Hoagies (loaded Italian and chicken cutlet sandwiches), roast pork (with garlicky broccoli rabe and sharp provolone), and cheesesteaks.

The cheesesteak's story began in the 1930s in South Philadelphia but has become a staple at corner shops across the region, given the gourmet remix by award-winning chefs, and even inspired international outposts in Tokyo and London. I've been eating cheesesteaks since my college days, and as a Philly lifer, I've got plenty of opinions. Consider this your beginner’s guide.

Cheesesteaks are as much a part of Philly's late-night food culture as they are a daytime attraction, especially on weekends and game days. Expect long lines, limited seating, and plenty of takeout orders at popular spots, and bring cash—many old-school shops don't accept cards. Like New York's pizza slice culture, cheesesteaks are typically eaten on the go or at a nearby outdoor table. Grab extra napkins and come hungry.

A classic Philly cheesesteak starts with thinly sliced ribeye steak, melted cheese, and a long Italian roll. But no two shops make it exactly the same, and everyone has their preferences.

The meat: Some shops finely chop their ribeye on the grill, while others leave it in thin slices or longer strips. It comes down to whether you prefer a finely chopped, cheesy mixture or more substantial bites of steak.

The cheese and toppings: American, Cheez Whiz, and provolone are the traditional choices. In Philly, you'll hear people order their preferred cheese "wit" or "without," referring to fried onions. For example, "Whiz wit" means Cheez Whiz with onions, while "American without" means American cheese without onions. Other popular toppings include mushrooms, sweet or hot peppers, which you can often request on the side.

The bread: A good cheesesteak roll is typically long and Italian-style, sometimes seeded, with a lightly crunchy crust and soft interior—similar to New Orleans French bread. Some shops scoop out the excess bread to make more room for the steak and cheese, while others leave the roll intact. Either way, the bread needs to hold up to all that juicy filling.

John's Roast Pork has a signature sandwich of the same name.

John’s on East Snyder Avenue has been a neighborhood fixture for nearly a century, thanks to the Bucci family. The James Beard Award-winning shop has also been voted Best Cheesesteak multiple times, known for its hefty portions of finely chopped, crispy ribeye steak served on crusty rolls sourced from nearby Carangi’s or Sarcone’s. Choose from American, provolone, or Cooper Sharp cheese. Expect long lines, but there’s outdoor seating and a semi-enclosed dining area where you can dig in. And if you’ve got the appetite, don’t leave without trying their signature roast pork sandwich.

You’ve probably heard the hype or seen the long lines on 9th Street. Every cheesesteak at Angelo’s is made with house-baked, crusty bread and fresh, peppery ribeye steak, with your choice of Cooper Sharp or the increasingly popular long-hot-pepper-infused Cheez Whiz. Since its Italian Market debut, the Michelin Bib Gourmand-recognized shop has expanded beyond its Italian Street location, including an outpost at a food hall in Wilmington, Delaware and a ghost kitchen deeper in South Philly, with more locations on the horizon.

400 South St. Philadelphia, PA 19147431 N. 62nd St. Philadelphia, PA 19151

Philadelphia is lucky to have two Jim’s Steaks, each with its own personality. The 50-year-old Jim’s South Street is where all walks of life congregate late into the night, plotting their orders (definitely get the famous Whiz wit), scrambling for cash (there’s an ATM inside that sometimes works), and hollering at motorbikes cruising by. Inside, there’s a first-floor diner-style dining room and a second floor adorned with rare mosaics by the late legendary Philadelphia artist Isaiah Zagar, whose Philadelphia’s Magic Gardens is just a few blocks west. Over in West Philly, Jim’s West—the original location, now under different ownership—sits on a residential corner where O.G.s line up to bring cheesesteaks home to family and friends or score a $20 combo special: a beef or chicken cheesesteak, a drink, and a side of banana pudding.

517 South St. Philadelphia, PA 19147337 South St. Philadelphia, PA 19147

Recently featured in season six of Abbott Elementary, the nearly 50-year-old Ishkabibble’s has long attracted celebrities, locals, and tourists alike, often captured on camera by local photographer South Street Sam. The shop helped popularize chicken cheesesteaks and hot pepper-and-onion Spanish fries, eventually expanding to a second, larger location with additional seating just two blocks away. Chicken cheesesteaks are the name of the game here, with nearly a dozen variations, including Pizza (mozzarella and pizza sauce), South Philly (roasted peppers, spinach, and provolone), and Broccoli (melted cheese and steamed broccoli). Wash it all down with their famous Gremlin, a half-grape soda, half-lemonade concoction. Trust us.

What began as a Northeast Philly corner shop in 1949 has changed owners, locations, and names over the decades, but one thing remains: its signature thinly sliced ribeye cheesesteaks, grilled to order with or without onions on fresh Liscio's rolls delivered daily. In 2013, the renamed shop landed at Fishtown's buzzy corner of Girard and Frankford avenues, transforming into a family-friendly, '50s-style diner with an expanded menu. Alongside its classic cheesesteaks, you'll find vegetarian versions with onions and mushrooms, gluten-free roll options, crinkle-cut fries, egg creams, and sundaes.

1338 S. 10th Street Philadelphia, PA 19147

Got cheesesteak FOMO because you're vegan? Or have plant-based loved ones who want in on the Philly experience? Triangle Tavern, a neighborhood bar on East Passyunk Avenue, has you covered. Most of the menu is vegetarian or vegan, including its only cheesesteak, which was crowned Best Vegan Cheesesteak in Philly by the American Vegan Center in 2019. The winning sandwich features locally owned Blackbird Foods' seitan, fried onions, and a Carangi Bakery roll, all smothered in house-made vegan Whiz (a blend of Daiya vegan cheddar, Tofutti cream cheese, miso, nutritional yeast, and seasonings).

For decades, Robert Perry has cultivated a community of artists, musicians, creatives, and beer lovers at this two-story rock-and-roll bar known for its sticker- and graffiti-covered walls. Affectionately called TMoms by locals, Tattooed Mom welcomes meat lovers and plant-based eaters alike with a savory, gooey vegan cheesesteak. Chunks of seitan and plant-based smoked Gouda replace the traditional steak and Whiz, all tucked into a crusty roll from local bakery Merzbacher's of Germantown. Even better, you can snag one for just $7 on Meatless Mondays.

4540 Baltimore Ave. Philadelphia, PA 19143

A West Philly institution, this husband-and-wife-run Ethiopian restaurant and bar is known for its mashup of East African and Philly staples, particularly its berbere-spiced beef cheesesteaks, served since 1996. Thinly sliced beef is coated in an earthy, fiery blend of chili peppers, coriander, ginger, cardamom, nutmeg, and allspice, then tossed with onions and melted American cheese. The result is a juicy, boldly seasoned cheesesteak with a kick.

1600 W. Girard Ave. Philadelphia, PA 19130

Fairmount may not be the first neighborhood that comes to mind for a Philly cheesesteak, but it's home to an 8,500-square-foot indoor mini golf course serving pan-Asian-inspired bar food. Opened in 2021 by three longtime friends, Libertee Grounds has a playful menu to match, including an Indian-inspired Lamb Kheema cheesesteak made with a masala-rubbed lamb and ribeye blend, melted Cooper Sharp, caramelized onions, and cilantro-lime aioli on a seeded long roll. It comes with fries, but for an extra kick, add pickled Fresno peppers or miso Cooper Sharp cheese Whiz.

3101 Tasker St. Philadelphia, PA 191453401 Walnut St. Franklin's Table Food Hall, Philadelphia, PA 191042563 Trenton Ave. Philadelphia, PA 19125

What began as a food cart in 2022 has grown into multiple Philadelphia locations for Korea Taqueria, where chef-owners Alexander Sherack and Rene Lopez blend traditional Korean flavors with Mexican street food staples. Their Korean-Mexican mashups include a signature slow-burn spicy bulgogi cheesesteak featuring thinly sliced halal ribeye marinated in bulgogi sauce, melted Cooper Sharp, gochujang mayo, and scallions on a seeded Liscio's hoagie roll. Add cucumber kimchi for an extra tangy crunch.

Dalessandro's sits in Roxborough, in the city's northwest outskirts.

Husband-and-wife team Steve and Margie Kotridis have kept this Northwest Philly cheesesteak shop humming with hungry customers since taking over in 2008. Now one of three Michelin Bib Gourmand-recognized cheesesteak shops in Philadelphia, alongside Del Rossi's and Angelo's, Dalessandro's is known for its juicy, gooey, squishy sandwiches. Finely minced ribeye, melted cheese, and generously diced onions meld together inside Amoroso's hearth-baked rolls (another local favorite bakery), which soak up all that goodness. Better yet, toppings are free. Grab your cheesesteak to go and, weather permitting, enjoy it beneath the trees at the park across the street.

3653 Germantown Ave.Philadelphia, PA 19140

This North Philly cheesesteak shop is a celebrity in its own right, having appeared in Creed and Creed II and attracted famous fans like Philly's own Colman Domingo. Since 1994, crowds have lined up beneath its glowing red neon sign near the Broad and Erie transit hub for finely chopped "100% sirloin steak," served in half, whole (12-inch), or Giant (two-foot) portions. Order yours Whiz wit (ketchup is a popular addition here), grab some cheese fries, and join the regulars eating off the hoods of their cars. Those in the know head next door to Eagle Bar for a beer before calling it a night.

3020 S. Broad St. Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19145

Heading down to the stadiums for a game? Consider Skinny Joey's your pre- or post-game cheesesteak fix. Former inmate turned podcaster turned restaurateur Joey Merlino has entered Philly's competitive cheesesteak scene, offering six beef and chicken variations that draw long lines of customers and parked cars along Broad Street on weekends. And he's not stopping there: Merlino has expanded to the Jersey Shore with a Wildwood outpost.

Competition and tradition run deep in Philly's cheesesteak scene, a challenge Nish Patel embraced when he took over Del Rossi's in 2020. He helped usher in a new wave of cheesesteak making by focusing on better ingredients and technique rather than reinventing the classic sandwich. First came a house-baked roll with a crunchy crust and pillowy-soft interior. Next, pasture-raised, hormone-free, hand-cut ribeye steak, followed by melted Cooper Sharp American cheese and onions. The upgrades paid off: Del Rossi's earned Michelin Bib Gourmand recognition in 2026.

One of Philly's newest cheesesteak sensations, Sal Burgese's Backyard Cravings began as pandemic-era home cooking for friends, family, and a few lucky guests at his South Philly rowhome. What started in his backyard grew into tailgating parties and, eventually, his first brick-and-mortar shop in October 2026. Like Del Rossi's, the focus here is on quality ingredients and cooking from scratch. The $20+ cheesesteak has a generous portion of finely chopped, salt-and-pepper-seasoned beef, onions, and creamy Cooper Sharp cheese on a long, crisp, sesame-seeded roll with a soft, scooped-out center. Burgese's cheesesteaks have drawn sold-out crowds wherever he's served them, so for now, the Eagles “Kelly Green” and cream-colored corner spot sells them only on weekends.

#6311. Faye Travel Insurance: The Best New Company Out there

We may receive compensation from Faye as an advertising partner. However, this does not influence our evaluations. Our opinions are our own.

I’ve been writing about travel for nearly two decades and, in that time, I’ve watched the travel insurance industry change at roughly the speed of a glacier. For years, the pitch was always the same: buy a policy, hope you never need it, and if something goes wrong, prepare for a paperwork marathon and a check that arrives somewhere between “eventually” and “you’ve forgotten you ever filed.”

I’ve personally been on the receiving end of that runaround. So have most travelers I know. It’s just something you kind of deal with. After all, you should never, ever, ever, EVER travel without travel insurance. You don’t want to end up needing a GoFundMe to pay your bills and get home if something goes wrong. (You can’t predict the future!)

Now, there’s a lot of players in this space but one I want to highlight today is Faye Travel Insurance, which I think is doing something unique.

Faye is a digital-first travel insurance company that launched coverage in the U.S. in 2022 so it’s pretty new to the US market when you consider that brands like World Nomads or Allianz have been offering coverage for over twenty years.

Faye is based on a pretty simple idea: travel insurance shouldn’t just sit there waiting for things to go wrong. It should actively help things go right.

That means whole-trip protection (your trip, your health, your stuff, even your pet), an app that’s actually useful while you’re traveling, 24/7 access to real human customer support, claims that get processed in days instead of months, and a digital wallet that pays you back almost instantly instead of waiting around for a check in the mail, which some companies still do in this day and age.

Faye has one plan for domestic and international trips, which makes things super easy. A lot of travel insurance companies have lots of plans and you end up squinting at coverage tables trying to figure out which one isn’t going to leave you stranded and has the coverage minimums you need. Faye built a single comprehensive plan that covers most of what travelers actually need:

These limits are pretty standard, especially on the medical coverage. If you want to add stuff on, they have a few optional addons that I think are really good and unique:

The CFAR insurance is really useful and I’ve rarely seen a company allow you to add it on to a policy. Usually, it’s already incorporated at a higher fee but this creates an affordable add on. I also love the pet care add on as more and more people travel with their pets.

Here’s where Faye really separates itself. Faye built something completely different! Here’s what you can actually do inside the Faye app:

Buy a policy in as little as 60 seconds – Plug in your trip details, get a quote, get covered.

Get real-time flight tracking and alerts – You’ll get delay info, gate changes, or baggage carousel numbers when you land! A lot of apps do this but this is a nice add on.

Telemedicine – Faye gives you access to a network of 20,000 telemedicine doctors in 21 languages when you travel abroad. If you wake up with food poisoning in a town where you don’t speak the language and don’t trust the local hospital reviews, you can talk to a doctor from your hotel bed. (As someone who has had to find doctors in other countries, this feature is amazing!)

Find a doctor, pharmacy, ER, or ATM nearby – The app does the work of figuring out where to go when you’re disoriented and just need to find the closest open pharmacy at 11 p.m. in a city you arrived in five hours ago. (As someone who has had to do this in other countries, this feature is amazing!)

Get free airport lounge access – If your flight is delayed by three hours or more, Faye gets you into a lounge – and who wouldn’t want lounge access with free food and drinks for a long delay?

Store your documents in Safekeeping – Securely u     pload your passport, visa, insurance card, vaccination records. If anything gets lost or stolen, you’ve got digital copies.

Check destination essentials before you go – Visa requirements, plug adapter types, local emergency numbers, weather, currency conversion, even local apps worth downloading.

Chat with real humans, 24/7 – Actual customer experience specialists, available every day of the year, including weekends and holidays.

Buy an eSIM – The app also enables you to purchase an eSIM meaning you can avoid pesky physical SIM swaps and get connected to the internet right when you land.

Here’s how Faye works: something bad happens. You open the app. You file a claim in a few minutes by uploading photos of your receipts. If it’s a qualifying issue like a baggage delay or flight delay, you may get reimbursed almost instantly. Funds go straight into Faye Wallet, a digital payment card built into the app that connects to Apple Pay or Google Pay. You tap and pay, right then and there, for whatever you actually need: a new outfit, toiletries, dinner, a hotel.

For larger or more complex claims, Faye aims to resolve them within 48 hours. of receiving the necessary documentation.

If you don’t want to use the digital wallet, you can transfer the funds to your bank account or get a paper check.

Pricing depends on your trip cost, destination, length, state of residence and age (same as every insurance product) but prices start at around $5.16 a day for international trips, which is a lot more competitive than other companies out there.

I’ve used a lot of travel insurance companies over the years. Most of them are fine. A few are awful. Faye is the first one that feels like it was designed by people who actually understand modern travel and get that we’re booking trips on our phones, communicating in apps, and expecting the same digital convenience from insurance that we get from everything else.

The combination of whole-trip protection, the app, Faye Wallet, real human support, and fast claims has genuinely changed how I think about this category. Travel insurance used to be the thing I bought and forgot.

If you’re heading out on a trip soon, check it out at withfaye.com, get a quote, and see for yourself.

#6310. 12 Airline Booking Traps That Could Cost You Money in 2026

Airline websites are not necessarily badly designed, even though they often feel that way. In many cases, the booking process is doing exactly what it was designed to do: get you focused on the lowest advertised fare before revealing the cost of everything else.

You start with a flight that looks like it costs $400. By the time you add a carry-on bag, choose a seat, and work through the final checkout screens, the total is suddenly $650.

After more than 18 years of travel to over 130 countries, we still catch ourselves slowing down to double-check airline bookings. The difference now is that we know where the expensive mistakes are usually hiding. We also use flight-search and tracking tools to compare routes and monitor changes. See our guide to the best travel apps for 2026.

The lowest price on the first screen is rarely enough information to tell you which flight is actually cheapest. You need to compare the complete journey, including baggage, seats, fare restrictions, connections, operating airlines, and the risk involved if something goes wrong.

To avoid costly airline booking mistakes, compare the total price of the journey rather than the advertised base fare. Check the conditions of the exact fare, baggage allowances, operating airline, cabin on every segment, connection times, and whether the flights are issued on one protected ticket.Before paying, compare the flight as a round trip, two one-way tickets, and a multi-city itinerary. Before leaving home, verify your passport, visas or travel authorizations, transit requirements, check-in deadline, and gate-closing time.

These airline booking traps—also common flight-booking mistakes—can turn an apparently cheap ticket into the most expensive option.

One of the first mistakes travellers make is comparing flights by airline logo.

You see the airline you normally use, remember the points sitting in your account, and stop comparing. But loyalty should not convince you to pay hundreds of dollars more for a worse schedule, a more restrictive ticket, or a fare that excludes everything you need.

Airline points can still be valuable, especially when you are close to earning useful status or have benefits such as complimentary baggage. But loyalty should be one part of the calculation, not the starting point.

The days of automatically paying more because “this is our airline” are over. Loyalty should follow value, not the other way around.

Basic Economy can be a perfectly reasonable fare. The trap is buying it without understanding what has been removed.

It may work well when you are taking a short flight, travelling with only a small personal item, do not care where you sit, and are confident your plans will not change.

The problem is that airline websites normally display the lowest available fare first. Once you are in booking mode, it is easy to select that number and move forward without reading the restrictions.

You may save $40 on the ticket and then spend $85 adding the carry-on bag you needed from the beginning.

Before booking Basic Economy, price the next fare category. A Standard Economy ticket may cost more initially but include a carry-on bag, checked luggage, seat selection, or greater flexibility.

Also consider whether seat selection genuinely matters. Travellers with children, mobility considerations, medical needs, or a strong need for an aisle or window seat should include that cost when comparing fares.

Do not buy the lowest number. Buy the fare that includes what you actually need.

Airlines do not necessarily sell every Economy Class seat at the same price. Seats are divided into fare classes or pricing tiers, often called fare buckets.

When the cheapest tier sells out, the price can jump even when the aircraft still has many empty seats.

That is one reason a flight might appear at $480 in the morning and $620 later that day. It does not always mean the plane suddenly filled up. It may mean the least expensive fare class is no longer available.

When you see a noticeable price increase, do not assume you must either pay it immediately or lose the trip.

A competitor may now be cheaper. In other cases, the next fare level may include baggage, seat selection, or flexibility that makes it better value than the stripped-down ticket you were originally considering. A fare jump is a signal to widen the search, not automatically accept the new price.

For the tools we use to compare dates, airports, and fare changes, see our guide to the best travel apps for finding flights.

The standard airline search box encourages travellers to enter a departure city, destination, outbound date, and return date.

That does not mean a traditional round trip is always the cheapest or most efficient way to book.

Before purchasing an expensive international itinerary, compare it three ways:

An open-jaw ticket means flying into one city and returning home from another.

For example, if you are travelling through Europe, you might fly into Paris and return from Rome. Even if the airfare is similar to a return ticket from Paris, you could avoid paying for a train or flight back to your starting point. You may also save a hotel night and an entire day of backtracking.

Different airlines can also be used in each direction. One carrier may offer the best outbound flight, while another has a much better return schedule.

When comparing separate tickets, check baggage fees, fare restrictions, connection risks, and cancellation policies. The goal is not to find the cleverest itinerary. It is to determine which option gives you the best total trip.

With a codeshare flight, the airline selling the ticket may not be the airline flying the plane.

You might purchase the journey through one airline’s website and then arrive at the airport to discover that a partner carrier operates the flight.

Before buying, look for the words “operated by” in the flight details.

Then check the itinerary on both airline websites. Confirm the aircraft, seat map, baggage allowance, terminal, and check-in instructions.

After booking, make sure you have the operating carrier’s reservation number. The confirmation number issued by the airline selling the ticket may not work on the partner airline’s website.

Codeshares are not automatically bad. They can provide more destinations and useful connections. The problem is that they create a handoff between companies, and that handoff can become confusing when you need assistance.

As we have learned, one of the most expensive sentences in travel can be: “You need to contact the other airline.”

Mixed-cabin fares are one of the easiest airline traps to miss.

The search result may display a large Premium Economy or Business Class label, making it appear that the entire journey is in the upgraded cabin.

Then you expand the flight details and discover that the 40-minute connection is in Premium Economy while the eight-hour overnight flight is in regular Economy.

We have come close to booking this type of itinerary several times.

Before paying, check the cabin listed beside every individual segment. Make sure the premium seat is on the flight where you will actually benefit from it.

Do not assume one premium segment provides premium benefits throughout the trip.

Screenshot the cabin shown for each flight and confirm that it appears correctly in the final reservation. A mixed-cabin fare is only a deal when the upgraded cabin is on the part of the journey that matters.

There is rarely one simple baggage policy that applies to every passenger flying with an airline.

Do not check only the airline’s general baggage page. Open the conditions attached to the specific fare and route you are considering.

This is especially important when connecting from a transatlantic flight to a smaller airline or low-cost carrier within Europe. A bag accepted on the first flight may be too large, too heavy, or not included on the next one.

A bag fitting inside the overhead compartment does not automatically mean it meets the airline’s rules. Wheels, handles, and outside pockets are normally included when the bag is measured.

Price your luggage before buying the flight. A ticket that appears $30 cheaper can quickly become more expensive once the necessary baggage is added.

Paying for bags online in advance is also frequently less expensive than waiting until the airport, although the difference varies by airline.

Finally, weigh your suitcase at home using a real scale. Picking it up and declaring that it “feels about 20 kilos” is not a reliable baggage strategy.

Once you know your allowance, follow our two-minute checked-bag routine before handing your suitcase over at the airport.

A self-transfer may be the most expensive mistake in this guide.

Some search and booking sites combine two separate tickets and display them as one journey. Look for warnings such as:

The critical detail is that the airlines may not recognize the flights as one protected itinerary.

If the first flight is delayed and you miss the second one, the second airline may consider you a no-show. You could lose the remaining flights on that reservation and be forced to purchase a new last-minute ticket.

The first airline may not be responsible for helping because it transported you to the destination shown on its ticket.

Leaving the international transit area can also trigger entry or transit requirements that would not apply during a normal airside connection.

Self-transfers can work when you have a long buffer, carry-on luggage, an airport you understand, and enough flexibility to absorb a disruption.

We would not use one when connecting to a cruise, wedding, organized tour, or once-daily long-haul flight.

Always compare the self-transfer price with a protected itinerary. The higher fare may not simply be buying convenience. It may be buying the airline’s responsibility to get you to your final destination.

Airlines can sell a connection that technically meets the airport’s minimum requirements.

That does not necessarily mean it is comfortable, sensible, or suitable for you.

A 45-minute connection at a large international airport might involve:

If a connection makes you nervous while sitting at home, it will not feel better when you are waiting for the aircraft door to open. Choose connection time based on the consequences of missing the next flight.

A long layover can be inconvenient. A missed connection can cost a full day or derail the entire trip.

We use third-party flight sites for research. They are useful for comparing airlines, dates, and routing options.

Buying through one is a separate decision.

A third-party fare may be genuinely cheaper, but make sure you are comparing the same product. It could involve:

The biggest issue normally appears when the schedule changes or the flight is cancelled.

The airline may tell you to contact the company that issued the ticket. The booking company may then tell you that only the airline can resolve the flight.

Before buying, find the itinerary through the search site and compare it directly with the airline. When the price difference is small, booking with the airline may be worth it for easier communication during disruptions.

Also check the payment currency. Some booking sites offer to convert the total into your home currency. This feels convenient but may include a less favourable exchange rate.

When your credit card does not charge a foreign transaction fee, paying in the original currency may be less expensive. Compare the final converted amount and check your card’s fees rather than choosing a currency based on familiarity.

Some of the most expensive travel problems do not happen during booking. They happen at the airport after your hotel, tour, rental car, or cruise has already been paid for.

A valid passport may not be enough to enter your destination or transit through a connecting country.

Depending on your nationality, route, and destination, you may need:

A passport can be valid on your departure date and still fail to meet the destination’s entry requirements. Complicated connections are also a good reason to review our international travel safety tips before departure.

Names matter too. The name on your airline ticket should match your passport and any visa or travel authorization. Do not assume that a nickname or commonly used name will be accepted.

Before an international trip, take five minutes to verify:

Canadian travellers should verify current destination-specific requirements using official government travel advisories and the relevant embassy or immigration authority, since entry and transit rules can change.

Five minutes at home can save the entire trip at the airport. For our complete pre-departure routine, read our travel safety checklist for 2026.

Departure time is when the aircraft is scheduled to leave. It is not the time you should arrive at the gate.

Boarding begins earlier, and the gate closes before departure. The exact cutoff depends on the airport, airline, route, and destination.

Once the gate is closed, seeing the aircraft through the terminal window will not save your seat.

If you miss the flight, the cost may extend far beyond a replacement ticket. You might also lose:

Build your airport schedule backward from the airline’s check-in, baggage-drop, boarding, and gate-closing deadlines.

Check current security conditions using the airport’s official app or website, but do not treat an estimated wait time as a guarantee. Add time for airport parking, shuttle transportation, baggage drop, security, passport control, terminal changes, and finding the gate.

It is better to have extra time near the gate than to spend the start of your trip running through an airport while your name is being called over the loudspeaker. Arriving early does not help much if your carry-on slows you down at screening. Read our airport security tips and common mistakes before packing.

Before confirming a flight, we recommend checking the entire itinerary one final time.

The best defence against airline booking traps is not a secret search setting or complicated flight hack. It is slowing down long enough to compare the complete journey.

All 12 of these traps work best when travellers are rushing.

We see a low fare, get excited about the trip, and want to finish before the number changes. The booking process then reveals the bags, seats, restrictions, connections, and other costs after we have already become emotionally committed to the flight.

The cheapest flight is not necessarily the one with the lowest number on the first screen. It is the flight that gets you to your destination without surprise charges, unrealistic connections, or an expensive problem at the airport.

After more than 18 years of travelling, experience has not made us immune to booking mistakes. It has simply taught us when to stop, reopen the details, and check everything one more time.

Take five minutes before pressing confirm. Those five minutes could save hundreds of dollars—or save the entire trip.

#6309. I Visited China as an American Without a Visa—Here’s How You Can Do It Too

Last month, I visited China as an American—without going through a multi-week visa application process. This is thanks to a recent policy introduced in 2024 that allows certain travelers to visit China for a maximum of 10 days while transiting between one country and another. Though the rule can feel intimidating in theory, it’s relatively straightforward in practice as long as you prepare accordingly.

Officially called the “240-Hour Visa-Free Transit Policy," the program is part of China’s goal to attract more inbound international travelers, according to Mei Zhang, the founder of WildChina and a Condé Nast Traveler travel specialist. “The idea is to make visiting China an easier decision,” Zhang says. “Most people are daunted by the idea of queuing for a visa at the Chinese consulate. Removing that step makes it easier for people to come.”

And even though the policy is designed for transiting between countries, 10 days is still enough time for a meaningful visit. “Beyond the quick business visits or short stopovers people may associate with China, ten days gives travelers time to explore several destinations, experience the culture, and develop a deeper appreciation for the country,” says Catherine Heald, CNT specialist and founder of Remote Lands, which specializes in travel to Asia.

However, because the program is relatively new, not all airline or airport staff are familiar with it—which almost resulted in me being denied boarding. To help you avoid ending up in a similar situation, here’s what travelers should know before booking your flight to China, so you too can see the Forbidden City in Beijing, the futuristic skyline glowing along the Bund in Shanghai, the terracotta warriors in Xi'an, and the mountainous megacity of Chongqing.

Officially called the “240-Hour Visa-Free Transit Policy,” this new rule was first introduced by China’s National Immigration Administration in December 2024. It permits a traveler to visit China without obtaining a visa ahead of time as long as the total length of their stay in the country does not exceed 240 hours. “It’s a great policy that has driven the growth of international travelers to China,” says Zhang, “but you do need to read the fine print before using it.”

The fine print: First of all, the operative word is transit. You have to enter China from one country, then leave it for another, different country. For example, flying from the US to China, then from China to Japan is allowed. However, going from the US to China, then back to the US, is not. Hong Kong, Macao, and Taiwan count as separate destinations for this policy, so a trip that goes from Hong Kong to mainland China to Taiwan would qualify for a visa-free transit in China that does not last longer than 10 days.

Second: Only holders of passports from 57 countries, including the United States, can take advantage of this policy. See the full list here. And third: You have to enter and exit via designated ports. The full list is here, and it conveniently includes the cities you might visit on a first-time visit to China, like Beijing, Shanghai, and Chengdu. If you want to travel beyond the areas permitted by the transit policy, you’ll have to apply for a Chinese visa.

“Remember that you can enter and leave through the same eligible Chinese city or choose different eligible cities,” says Heald of Remote Lands. So you could come to China through Shanghai, spend three days there, then take the high-speed train to Beijing, stay for another three days, then depart for a third destination like nearby South Korea to make the most out of your trip.

The Forbidden City was the Chinese imperial palace from the Ming dynasty to the end of the Qing dynasty (1420-1912).

To try the transit policy for myself, I kept my first-ever trip to China simple. I arrived in Shanghai on September 30 and departed on October 5, entering and exiting through the same qualifying port, Shanghai Pudong International Airport (PVG). I stayed in the country for a total of five nights, well under the 240-hour limit. (For what it’s worth, I stayed at the good-looking PuLi Shanghai, the very cool Upper House Shanghai, and the historically rich Capella Shanghai, Jian Ye Li, to explore different parts of the city.)

I’m an American citizen, so my US passport made me eligible for the transit policy. As for my routing, I departed from Paris, where I live, on a direct flight to Shanghai; from there I flew onward to Manila. The logic is that this made my visit to China count as a long layover since my final destination was actually the Philippines.

As you prepare your itinerary, check—and double check—that your passport, routing, entry and departure ports in China, and destinations within China all qualify under the 240-hour visa-free transit policy before you make your bookings. The list of qualifying passports and entry-exit ports in China can be found here.

Once you have all your confirmation info, it’s a good idea to get organized and put together a folder with all your bookings as proof of your plans to stay no more than 10 days in China. “Carry printed copies of your confirmed onward tickets, hotel reservations, and itinerary,” Heald says. She also recommends calling your airline before departure and confirming your transit eligibility with them. You might even print the official page describing the policy (again, here!) so you can present it to anyone you encounter, like a check-in agent, who might be unfamiliar with the relatively new 10-day rule.

Consider this your heads up, says Zhang: “It’s a great policy but sometimes the implementation on the ground can be uneven.” For an added layer of security, consider booking your travel to China with local tour operators or travel specialists like WildChina or Remote Lands. They can design a trip that will definitely qualify for the transit policy, and can help you out in case you run into issues while you’re traveling.

Well, I did none of the above. I arrived at Paris-Charles de Gaulle for my flight to Shanghai without any printed confirmations of my onward ticket to Manila, my three hotel stays, or the official policy from the Chinese National Immigration Administration’s official website.

The Air France check-in agent asked me to present my Chinese visa, which, of course, I did not have. I tried to explain in French that I could go to China through this new policy, but the agent insisted, “Non, c’est pas possible.” Foolishly, I plugged “10-day visa-free transit China” into Google on my phone and presented the results to him. He sighed, switched to English, and said, “That is not official. That is AI Overview.”

I asked if there was anyone at Air France I could talk to, and the agent shook his head. Maybe he softened when he saw the panic creep across my face because he then phoned a colleague, an Air France agent who was Chinese. The other agent explained that I was correct, there is indeed a new 10-day transit policy, and all I had to do was present my onward ticket to the Philippines, which I did have saved as a screenshot on my phone.

May my failure to properly prepare be your reminder to print out everything, including your flight and accommodation info, as well as the official visa-free transit policy. If there was ever a time to be a type-A traveler, it’s this.

Once in China, the process becomes much smoother. All international travelers are required to fill out a digital arrival form, whether they have a visa or not. The form asks if you have a visa for China and, when you select no, offers a drop-down menu where you can declare that you are visiting through the 240-hour visa-free transit policy. Once that’s done, the form gives you a QR code that confirms you’ve completed the form; screenshot this code, just in case. Then go through the immigration line, approach the immigration officer, and present whatever is asked of you, like that QR code or your onward ticket, when prompted. That’s it!

For my journey, I got to Pudong Airport in Shanghai, logged onto the airport Wi-Fi, completed the form, and went into the immigration line. They didn’t ask for the QR code but they did ask for my ticket to Manila. Once everything looked good to them, they stamped my passport with a transit visa—a little sticker that declared my date of entry into China and when they expected me to leave. I was cleared to go, and I stepped into the duty-free shopping area, located right before baggage claim, feeling giddy and satisfied that it all worked out.

Zhang says working with a travel company could help relieve some of the stress on the arrival side too: “WildChina normally would book a VIP airport pickup if any of our travelers are using the 10-day transit visa. This way, an airport concierge would meet the guests at the gate and walk them through the visa step-by-step. This eases the stress of facing an unfamiliar bureaucratic process.”

One of the things that greatly intimidated me about visiting China was how different the tech is. There’s no Uber or Google Maps, which has been very helpful for me on my solo travels in new-to-me countries. The very fine teams at PuLi Shanghai and Upper House Shanghai helped me get set up with the right apps, and I was zipping around the city in no time. (For a map app, Apple Maps worked like a charm, to my surprise.) Here are tips for what Chinese apps to download before traveling.

First, set up Alipay, which is a do-it-all app and a total lifeline in China. You can link an international bank card and use it for all payments everywhere you go; call a DiDi car (China’s equivalent of Uber or Lyft), use its translation tool, and more. “Alipay is part of everyday life here,” Zhang says. “At most restaurants, you can scan the QR code on your table with Alipay, choose your dishes—already translated on the interface—and pay through the app.” Be sure to set it up and link your bank account or card before you arrive in China; some verification steps require authorization via your phone number, which you may not have access to while in the country.

Second, everyone in China is on WeChat, so you’d do well to download that too; it’s how I communicated with the guest experiences team at Capella Shanghai, Jian Ye Li, who took me on cultural tours in the hotel’s neighborhood. Think of it as Chinese WhatsApp.

And to stay connected online, Heald suggests checking if your existing carrier offers roaming in mainland China (helpful for any verification texts you may need to receive). Otherwise, get a compatible travel eSIM that explicitly covers it. A home carrier or a travel eSIM will allow you to connect to sites like Google Workplace and apps like Instagram that you would not be able to normally access through the internet while in China. For my phone, Airalo, a travel eSIM, and Free, my French home carrier, worked perfectly.

“If you'll be using a laptop or tablet on Wi-Fi and need access to services such as Google, WhatsApp, or Instagram, install a VPN and arrange any paid subscription before you leave,” Zhang says. “Downloading and setting it up can be much trickier once you're in China.” I, for one, used Astrill VPN to stay connected on my laptop to sites like Gmail and YouTube.

And finally, both Zhang and Heald recommend keeping an open mind. “China can feel very different from what you know,” Heald says. “Give yourself the chance to observe, ask questions and learn, rather than expecting everything to feel familiar.” Zhang adds, “That's part of getting to know a place. Don’t be afraid to ask for help or start a conversation, even if you only have a few words in common. You'll often find people are curious about you too, and pleased that you've come to see where they live.”

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6308. Brisbane Gets Its Moment in the Sun

Late one afternoon last November, Ty Simon works the room at Golden Avenue. He laughs with a pair of men in suits, tops off the glasses for a table of women in flower-patterned dresses, squeezes shoulders, and nods and smiles his way across the rest of the floor. Waiters ferry wine and coffee and platters of hummus and salads between the kitchen and the split-level dining space. Sheets of bright Queensland sun pour in through the open walls. It's Tuesday, it's lunch, and the place is full, unrushed, and lovely; it feels good to be here. Golden Avenue opened in the middle of last year as the ninth restaurant from Simon and his wife, Milan-born Biànca Marchi-Simon, through their Anyday hospitality group, which started with the Asian-inflected Longtime and went on to include Agnes, a dimly lit open-flame spot that won Australia's Restaurant of the Year in 2023. When Simon returns to our table, I remark on the hospitality that I've just seen. “Here we take a community approach,” he says. “My goal has always been to make sure that the people who like us, love us.”

The community approach may be the key to his city's success. Brisbane—Australia's perpetually distant-third city—has long been reduced by the Aussies to a “big country town.” (Their words—not mine!) Though a good-natured and happy place, it lacked the natural beauty and trendsetting of Sydney and the cultish urban creativity of Melbourne. For decades Brisbane seemed to succumb to the belief that it could never compete. It lacked personality in its Central Business District (CBD) and had pretty much no public transport. Even geography worked against it: In a state prized for its coastline, Brisbane is nearly 50 miles from a surf beach. Locals would often zip overseas or migrate south, perhaps on the assumption that their ambition could never be realized at home. The big country town endured.

The astounding Kith and Kin, from Queensland artist Archie Moore, which won the Golden Lion at Venice’s 60th biennale, on display at GOMA

Then a shift began. The city council embarked on an ambitious rebranding in 2010 to position Brisbane as globally connected and dynamic, giving it the nickname of New World City (“It was about shedding the idea of being the poor cousin,” Simon says). The magnificent Gallery of Modern Art (GOMA) had opened just a few years before, attracting world-class works from the Pacific and beyond. The council leveraged the city's billion-dollar location, just north of the booming Gold Coast, with its high-rises and killer beaches, and south of the covetable Sunshine Coast, with the Great Barrier Reef just off its shores. Millions traveled in from all over each year for what lay on either side of Brisbane, so why not make the city bait for some of their money and time? Many Brisbanites, Simon included, began to grow this place together, creating a city that reflected their own ambitions—and themselves. In the 2010s the city developed sharply designed precincts filled with glamour shopping and higher-level dining, all under year-round sunshine and with Brisbane's noticeable good cheer and friendliness. In 2021 the IOC announced that Brisbane would host the summer Olympics in 2032, following Los Angeles.

And right around that same time, COVID hit. While the rest of Australia struggled with lockdown and tight regulations that dragged on, Queensland fared generally well, with looser rules and relatively low numbers of cases after the initial shutdowns. “We had Melburnians coming into Brisbane just to feel normal again,” says entrepreneur and developer Catherine Malouf.

Malouf may be the most recognizable face of Brisbane's new chapter. Her family is one of the key forces behind the James Street precinct, a fig-tree-studded melange of open-air coffee houses, Champagne bars, and high-end restaurants strung together with designer shops selling top local labels. “I wanted to create somewhere where we could have a good lunch, a glass of wine, and go shopping in a place that felt like the best of Australia,” she says as we eat grilled chicken and salads at her Hellenika restaurant. Stylish and elegant, Malouf exudes the kind of sophistication you may more often associate with the places she formerly called home, like Italy and California, but her good nature and easy friendliness is all Brisbane. In a sense she personifies the version of Brisbane she is invested in creating: global and chic but anchored in hometown charm. “It took me 20 years to come back and realize that this is the place I want to live in, and a lot of people have realized that too,” she says. “It is comfortable. It is easy.”

The precinct's architecture is heavy, concrete, and borderline Brutalist, but not at all ugly. It creates an aura of strength and permanence that's almost symbolic for the next chapter of a city whose heritage architecture was mostly knocked down and whose locals have often fled elsewhere for opportunity. And amid it all is the anchor of the precinct, The Calile, an urban resort hotel whose execution feels Aussie but whose ambition and hospitality would work in any major global city. Its opening—along with its smartly designed rooms and mezzanine-level pool, bars, and restaurants that spill over into the general precinct sidewalks—catapulted the James Street precinct onto the radars of international travelers. “We are very much an Aussie hotel, but we are increasingly hosting people from around the world,” Malouf says.

Designer Heidi Middleton inside her atelier, Artclub

The James Street precinct serves as a gateway to Australia. The stores here, high-end and, for the most part, independent, are nearly all Australian brands such as P. Johnson, St. Agni, and Brisbane's own Gail Sorronda. A centerpiece is Artclub, from fashion designer Heidi Middleton, which launched here last year. Like many of her fellow Brisbanites, Middleton left to start and grow a business whose ambitions, she felt, would never flourish in Brisbane. After spending decades in Europe and selling her globally renowned Sass & Bide, she alleviated her homesickness and moved back. Artclub is a sustainably minded fashion brand that focuses on small production and renewable materials. Middleton remarks that the key to the precinct's success is the curation: high-end and never high street. “They have created a genre that is all their own,” she says.

Brisbane is called the River City for the coffee-hued eponymous waterway that snakes through it. Like the James Street precinct, the river, too, has been a focus for a lot of redevelopment. The work here—walkways, bridges, cycling and jogging lanes, dining districts, and green spaces—has pulled the city together and been a catalyst for a revamped relationship between people and place. On the banks near the James Street precinct, where a once industrial wasteland lay abandoned and uninspired, now sits the reimagined Howard Smith Wharves, alive with breweries, green parks, and restaurants. It's located on the Brisbane Riverwalk, a network of overwater walkways that are dotted with bright red royal poinciana flame trees, which didn't exist 10 years ago. Along the walk sits Stanley, an excellent Chinese spot that conjures a Hong Kong evening parlor and was opened by Louis Tikaram, who made a name on the global culinary stage as executive chef of EP & LP in West Hollywood. A 15-minute stroll away is Supernormal, the only sister restaurant to the hit Melbourne joint of the same name, whose 2024 opening unofficially announced Brisbane as a serious foodie city.

A signature steamed dumpling basket from Stanley

Four new pedestrian bridges have opened to decrease car traffic, promote sustainable living, and solve some of the city's connectivity issues. The latest, Kangaroo Point Bridge, connects the suburb of Kangaroo Point to the CBD, and it's bookended with coffee bars and has green spaces so that pedestrians can relax while looking out over the water. Zigzagging underneath them all is the beloved CityCat ferry, which zips from bank to bank, chartering passengers throughout town and beyond. Stops include the wonderful South Bank cultural district, where you'll find GOMA and the Queensland Art Gallery (QAG). It chugs its way to West End, Brisbane's perennial counterculture neighborhood, which has a funky retro cinema, indie shops selling Japanese crafts and fashion, and solid food.

Take the ferry north and you'll arrive at Brisbane Powerhouse. A hulking industrial building that powered the city starting in the 1920s, it was reborn in 2000 as the city's contemporary art center, complete with sprawling grounds, rooftop areas, bars, restaurants, and untouched industrial spaces that can host interactive exhibitions. It's raw and cool, and its scale is enormous. When I meet Louise Bezzina there, she is in her second week as the Powerhouse's artistic director and CEO. Kind and unassuming, she is the type of person you might casually meet at a mutual friend's birthday dinner and, 15 minutes into the conversation, realize you are sitting next to someone brilliant. “As Australia develops it allows for more cities to grow—it is not just Sydney and Melbourne,” she says. “Brisbane has long been an untapped city of opportunity.”

She is part of the cohort of local leaders drilling into its potential. Prior to the Powerhouse, Bezzina was the creative director of Brisbane Festival, the largest international festival in Australia by attendance numbers, for which she secured the Jean Paul Gaultier show over creative capitals like Melbourne in 2024. “My edgy style suits Brisbane,” she believes. For her first project at the Powerhouse, she launched “Swingers: The Art of Minigolf,” an interactive statement on female empowerment in a male-dominated world, pegged to the origin story of the putting game, which was founded in the 19th century by Scottish women who had been banned from 18-hole golf on account of their gender; each of the nine holes here was designed by a different female-identifying artist. Bezzina has begun ideating plans to partner with Los Angeles and Pacific dance groups in the lead-up to (and handoff of) the Summer Olympic Games.

But to suggest that creativity is new to Brisbane would be misleading. Designer Lydia Pearson is a local loyalist who has long believed in the power of her hometown. “It used to be that if you wanted to be successful, you had to either leave or create it yourself,” she says. She chose the latter. In 1989 Pearson cofounded the fashion brand Easton Pearson with fellow designer Pamela Easton, which focused on circular fashion through textiles and hand embroidery. It took off, showing during Paris Fashion Week in 1999 and selling in 20 countries before the label closed in 2016. The following year the Museum of Brisbane acquired more than 3,000 pieces from the Easton Pearson archive and has put some of the items on permanent display. “The hard part was getting people to believe you could make a brand in Brisbane that wasn't simply a hibiscus-patterned dress,” Pearson says.

We meet in the leafy suburb of Red Hill, where she and her current partner, the artist Shilo Engelbrecht, work diligently to upcycle old fabrics into a new life through their label, ShiloLydia. This could mean turning an antique tablecloth into a sheer, soft dress, or reworking discarded linens into sharp shirts whose silhouettes could compete with any on a global catwalk. The work is slow, careful, and considered—a preservation effort as much as it is a creative one. The results are delicate and beautiful, a quiet and enduring counter to the louder creativity happening across the city.

Their studio sits inside a Queenslander, an old, iconic style of house that started to appear in Brisbane in the mid-1800s. The structures are wood, often colorful but always fragile, with large verandas designed to catch and route cooling breezes through the home. Queenslanders are delightful and charming, and have become recognizable to millions of viewers around the world who tune into Brisbane's most famous export, Bluey. The beloved animated show about Bluey, a blue heeler dog, who is likely known to more people around the world than her real-life fellow Brisbanite Jacob Elordi, is the creation of animator Joe Brumm. The show airs in 28 languages and more than 140 countries. For several years it was the most streamed show in the United States of any genre, and it has an empire worth $2 billion. Brisbane is a main character, and the city is unmistakable via the iconic Queenslander wood homes, the ibis birds pecking around, the sun and steep hills, the hours of imaginative outdoor play that Brumm says is modeled after his own upbringing in Queensland. Bluey resonates with parents and children of the world due to the heart and the humor at the show's core, something Brumm says defines Brisbane. “It is about the cheer that I feel when I come back,” he says. A good reminder, then, that a place's most resonant selling point is often something that can't be built.

True urban resort The Calile Hotel helped put Brisbane on the traveler map. The hotel has a phenomenal pool and fitness space; even if you're not staying here, swing by for its Lobby Bar and excellent restaurants, including Hellenika, which serves Greek favorites.

Inside a restored heritage Queenslander, the intimate Spicers Balfour Brisbane is well-located in New Farm: It's walking distance from the James Street precinct, the Howard Smith Wharves, and Brisbane Powerhouse.

The dimly lit, decidedly grown-up restaurant Agnes, which was named Australia's Best in 2023, is known for its exceptional wood-fired cooking of duck, steak, and more.

Housed inside a former church in West End, August is a nod to the reverence of Sunday lunch, with considerately prepared plates of Noosa snapper and Jerusalem artichoke risotto.

Sleek and light-flooded, the 15-month-old Middle Eastern spot Golden Avenue has great eggplant and grilled meats.

Do an outdoor table and load it up with all the dumplings and noodles you can order at superb riverside restaurant Stanley that feels like high-end Hong Kong parlor dining.

The Brisbane outpost of the hot Melbourne restaurant Supernormal has a glamorous dining room with large water-facing windows and a fun, Asian-inflected menu that leads with local produce and protein.

Located near the funky Fish Lane, Southside is the spot for dumplings and siu mai after strolling the museums of South Bank.

The French Exit, the newest venture from Ty and Biànca at Anyday, has Parisian-style interiors by star designer Tamsin Johnson and cool bars and dining rooms spread over multiple floors in a heritage building.

Brisbane's cultural hub is South Bank, with Gallery of Modern Art (GOMA) and other institutions featuring Indigenous, Australian, and Pacific Island artists. The riverfront Brisbane Powerhouse has ambitious and edgy festivals, exhibitions, and events throughout the year.

For the best Australian labels, head to the James Street precinct for objects from Dinosaur Designs; stylish dresses from St. Agni; and sustainable, one-off fashions from Heidi Middleton's atelier, Artclub. Over in Red Hill, drop into ShiloLydia as well as the other ateliers that share space in the same Queenslander. Shilo Engelbrecht also hosts collage and meditation workshops in her studio out back by appointment.

The best way to see (and travel) Brisbane is the CityCat ferry, which bounces between 22 stops along the river. But the city has made walking easier too. Stroll the overwater footpaths on the waterfront up to the gorgeous City Botanic Gardens. If you‘re keen for a longer walk after checking out the exhibitions at GOMA, find your way to West End for funky vintage shopping and phenomenal food.

There is no shortage of worthy weekend getaways from Brisbane, including the Gold Coast and Noosa on the Sunshine Coast. But drive an hour inland to the artsy, beautiful Tamborine Mountain for a lovely look at a lesser-explored side of Queensland. Stay at the chic, two-year-old Tamborine Boutique Hotel, where a pantry and bar stock local snacks. Have lunch at the petite Picnic Real Food Bar, and don't worry if it's already run out of the plump and delicious pies (everything is worth trying). Then head around the corner for local amaro tastings at Loborn. Restore yourself after mountain hikes at the floating Sol Elements spa, whose soaking baths and salt room all seem to hover over a lake.

#6307. Can You Pack Power Banks in Checked Luggage? 2026 Airline Battery Rules Travellers Need to Know

Most travellers now fly with several battery-powered items: a phone, laptop, tablet, camera, headphones, smartwatch, portable charger or vape. But packing one of them in the wrong bag can cause real problems at the airport.

In 2026, aviation safety authorities are warning travellers to pay closer attention to lithium batteries after reports that millions of batteries are still being packed incorrectly. The biggest mistake is simple: power banks, portable chargers and spare lithium batteries should not go in checked luggage.

They belong in your carry-on bag or personal item, where they can be reached quickly if they overheat, smoke or catch fire. This matters even more when your carry-on gets taken away at the gate and sent underneath the plane.

No. Power banks, portable chargers and spare lithium batteries should not be packed in checked luggage. They belong in your carry-on bag or personal item, where they can be reached quickly if they overheat.The same goes for loose camera batteries, spare laptop batteries, rechargeable battery packs, vape devices and phone battery charging cases. If your carry-on bag is taken away at the gate and checked underneath the plane, remove all power banks and spare batteries before handing it over.Phones, laptops, tablets and cameras with batteries installed are treated differently from spare batteries, but the safest habit is still to keep valuable battery-powered electronics in the cabin whenever possible. If an airline allows a device to be checked, it should be completely powered off, protected from damage and prevented from turning on accidentally.

The safest habit is simple: power banks, spare batteries and removable batteries stay with you. Valuable electronics are usually better in the cabin too.

Power banks are not allowed in checked luggage because they contain lithium batteries that can overheat if damaged, poorly packed, overcharged, exposed to heat or affected by a defect.

In rare cases, lithium batteries can enter thermal runaway. That means the battery heats faster than it can cool itself down. It may swell, smoke, burn or ignite.

If that happens in the cabin, passengers and crew can spot the problem quickly. Cabin crews are trained to respond to battery incidents. If the battery is hidden inside a suitcase in the cargo hold, it is much harder to access.

That is why this rule is not just airport red tape. A small charger in the wrong bag can become a serious safety issue.

Before you check a suitcase, look for anything with a loose, spare or removable lithium battery.

These items should stay in your carry-on or personal item:

You should also think carefully before checking valuable electronics with installed batteries, including:

Some airlines may allow certain devices with batteries installed in checked luggage if they are completely powered off and protected from damage. But for most travellers, the smarter choice is to keep electronics in the cabin.

Checked bags get dropped, delayed, searched and occasionally sent on their own little vacation. Your laptop does not need that character-building experience.

This is where the rules confuse a lot of travellers.

A spare battery is any battery that is not installed inside the device it powers. A power bank also counts because it is an external battery used to charge other devices.

A battery installed in a device is different. This includes the battery built into your phone, laptop, tablet, camera, headphones or smartwatch.

If the battery is loose, removable or used to charge something else, do not check it. The FAA’s lithium battery guidance says power banks and spare lithium batteries must travel in carry-on baggage, not checked luggage.

Gate-checking is one of the easiest ways to accidentally break the battery rule.

You may pack your power bank correctly in your carry-on at home. Then you reach the gate, the overhead bins are full and the agent tags your carry-on to go underneath the plane.

At that moment, your carry-on has become checked luggage.

The easiest system is to keep all power banks and spare batteries in one small pouch inside your personal item. If your roller bag gets gate-checked, you can remove the pouch in seconds instead of digging through your suitcase while the boarding line gives you the collective death stare.

Airlines measure lithium-ion battery size in watt-hours, written as Wh.

Most standard phone power banks are under 100 Wh and are usually allowed in carry-on baggage. Larger batteries may require airline approval, and very large batteries are generally not allowed in normal passenger baggage.

The 100 Wh rule matters most for large laptop power banks, professional camera gear, video equipment and drone batteries.

A typical 10,000 mAh power bank is often around 37 Wh. A 20,000 mAh power bank is often around 74 Wh. Larger power banks can get close to the limit, so check before you pack.

According to CATSA’s battery packing guidelines, travellers should keep batteries and electronic devices containing batteries in their carry-on baggage, avoid damaged or recalled batteries, and protect spare batteries from short-circuiting.

Look for the Wh rating printed on the back, bottom or side of the power bank. Newer batteries often show this number clearly.

If the label only shows mAh and volts, you can calculate watt-hours with this formula:

Since 1,000 mAh equals 1 Ah, a 20,000 mAh power bank is 20 Ah.

That would usually fall under the 100 Wh carry-on limit.

If the label has rubbed off and the airline cannot confirm the battery rating, the item may be refused. Do not rely on guessing at the airport.

Laptops, phones and tablets have batteries installed inside the device, so they are not treated the same way as loose spare batteries or power banks.

However, airline rules vary. If an airline allows these devices in checked luggage, they should be completely powered off, protected from damage and packed so they cannot accidentally turn on.

That means fully powered off, not sleeping, hibernating or sitting there quietly planning to wake up mid-flight.

In practice, keep phones, laptops and tablets in the cabin whenever possible. They are valuable, easy to damage and often essential if your checked bag is delayed.

No. Vapes and e-cigarettes should not be packed in checked luggage because they contain batteries. They should travel in the cabin and must not be used or charged during the flight.

Rules for vaping products also vary by destination, and some countries restrict or ban them. If an adult is legally travelling with one, it still needs to follow airline battery rules.

If you are packing for someone else, check for these before closing a checked suitcase. A vape tossed into checked luggage can create the same battery issue as other lithium-powered devices.

Smart luggage can usually be checked only if the battery can be removed.

A smart bag is luggage with built-in charging, tracking or other battery-powered features. If the bag is going into the cabin and meets carry-on size limits, it may be accepted as a carry-on. If it has to be checked, the battery must usually be removed and brought into the cabin.

If the battery cannot be removed, the airline may refuse to accept the bag as checked luggage.

Before travelling with smart luggage, find the battery compartment at home. Do not wait until the check-in counter to discover that the “removable” battery requires a tiny screwdriver, a prayer and the patience of a saint.

The drone or camera body may be allowed in checked luggage by some airlines, but spare lithium batteries should be removed and carried in the cabin.

Spare camera batteries and drone batteries should be individually protected so the terminals cannot touch metal or each other. Use the original packaging, a battery case, a protective pouch or tape over exposed terminals.

If you travel with several batteries for photography or video work, check your airline’s quantity limits before you fly. Battery rules can be stricter for professional video gear and larger drone batteries.

Loose batteries should never be thrown into a bag with coins, keys, jewellery, cables or other metal objects. Battery terminals can short-circuit if they touch metal.

This is especially important for camera batteries, drone batteries and loose rechargeable cells.

Do not travel with a battery that is swollen, cracked, leaking, unusually hot, damaged or recalled.

A swollen power bank is not “probably fine.” It is a damaged battery and should be taken to an appropriate recycling or disposal location.

Before flying with an older power bank, check the model number and look for current recall notices from the manufacturer or your government recall site. Some recalled power banks may be prohibited onboard entirely.

If a battery looks questionable, leave it at home. Replacing a charger is cheaper than dealing with a safety incident at the airport.

If a battery or device becomes hot, starts swelling, smokes, sparks or smells strange during a flight, tell the cabin crew immediately.

Do not put it in the overhead bin. Do not hide it in a bag. Do not take it to the washroom. Cabin crew are trained to respond to battery incidents, but they need to know right away.

The goal is not to handle the problem yourself. The goal is to alert the people trained to deal with it.

Before leaving for the airport, do this quick check:

This takes less than two minutes and can prevent a pulled bag, confiscated item or airport delay.

Before you check a suitcase or hand over a carry-on at the gate, make sure:

Before you check any bag, open it and look for batteries.

Power banks, portable chargers, spare batteries and removable lithium batteries stay with you in the cabin. Phones, laptops, tablets and cameras are usually safer in your carry-on. If your carry-on gets taken at the gate, remove your battery pouch before the bag goes underneath the plane.

The goal is not to stop travelling with electronics. The goal is to stop packing them on autopilot.

A two-minute battery check before every flight can save your bag, your gear and possibly your travel day.
