#6299. Best Day Trips from Toronto: Easy Escapes for 2026

Looking for the best day trips from Toronto? Whether you’re craving waterfalls, wineries, beaches, or small towns, Ontario is packed with incredible places to explore just a short drive from the city. The best day trips from Toronto include Niagara Falls, Elora, Blue Mountain, and Prince Edward County, all within 2 to 3 hours from the city.

We’ve lived in Toronto and traveled all around the province—and trust us, you don’t need to go far to find adventure. From hiking trails along the Niagara Escarpment to paddling the Grand River or sipping wine in Prince Edward County, there’s a day trip here for everyone.

Most of these destinations are within a 2-hour drive from Toronto, so you can head out in the morning and be back home in time for dinner. If you’re short on time but big on wanderlust, these are the top 25 Toronto day trips to add to your weekend plans in Ontario.

The best day trips from Toronto include Niagara Falls for first-time visitors, Hamilton for waterfalls and food, Elora for small-town charm and the gorge, Stratford for theatre, Blue Mountain for outdoor adventure, Prince Edward County for wineries and beaches, and the Toronto Islands for an easy car-free escape. Most are within 1 to 2.5 hours of the city, but places like Algonquin Park and Bruce Peninsula are better as long day trips or overnight getaways.

Hamilton is one of the best day trips from Toronto because it combines history, nature, food, art, and outdoor adventure in one easy-to-reach city.

The best day trips from Toronto include popular destinations like Niagara Falls, Hamilton, Elora, and Prince Edward County, all within 2 to 3 hours of the city.Toronto Islands and Canada’s Wonderland offer easy escapes under an hour, perfect for families and low-stress outings.Elora and Stratford are ideal for those seeking small-town charm combined with nature and culture.Longer trips such as Muskoka and Algonquin Provincial Park provide stunning wilderness experiences but require more travel time.

Best for: skyline views, beaches, biking, picnics, and car-free exploringTravel time from Toronto: 10–15 minute ferry from downtownSuggested day: Take the ferry in the morning, explore Ward’s Island or Centre Island, rent bikes, have a picnic, and return near sunset for skyline views.

The Toronto Islands are the easiest day trip from Toronto because you don’t even need to leave the city. Once you step off the ferry, it feels like a completely different world, with beaches, bike paths, picnic areas, and one of the best views of the Toronto skyline.

This is a great option if you want a low-stress day trip without a long drive. You can spend the day walking, cycling, swimming in summer, or simply relaxing by the water.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Go late afternoon if you want the best skyline photos. The view of downtown Toronto from the islands is one of the classic shots of the city.

Best for: families, thrill rides, water park fun, and summer day tripsDrive from Toronto: about 30–45 minutesSuggested day: Arrive early, hit the big roller coasters first, cool off at Splash Works in the afternoon, and stay into the evening if the park has special events.

Canada’s Wonderland is one of the easiest family day trips from Toronto. It has roller coasters, kids’ areas, live entertainment, water rides, and Splash Works, which is perfect on a hot summer day.

This is a full-day outing, especially if you are visiting with kids or trying to ride the major coasters. It’s busy in summer, but that is part of the experience.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Buy tickets online and arrive before opening if you want to make the most of the day. The biggest rides get long lines quickly.

Best for: hiking, conservation areas, mountain biking, skiing, and quick nature escapesDrive from Toronto: about 40–60 minutesSuggested day: Start with a hike at Rattlesnake Point or Kelso, have lunch in town, then add Mount Nemo or Crawford Lake if you want a second outdoor stop.

Milton is one of the best quick nature escapes from Toronto. It sits along the Niagara Escarpment and gives you access to hiking trails, lookout points, conservation areas, and outdoor activities without committing to a long drive.

Kelso Conservation Area is great year-round, with hiking and mountain biking in warm weather and skiing or snowboarding in winter. Rattlesnake Point and Mount Nemo are also excellent for escarpment views.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Milton is ideal when you want a real outdoor day but don’t want to spend half the day in the car.

Best for: waterfalls, hiking, food, art, museums, and waterfront trailsDrive from Toronto: about 1 hourSuggested day: Visit a waterfall in the morning, explore Dundurn Castle or the waterfront in the afternoon, then head to James Street North for dinner or Art Crawl if it’s the second Friday of the month.

Hamilton is one of the best day trips from Toronto because it combines nature and city energy in one easy trip. You can hike to waterfalls, visit museums, walk the waterfront, eat downtown, and still be back in Toronto by evening.

The waterfalls are the main draw, but Hamilton has become much more than an outdoor stop. James Street North, King William Street, the waterfront, and the city’s food scene make it worth a full day.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If you want the full city-and-nature experience, see our guide to the best things to do in Hamilton, Ontario.

Best for: scenic drives, hiking, fall colours, cider, and countryside escapesDrive from Toronto: about 45–60 minutesSuggested day: Visit the Cheltenham Badlands, go for a hike, stop at a cidery or café, and enjoy a relaxed countryside drive.

Caledon is a great day trip when you want fresh air, rolling hills, and a slower pace. It’s close to Toronto but feels rural, making it perfect for a scenic drive or a low-key outdoor day.

The Cheltenham Badlands are the most famous stop, but Caledon also has trails, conservation areas, farm shops, and cideries that make it easy to turn a short drive into a full afternoon.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Caledon is especially beautiful in fall. Go early if you are visiting popular spots during peak colour season.

Best for: first-time visitors, waterfalls, wineries, romance, and classic Ontario sightseeingDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 to 2 hoursSuggested day: Visit Niagara Falls in the morning, then drive 20 minutes to Niagara-on-the-Lake for wineries, heritage streets, boutique shopping, or dinner.

Niagara Falls is one of the most famous day trips from Toronto, and it still delivers every time. Start with Horseshoe Falls, then add Journey Behind the Falls, the Niagara SkyWheel, Clifton Hill, or the Hornblower boat cruise if you want the full experience.

After the falls, slow the pace down in Niagara-on-the-Lake. The town is known for wineries, pretty streets, historic buildings, theatres, and one of the most charming main streets in Ontario.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If it is your first visit, do the falls first while you still have energy, then end the day with wine country and dinner in Niagara-on-the-Lake.

Things to do in Niagara Falls Where to Stay in Niagara FallsNiagara on the Lake Day Tours Niagara Day Tours from TorontoNiagara on the Lake

Best for: small-town charm, gorge views, tubing, kayaking, boutiques, and river adventuresDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 hoursSuggested day: Walk the town in the morning, hike along the Elora Gorge, have lunch downtown, then go tubing or kayaking if you are visiting in summer.

Elora is one of Ontario’s prettiest small towns and one of the best day trips from Toronto for people who want both nature and charm. The town has boutiques, bakeries, cafés, stone buildings, and a relaxed weekend feel.

The Elora Gorge is the highlight. The cliffs rise above the Grand River, and the trails offer beautiful views. In summer, tubing and kayaking add a little adventure to the day.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Elora gets busy on summer weekends, so arrive early if you want parking, lunch, and time on the river.

Best for: theatre, food, culture, gardens, romantic day trips, and small-town charmDrive from Toronto: about 2 hoursSuggested day: Explore downtown, walk along the Avon River, have lunch, browse the shops, and see a Stratford Festival performance if one fits your schedule.

Stratford is one of the best cultural day trips from Toronto. It’s known for the Stratford Festival, but even without a show, the town is worth visiting for its riverfront, restaurants, gardens, heritage buildings, and independent shops.

This is a slower, more polished day trip. It’s ideal for couples, theatre lovers, and anyone who wants a break from the city without heading into the wilderness.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If you are seeing a show, build extra time into the day. Stratford is made for wandering before or after the theatre.

Best for: small towns, paddling, biking, river views, history, and easy food stopsDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 hoursSuggested day: Start in Paris for river views, shops, and lunch, then continue to Brantford for the Bell Homestead, Grand River trails, or a bike ride.

Paris is one of the prettiest small towns in Ontario, with the Grand River running through town, a compact downtown, cafés, bakeries, and great views from the riverfront. It’s a perfect low-key day trip when you want somewhere pretty but not overcomplicated.

Nearby Brantford adds history and trails to the day. The Bell Homestead tells the story of Alexander Graham Bell and the first long-distance telephone call, while the Grand River trails are excellent for walking, biking, and paddling.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Pairing Paris and Brantford makes the day feel more complete. Do Paris for the charm and Brantford for the history and trails.

Best for: markets, food, Mennonite culture, tech-meets-tradition, families, and easy wanderingDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 hoursSuggested day: Visit St. Jacobs Farmers’ Market in the morning, explore the village, then head into Kitchener-Waterloo or Cambridge for food, history, or the Butterfly Conservatory.

Kitchener-Waterloo and St. Jacobs make a great day trip because they offer such a mix of experiences. You can visit one of the best-known markets in Ontario, see Mennonite farms and horse-drawn buggies, then head into a modern university and tech region.

St. Jacobs is the classic stop, especially if you love markets, bakeries, crafts, and small-town shopping. Nearby Kitchener, Waterloo, Cambridge, and Galt add more food, history, and riverside exploring.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Go on a market day if you can. St. Jacobs Farmers’ Market is the anchor of this day trip.

Best for: beach-town nostalgia, Lake Erie, fish and chips, pier walks, and casual summer daysDrive from Toronto: about 2 hoursSuggested day: Walk the pier, have lunch at The Arbor or a local fish-and-chips spot, relax by the beach, then continue along Lake Erie if you want a mini road trip.

Port Dover is a classic Ontario beach town. It has a sandy beach, a pier, casual restaurants, shops, and that old-school summer feeling that makes you want to slow down.

This is not a polished luxury escape, and that is exactly the point. Port Dover is relaxed, nostalgic, and easy. It’s the kind of place where a hot dog, a walk by the water, and a sunset can be the whole plan.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Use Port Dover as the starting point for a Lake Erie mini road trip to Turkey Point, Port Rowan, or local wineries and breweries.

Best for: paddling, cottage-country scenery, lift locks, museums, Indigenous art, and relaxed exploringDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 to 2 hoursSuggested day: Visit the Peterborough Lift Lock, explore the Canadian Canoe Museum, paddle or walk along the water, then stop for food or local shopping before heading home.

Peterborough sits at the gateway to the Kawarthas and gives you a taste of cottage country without driving too far. It’s a good choice if you want water, history, culture, and a relaxed pace.

The Peterborough Lift Lock is the classic stop, and the Canadian Canoe Museum adds a meaningful look at paddling history and Indigenous craftsmanship. The area also has riverside trails, breweries, and access to the Trent-Severn Waterway.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Don’t treat Peterborough as just a place to pass through on the way to cottage country. It has enough to fill a full day.

Best for: skiing, hiking, biking, spa days, village atmosphere, and four-season adventureDrive from Toronto: about 2 to 2.5 hoursSuggested day: Spend the morning hiking, skiing, or visiting Scenic Caves, then explore Blue Mountain Village and finish with Scandinave Spa if you want a slower end to the day.

Blue Mountain and Collingwood are technically a longer day trip, but they are worth it if you start early. In winter, Blue Mountain is one of the most popular ski and snowboard areas near Toronto. In summer, it becomes a hub for hiking, biking, patios, and outdoor activities.

Scenic Caves, Blue Mountain Village, the waterfront in Collingwood, and Scandinave Spa all make this area easy to customize depending on your travel style.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If you want the day to feel less rushed, pick one main activity. Don’t try to ski, spa, hike, shop, and eat your way through the whole region in one day.

Best for: beach days, families, swimming, paddleboarding, summer energy, and easy sand-and-sun escapesDrive from Toronto: about 2 hoursSuggested day: Arrive early, set up on the beach, swim or paddleboard, grab lunch nearby, and stay for sunset if traffic is manageable.

Wasaga Beach is one of Ontario’s classic summer day trips. It is known for its long sandy shoreline, shallow water, and big beach-day energy.

This is a good choice when you want a simple day: cooler, towels, sunscreen, water, snacks, and sand. It can get very busy in summer, but that is part of the Wasaga experience.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Go early on hot weekends. Parking and prime beach spots fill up fast. Book ahead with Ontario Parks or you can pay at parking lots.

Best for: lakes, paddling, fall colours, cottage-country scenery, breweries, and small townsDrive from Toronto: about 2 to 2.5 hoursSuggested day: Pick one town as your base, such as Gravenhurst, Bracebridge, or Huntsville, then add a lake stop, short hike, brewery, or boat cruise.

Muskoka is one of Ontario’s most famous cottage-country regions, with lakes, forests, docks, small towns, and that unmistakable smell of pine trees and campfires.

It is a bit of a long day trip from Toronto, but it works if you choose one area instead of trying to see the entire region. Gravenhurst, Bracebridge, Huntsville, and Port Carling all make good anchors.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Muskoka is better when you slow down. Choose one town, one lake, and one great food stop instead of racing between too many places.

Best for: wineries, beaches, food, art, romantic getaways, and summer road tripsDrive from Toronto: about 2.5 hoursSuggested day: Visit a winery or two, explore Picton or Wellington, stop at Sandbanks or a beach, and have dinner before heading back.

Prince Edward County is one of the best food-and-wine day trips from Toronto, though it also works beautifully as an overnight getaway. It has boutique wineries, cideries, beaches, farm stands, restaurants, art galleries, and small towns.

Sandbanks Provincial Park is the major beach draw, but the whole county is made for slow exploring. It’s ideal for couples, food lovers, and anyone who wants a countryside escape.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: For a true day trip, don’t overbook tastings. Pick one area of the county and enjoy it properly.

Best for: wilderness, paddling, hiking, fall colours, wildlife, and big nature daysDrive from Toronto: about 3 hoursSuggested day: Leave before sunrise, choose one hiking trail or guided paddling experience, stop at a lookout or visitor centre, and head home before you are too tired.

Algonquin is a stretch as a day trip, but it can be done if you start early and keep the plan simple. This is one of Ontario’s most iconic wilderness areas, with forests, lakes, hiking trails, canoe routes, and wildlife.

You won’t see all of Algonquin in a day, and you shouldn’t try. But a single hike, paddle, or scenic drive can still give you a taste of why the park is so special.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Algonquin is much better as an overnight, but if you only have one day, choose one trail or activity and make that the focus. Algonquin Outfitters offers excellent one-day guided tours .

No car? Book this Toronto to Algonquin Provincial Park private Tour.

Best for: The Grotto, Georgian Bay, hiking, turquoise water, cliffs, shipwrecks, and big adventure daysDrive from Toronto: about 3.5 to 4 hoursSuggested day: Leave very early, visit the Grotto or hike a section of the Bruce Trail, stop in Tobermory if time allows, and expect a long drive home.

Bruce Peninsula National Park is one of the most spectacular places in Ontario, but it is a very long day trip from Toronto. The Grotto, Georgian Bay cliffs, turquoise water, and Bruce Trail scenery make it unforgettable.

This is best for travellers who do not mind a long drive and a full day outdoors. For most people, it works better as an overnight getaway, but it can be done in a single ambitious day.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Reservations and parking rules matter here. Plan ahead, start early, and don’t wing it on a summer weekend.

Hamilton, Elora, and Niagara Falls are the best day trips from Toronto for waterfalls. Niagara Falls is the most famous, Hamilton has the greatest variety, and Elora gives you dramatic gorge scenery along the Grand River.

Wasaga Beach, Port Dover, Sandbanks in Prince Edward County, and the Toronto Islands are the best beach day trips from Toronto. Wasaga is best for a classic summer beach day, while Sandbanks is better if you want dunes and a longer road trip.

Niagara-on-the-Lake and Prince Edward County are the best wine-focused day trips from Toronto. Niagara-on-the-Lake is easier for a one-day trip, while Prince Edward County feels more relaxed if you can stay overnight.

Canada’s Wonderland, Toronto Islands, Niagara Falls, the Toronto Zoo, and Wasaga Beach are some of the best family-friendly day trips from Toronto. They offer easy activities, food options, and enough to fill a full day without complicated planning.

Milton, Hamilton, Elora, Algonquin Provincial Park, and Bruce Peninsula National Park are the best hiking day trips from Toronto. For an easy hike close to the city, choose Milton or Hamilton. For a bigger adventure, choose Algonquin or Bruce Peninsula.

Stratford, Elora, Paris, and Niagara-on-the-Lake are the best small-town day trips from Toronto. Each has a walkable centre, good food, independent shops, and enough charm to fill a relaxed day.

The best day trips from Toronto under 2 hours include Hamilton, Niagara Falls, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Elora, Stratford, Paris, Caledon, Milton, Kitchener-Waterloo, and Wasaga Beach. These are the easiest options if you want to leave in the morning and be back home by dinner.

Yes, Niagara Falls is one of the easiest and most popular day trips from Toronto. It takes about 90 minutes by car, and you can visit the falls, Journey Behind the Falls, Clifton Hill, the Niagara SkyWheel, and the Hornblower boat cruise in a single day if you start early.

For nature close to the city, Hamilton’s waterfalls, Milton’s conservation areas, Elora Gorge, and Caledon are some of the best choices. For bigger wilderness, Algonquin Park and Bruce Peninsula are spectacular, but they work better as long day trips or overnight escapes.

Yes, but your options are more limited. Niagara Falls, Hamilton, Toronto Islands, and some towns along GO Transit or VIA Rail routes are possible without a car. For waterfalls, conservation areas, beaches, and rural towns, driving is usually much easier.

#6298. Editor's Letter: Introducing Our Winter Travel Issue

It was a long and hot summer, and I welcomed the cooler weather as soon as the leaves started to turn. My closet full of coats and jackets had sat sadly neglected for many months; the new boots I bought in April on a clearance rack are only now about to get their moment. I'm excited for the Christmas lights in London and New York, the festive trees, chestnuts roasting on street corners—and yes, my Christmas wish list (featuring a dangerous number of watches and pieces of jewelry) is ready too. There is something about the winter that still feels exotic and enthralling to me. I saw snow a few times in Kashmir as a kid, but the first real blizzard I encountered was when I was a freshman in college in Pennsylvania. It was late at night, but my roommate dragged me out of bed to make snow angels. I still remember lying on my back, waving my arms around—the sensation of cold all along my body was surreal, as was the way in which white feathery bits floated down from the sky. I recall thinking, What a strange but wonderful feeling! I discovered two things quickly: One, I was a terrible skier. And, two, I loved après-ski—to be nursing hot chocolate by crackling fireplaces and snuggled in blankets.

Our story on Banff perfectly encapsulates the promise of winter: the adventure, the exhilaration, the romance of a landscape transformed overnight. But equally seductive is the prospect of winter sun. Come January I'll happily trade snow boots for sandals and fly to Tenerife, Spain, or Boracay, in the Philippines, or Brisbane, Australia. That dose of vitamin D is essential by then, when the Christmas lights have come down and everything seems gray and empty. At that point I need a beach—and something colorful and sparkly to wear on it. So often I close my eyes and return to the end-of-year trips I've made to Maldives, Indonesia, Mexico, and remembered the sunrises, the sound of the waves, the palm trees swaying in the breeze, the fiery red chiles, and fresh coconut water. It's been a strange year. But as we navigate the final months ahead, this issue is filled with reasons to feel excited about what comes next. I hope it gives you plenty to dream about—and somewhere to go.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. #6297. Don’t Scan This Abroad: The QR Code Travel Scam Tourists Miss

QR codes are everywhere when we travel now, on restaurant tables, parking meters, hotel signs, airports, train stations, and transit machines. This travel scam known as Quishing or QR code phishing is becoming the fastest growing travel scam warning out there. Most QR codes are legitimate, but scammers are using fake QR code stickers and fake payment pages to catch travellers when they are tired, rushed, or distracted.

QR code travel scam happens when a fake QR code sends travellers to a fraudulent website. The code may be placed over a real QR code on a parking meter, restaurant table, hotel notice, airport sign, or transit machine, or it may arrive by text or email pretending to be a fine, toll, ticket, or check-in request. The safest rule is simple: Pause. Check. Then pay.Read out post: 20 Common Travel Scams and How to Avoid Them

A scammer does not always need to hack a system or damage a payment machine. Sometimes they print a fake QR code sticker and place it directly over a legitimate code.

From a quick glance, the sign still looks official. The logo may look familiar. The instructions may seem normal. The page that opens may copy the colours, layout, and branding of the real company.

You think you are paying for parking, ordering food, checking into a hotel, or settling a toll. Instead, criminals may be collecting your credit card number, password, phone number, licence plate, email address, or other personal information.

The FTC has also warned about fake traffic violation texts that begin with a QR code and try to scare people into paying a fake unpaid balance.

The FTC has warned that scammers hide harmful links in QR codes to steal personal information, including by placing fake QR codes over real ones on parking meters.

Many restaurants now use QR codes for menus, ordering, or payment. Most are legitimate, but travellers should still be cautious. This is the easiest travel scam for QR code phishing as everyone uses it.

A menu QR code should usually show a menu. Be careful if it asks for information it does not need, such as your passport number, banking details, hotel room number, or a password.

Before scanning a QR code on a restaurant table, look at the surface. Does it look printed into the menu or table sign, or does it look like a sticker placed on top? If it looks raised, crooked, bubbled, or mismatched, ask staff for a printed menu or the restaurant’s official website.

Parking is one of the easiest places for this scam to work because travellers are often rushed and confused.

You may not know the local parking app. You may be dealing with another language. You may be worried about getting a ticket. That pressure makes a “scan to pay” sticker feel helpful.

Before paying through a parking QR code, inspect the sticker, read the URL preview, and check whether the payment page matches the city, parking authority, or official app named on the machine.

If anything feels off, do not use the QR code. Type the official website yourself, use the official parking app, pay at the machine, or ask local staff for help.

Airports and transit stations are full of QR codes: Wi-Fi, directions, tickets, luggage storage, forms, lounge access, and service information. Travel scams often happen when travelers are in a hurry. If you need wifi, a taxi, some food, QR codes are often the easiest way to catch you off guard.

That does not mean every code is unsafe. It means you should slow down when a public QR code asks for payment, passwords, ID documents, or personal information.

The FBI warns that malicious QR codes can send people to fake sites, steal victim data, embed malware, or redirect payments. The FBI warns that criminals can tamper with QR codes to redirect payments, steal login and financial information, or send people to malicious websites.

The easiest way to avoid this scam is to build one habit before you scan a public QR code.

Do not scan just because a sign looks official. Public signs, parking meters, table cards, and posters can be tampered with.

If the message says you must pay immediately, avoid a fine, settle a toll, confirm a booking, or prevent a penalty, slow down. Urgency is one of the biggest warning signs.

Before your phone opens anything, look at the QR code itself.

We call this the scratch test. You are not damaging the sign. You are simply checking whether the QR code feels or looks different from the rest of the surface.

Canadian readers can also check the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security’s QR code safety guidance and report fraud through the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre.

Most phones show a preview of the website before opening the page. Read it.

Look for misspellings, extra words, strange endings, random letters, shortened links, or a domain that does not match the company, hotel, restaurant, city, or attraction.

Do not rely only on the padlock symbol. A secure connection does not automatically mean the site is legitimate. The real question is whether you are on the correct website.

The FTC has also warned about fake traffic violation texts that include a QR code and pressure people to pay a fake unpaid balance.

For payments, passwords, account logins, or identity information, the safest option is often to bypass the QR code.

Open your browser and type the official website yourself. Use an app you already installed from the official app store. Ask an employee for the correct payment method. Contact your hotel, airline, rental car company, or bank through the phone number on your booking or card — not through the number on a suspicious page.

First, do not panic. Scanning a QR code does not automatically mean your information has been stolen. The bigger risk usually begins when you enter payment information, type a password, download a file, or provide personal details.

Close the page immediately if the link looks wrong, the message creates urgency, or the site asks for information you did not expect to provide.

Do not download an unfamiliar app or file from a QR code.

If you entered credit card information, contact your bank or card issuer using the official number on the back of your card or through the official banking app.

If you entered a password, change it through the official website or app. If you reused that password anywhere else, change it there too.

Watch for follow-up messages. A scammer who has some of your information may later pretend to be your bank, hotel, airline, rental car company, or payment provider.

Report the fake QR code to the business, parking authority, hotel, airport, or local authority so they can remove it.

A QR code may be suspicious if it looks like a sticker placed over another code, has peeling edges, opens a strange URL, uses a shortened link, creates urgency, asks for information that does not make sense, or directs you away from the official website or app.

At a restaurant, a QR menu should not need your passport or banking password. At a parking meter, the payment page should match the city or parking authority. At a hotel, a check-in code should not send you to a random payment page outside the official booking system.

The BBB has also warned consumers to double-check QR codes before paying for parking.

No. QR codes are part of modern travel, and many are perfectly safe.

The goal is not to panic every time you see one. The goal is to stop treating every QR code as automatically trustworthy.

A few seconds of inspection can protect you from a much longer financial or account-recovery problem later.

QR codes are convenient, but convenience is exactly what scammers are using against travellers.

Before scanning a public QR code at a restaurant, parking meter, hotel, airport, train station, attraction, or transit stop, remember the rule:

Inspect the code. Read the link. Go directly to the official website or app when money, passwords, or personal information are involved.

That tiny pause may be the thing that saves your trip.

Scanning a QR code is not automatically dangerous. The danger usually begins when you open a suspicious page, enter payment details, type a password, download a file, or provide personal information without checking whether the site is legitimate.

Inspect the physical code for stickers, raised edges, bubbles, peeling corners, or anything placed over another code. Then check the URL preview before opening the page. If the link looks strange or does not match the official company, city, hotel, or attraction, do not use it.

Before entering payment information, make sure the website belongs to the official business or authority. When in doubt, use the official app, type the website manually, pay directly at the machine, or ask staff for the correct payment method.

Contact your bank or card issuer immediately using the official number on the back of your card or your banking app. Watch for suspicious charges, replace the card if needed, and do not use any contact information from the suspicious website.

#6295. In Winter, Canada's Banff National Park is So Much More Than a Skiers' Paradise

My view from the foot of gleaming Victoria Glacier was straight out of a snow globe. Two shaggy ebony draft horses pulled a vintage sleigh along a powdery path that hugged the shores of frozen Lake Louise. Lycra-clad Nordic skiers glided across the snow-dusted ice, navigating around life-size snowmen. In the far distance a ray of sun glinted off the turret of an ice-sculpted castle, a mini version of the grand Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise hotel, which stands sentinel over this unbelievably pretty patch of wilderness in Banff National Park. A soft gust of wind swirled a flurry of flakes across the scene. The winter wonderland in front of me was magical enough to make even the most die-hard snowbirds reconsider the season.

I've always felt winter could be approached in two ways: You could be lazy and binge Netflix for three months, or you could be sporty and get after it in the mountains. But a weeklong trip to the Banff and Lake Louise region of Alberta opened my eyes to a gratifying middle ground. This area is a true winter playground, where you could downhill-ski or engage with the elements in so many other ways: snowshoeing, going for a horse-drawn sleigh ride, or watching the snowflakes fall while you're soaking in an outdoor hot tub. My time ended up being more about appreciating nature than conquering it on the slopes.

A seat with a view inside Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise

I arrived in early January on the tail of one of the area's snowiest Decembers on record, though you couldn't tell from the landscape around Calgary airport. Umber-hued prairies and agricultural land surround the gateway city, and it wasn't until 40 minutes into my 90-minute drive west on the Trans-Canada Highway that the Great Plains transitioned to the Canadian Rockies and the sky started nuking snow.

Home to SkiBig3—a trio of resorts that include Banff Sunshine, Lake Louise Ski Resort, and the mom-and-pop Mount Norquay—Banff National Park was the place to be during a winter in which most of the American West suffered a snow drought. In my 20s I would have driven straight from the airport to the ski slopes. Now in my mid-40s, with an unpredictable knee, back-to-back, bell-to-bell days have lost their appeal. But the childlike joy of playing in the snow has not. And Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise was the perfect base for “soft” winter adventure.

The resort's address, in the heart of Banff National Park overlooking glacier-fed Lake Louise, envelops guests in nature. No surprise—Lake Louise was originally developed for outdoor tourism. In 1885, after the last spike of the Canadian Pacific Railway was driven in, future company president William Cornelius Van Horne built hotels along the route. Among the first, the Banff Springs Hotel was designed for horseback sightseeing. The Chalet at Lake Louise, a humble log cabin, was marketed as a destination for fishing, canoeing, and alpinism. Van Horne hired Swiss guides to teach his guests to safely navigate the mountains, and they are partially responsible for introducing locals to the sport of skiing.

A horse-drawn sleigh ride around Lake Louise

In 1925 the original Chalet, which had been damaged in a fire, was reimagined as Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise, a grand, Renaissance Revival–style resort with 539 rooms and suites. Today, a century after opening, some characteristics—like its staff dressed in lederhosen-inspired uniforms and its fondue-focused restaurant, Walliser Stube—nod to the original Swiss influence, and the lobby-level Guide's Cabin, decorated with vintage photos and stocked with books on alpine living, continues the property's mountaineering legacy. Through the hotel, guests can sign up for snowshoe hikes or Bavarian curling lessons and rent ice skates and Nordic skis.

My first morning, I met guide Kevin Kirkpatrick at the cabin for an activity called Powderfest Snowshoeing. I've long found snowshoeing a little snoozy and worried how we'd fill the allotted three hours. The activity's name, it turned out, wasn't a cutesy marketing ploy. The resort has seven snowshoe trails, but because there was a base of 61 inches and another foot of fresh powder, we went “off-roading.”

Leaving behind the groomed lakeshore trail, we trekked up the shoulder of Fairview Mountain, and all signs of civilization disappeared as we entered a frosted forest straight out of a Dr. Seuss story. “Really get in there and explore,” he encouraged as we wandered past fir and larch trees bent at cartoonish angles, their limbs heaving with snow. I followed him up a massive mound of powder only to catch the metal cleat of my snowshoe on a branch and topple backward, leaving an imprint like a gigantic snow angel.

Time flew as Kirkpatrick shared wisdom on everything from the current weather anomaly to how, in 1882, Edwin Hunter, a member of the Stoney Nakoda, first led a young European wrangler, Tom Wilson, to what the Indigenous people of this area called Ho-run-num-nay (Lake of the Little Fishes). He chose to ignore the name and anointed it Emerald Lake for its jewel-colored waters. Two years later the government changed the moniker to Louise to honor a daughter of Queen Victoria, Princess Louise Caroline Alberta.

An ice climber on the Lake Louise Lakeshore Trail

I returned to the hotel thoroughly exhausted from hours of high-stepping and grateful that I was booked for a session at Basin Glacial Waters, Fairmont's new, guests-only thermal bathhouse. Designed by Italian architect Matteo Thun, the building, with floor-to-ceiling windows that frame the lake and towering peaks at every turn, feels like part of the landscape. This is the epitome of nature bathing, I thought as I took in the views from the hot-stone room, silent salt chamber, and indoor-outdoor vitality pool.

I didn't think it was possible to distract me from the dramatic vista, but Basin's signature Aufguss sauna ritual, the conclusion to my multisensory journey, was impossible to ignore. This choreographed sauna performance popular across Europe has only recently been introduced to North American spas. For 15 minutes our sauna master, Kyan Van Haasteren, a young, blond Dutchman, theatrically waved a towel over scorching sauna stones to waft steam toward me and 32 other guests. He danced around the 185-degree-Fahrenheit space to an upbeat soundtrack of Luis Fonsi while smashing snowballs scented with aromatic oils over the hot stones to release the fragrance of Siberian fir. It felt more like a Vegas show than a wellness ritual, but the entertainment took my mind off the discomfort of the heat. I exited in a sweaty daze and willed myself to follow Van Haasteren's lead and dunk myself into the outdoor cold plunge. In seconds the tingling numbness gave way to a heady euphoria. I looked up to see the start of a steady snow spiraling down, one that wouldn't let up until late the next day.

I may not be a first-to-last-chair skier any longer, but I'm still motivated to score fresh tracks on a powder day. By 8 a.m. the next morning, I was on the complimentary Fairmont shuttle with a throng of stoked skiers for the 10-minute transfer to Lake Louise Ski Resort. With three ways up the front of the mountain, there's rarely a line. And once you're on the mountain, it's easy to spread out. With this season's addition of Richardson's Ridge, 200 acres of beginner- and intermediate-friendly glades and groomers, the resort owns bragging rights as the third biggest ski area in Canada, with 4,200 acres of skiable terrain. Throughout the day I experienced moments that felt more like backcountry than resort riding, especially in the rowdy inbounds steeps of the West Bowl.

Gearing up to snowshoe at Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise

I spent the morning lapping bowl runs off the Summit Chair, but in the afternoon the visibility disappeared, making a drop down black diamond Rodney's Ridge downright vertigo-inducing. I'd gotten my fix of SkiBig3's “Prosecco Powder” (wonderfully light, dry snow), and I won't lie—the other incentive that got me up and out early was the promise of lunch at Whitehorn Bistro. The acclaimed views from this upscale, on-mountain restaurant were obscured, but that didn't damper the deliciousness of its farm-to-table dishes, like pickled beet carpaccio with goat cheese and crispy duck with black cherry jus.

With a solid half day of riding under my belt, I left the resort to work off my lunch on the Nordic trails of the Lake Louise campground with Clare McCann, the high-energy owner of Bikescape. Her lighthearted guiding philosophy was an ideal match for my novice cross-country ski skills and the tricky conditions. Heavy wet snow would cement our skis to the ground the minute we stopped propelling forward. “Shimmy, shimmy, shimmy, glide,” she repeated like a mantra as we haltingly made our way around the four-mile Bow River Loop. The trail was so silent that the only sound was my retro SkiBig3 pass flapping on the side of my jacket.

Those words stuck with me as I drove 50 minutes southeast to the town of Banff. Compared with Lake Louise, it's a bustling tourism hub, but thanks to strict design guidelines, the businesses downtown—even the Starbucks and the McDonald's—are housed in intentionally rustic spaces built from local stone and wood. Over the last few years, new businesses have enlivened the downtown area. Some of these arrivals include locavore-focused restaurants Good Folk and Farm & Fire, and the 67-room boutique Kenrick Hotel, a hip remodel of the former High Country Inn that added a third-wave coffee shop, a thermal circuit spa, and a stellar Italian restaurant, The Fat Ox. Even the classic sticky-floored late-night club, the Dusty Boot Saloon & Dance Hall, has been reinvented as Banff's take on Jackson Hole's Million Dollar Cowboy Bar, complete with a shiny, boot-shaped disco ball and a karaoke room.

I kept things old-school and checked in to Fairmont Banff Springs, nicknamed the Castle in the Rockies for its Scottish-baronial-style architecture and perch overlooking the town. The hotel was another vision of railway executive Van Horne, who famously said, “If we can't export the scenery, we'll import the tourists.”

Today Banff National Park sees more than 4.25 million visitors every year; nearly two thirds come during summer. But a week into my trip, I began to think that winter might be the more enchanting season. On my final day I joined Discover Banff Tours on an excursion to Johnston Canyon for its Icewalk experience. In the parking lot our guide, Jeff Doherty, outfitted our group of six in Yaktrax—ice-gripping cleats that attach to shoes—then had us briskly hike a half mile over slick paths and bridges to the lower falls before the big bus tour groups arrived.

The canyon was pure quietude, and we had it to ourselves. When the pace slowed, I was able to admire the feathery moss suspended in frost on the forest floor, the icy old man's beard lichen dangling from the trees, and, most of all, the frozen ribbons of electric blue cascades. About a mile of slippery uphill trail led us to the upper falls, a stream of water plunging behind a veil of ice. I stood in front of Mother Nature's ice sculpture in awe. “It's like seeing the Mona Lisa alone in the Louvre,” said Doherty. “In summer you'd be elbowing iPhones out of the way for a view, let alone a photo.”

A few weeks after I'd returned home to Colorado, I read that Alberta had been hit by a warm spell that doused the mountains in rain, turning the slopes into sheets of ice. Some friends had taken their family on a ski trip per my recommendation. When I asked about their vacation, they told me they hadn't skied once, but they had the best time dogsledding, night tubing, and ice-skating. In an age when weather is unforgivingly unpredictable, Banff, with its buffet of activities, might be the closest thing to a guaranteed winter escape, no matter your preferred pace of adventure. My trip showed me that winter isn't just about high-voltage powder days at the ski resort. It can be enjoyed at a slower pace. I was even inspired to buy a pair of my own snowshoes.

Direct flights to Calgary International Airport are available from more than a dozen major US hubs. Banff National Park is an easy 90-minute drive west on the Trans-Canada Highway.

Lakefront grande dame Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise offers every imaginable snowy activity, from horse-drawn sleigh rides to curling. In winter an outdoor bar built from 240 blocks of ice serves mulled wine and spiked cocoa. Only hotel guests have access to Basin Glacial Waters, a sprawling thermal bathhouse. Don't miss the excellent hotel bookshop, curated with out-of-print editions on the area's mountaineering history.

One of the park's first hotels, Fairmont Banff Springs, recently added a new wing of larger, family-friendly suites with bunk beds and adjoining rooms. An on-site skating rink has a pop-up sugar shack that serves maple treats, and the adventure center rents fat-tire bikes and arranges guided evening snowshoe tours. Of the 13 dining venues, 1888 Chophouse, known for its Alberta Wagyu, is a standout.

A refreshing boutique alternative to Banff's palatial resorts, the reimagined Kenrick Hotel has an outpost of Calgary's Analog Coffee, a guests-only hydrotherapy spa that stays open until midnight, and one of the town's top tables, Alpine Italian–inspired Fat Ox.

Tucked away on Sulphur Mountain, 320-room resort Rimrock Banff, Emblems Collection debuted a sleek makeover last summer. The first property in Accor's new über-luxe Emblems Collection features a bathhouse of saunas, glacial plunges, and infinity pools, plus a cocktail-forward vinyl listening room and in-house guides who can take guests on glacier treks and ice canyon walks.

Reservations are a must at white-tablecloth Dining Room at the Post Hotel and Spa, known for its 25,000-plus-bottle wine cellar and European-inspired menu of dishes like roasted chateaubriand and Dover sole with saffron beurre blanc.

The house-made sourdough alone makes it worth pausing on a powder day for lunch at ski-in, ski-out restaurant Whitehorn Bistro off the Grizzly Gondola of Lake Louise Ski Resort. On a bluebird day request a patio seat.

The Dusty Boot Saloon and Dance Hall was recently spiffed up and turned into an Old West saloon with a stage for live music and a menu of excellent cocktails, like the Cattleman's Old Fashioned, and elevated bar food, including addictive popcorn chicken and shrimp spiked with wasabi peas.

At Good Folk, hearty breakfast dishes like banana caramel French toast will fuel your day's adventure. In the evening the menu showcases the local bounty in dishes like Alberta wild boar chop and a decadent bison burger topped with smoked cheddar and pepper bacon.

Johnston Canyon, a labyrinth of limestone rocks and cascades, sees a fraction of the visitors in winter than in summer. But to make sure you have the frozen falls to yourself, book the morning Icewalk experience with Discover Banff Tours.

Local outfitter Bikescape runs beginner-friendly Nordic ski tours on the trails within Banff National Park as well as electric fat-tire bike tours that include a backcountry lunch.

Sit back and enjoy the views of Lake Louise from the seat of a horse-drawn sled. Brewsters Lake Louise Stables runs hour-long trips that follow the lake path; evening tours under the stars are extra special.

SkiBig3's resorts offer something for everyone. Family-friendly Mount Norquay has night skiing and a thrilling tubing park. Every chairlift on the front side of Lake Louise Ski Resort has both an easy (green) and challenging (black) way down. Sunshine Mountain Lodge at Banff Sunshine Village has the area's only ski-in, ski-out lodging, and its big alpine views make you feel like you're downhilling in Europe.

For the perfect detour en route to Calgary International Airport, Everwild Canmore, a new Nordic spa at the Everwild hotel in the town of Canmore, features a DIY outdoor thermal circuit as well as five-elements rituals, ranging from an herbal steam cleanse to an Aufguss ceremony. The spa lounge serves a shareable charcuterie and cheese board for two along with cocktails.

#6293. Headed to Puerto Rico? These Beaches Belong on Your Bucket List

My father grew up on Puerto Rico's west coast, where beach days began with a barefoot walk to the sand around the neighborhoods of Isabela or Aguadilla and often ended wherever the waves happened to be breaking next. I grew up on stories of salty hair, sun-warmed sand, and long, glittering afternoons in the water. Eventually, I started following in his footsteps, exploring the island’s beaches for myself and discovering just how many different shades of paradise fit along its 300 miles of coastline. There are the rollicking Atlantic surf breaks at Jobos and Middles, the impossibly blue waters and colorful fishing boats of Crash Boat, the mangrove-fringed coastline around La Parguera, and the powdery white sands of Culebra's Flamenco Beach. Some days call for a boat ride out to Culebrita’s secluded Tortuga Beach; others are better spent under the palms in Luquillo, with a plate of fresh seafood and a cold Medalla from the nearby kiosks.

The island is filled with beaches, all with a slightly different personality. Whether your plan is to wake up early and arrive with a surfboard, head out on a boat ride, snorkel, or lounge on the sand with absolutely no plans at all, I've got a rec for you. From well-loved surf towns to far-flung island hideaways, these are the best beaches in Puerto Rico worth building a trip around—plus, where to stay when you get there.

Head to dreamy Playa Jobos (or Jobos Beach)…

…for local vibes, sublime swells, a colorful coast

Head to Culebra, a lush island off the east coast, and you'll find Flamenco Beach, a gorgeous white-sand beach that's just over one mile long. It sits inside a broad, horseshoe-shaped bay, where the curve of the land shields the coastline from heavy Atlantic swells, so the water remains calm and clear for long stretches. The layers of color can be seen overhead: pale green near the shore, then deeper blue as the floor drops away. A quintessential tropical beach, the sand here is as fine as flour, remarkably pale and cool. While the shore is relatively short, it is wide enough that you can always find a spot to claim as your own, even on busy peak weekends.

Not to mention, the beach was ranked one of the top 50 beaches in the world for 2026—the Caribbean gem landed the 41st spot globally and 10th in North America on The World’s 50 Best Beaches list for 2026.

Jobos Beach is one of those stretches that captures the easygoing, salt-in-your-hair spirit of Puerto Rico’s northwest coast. Tucked into Isabela’s Bajuras neighborhood, the sandy bay is framed by a rocky headland, with a well-known reef break that draws local surfers and visiting wave-chasers alike. Even if you don't surf, there's plenty to keep you busy here: watch the lineup from the shore, book a lesson with Moku Surf Shop, or settle in at one of the beachside restaurants next door for fresh seafood and a table with an ocean view. The surrounding stretch of coast is dotted with little places to eat and drink, so it's easy to make an afternoon of it, whether you're coming straight from the water or just looking for a laid-back lunch with a view. Jobos is a proper surf beach, though, not a reliably calm swimming cove; strong currents and changing conditions are part of the picture, so take care before heading in.

The path to this beach is a bit of a trek: Starting in Ceiba, a small town to the northeast of the main island, travelers will need to take a ferry to Culebra followed by another 30-minute boat ride via water taxi or tour group to Culebrita (little Culebra). But trust that the ride is well worth the reward of unspoiled paradise—it's even sea-turtle-approved. The beach's name Tortuga nods to the herds of turtles that visit its shores from February to August and make for superb snorkeling companions. Above water, the beach welcomes a Robinson Crusoe variety of fun with its lush untamed jungles and powder-soft white sands. Make sure to grab everything you'll need for a few hours of fun—because of Tortuga's removed location, you won't find amenities like bathrooms or food stands close by.

The piers here were initially built so the US military could quickly recover downed airmen from Ramey Air Force Base, thus explaining the name, “Crash Boat Beach.” Located on the west side of the island in Aguadilla, this beach's past life as a military outpost feels far behind it—dinghies and fishing boats of all shapes, shades, and sizes line the highlighter-painted piers and the unofficial soundtrack of the shore comes from the speakers and boomboxes pulsing to reggaeton beats. Whether you're here to party at some of the best bars in Puerto Rico or enjoy the calmer life that carries on at sea, visitors are welcome to take their sweet time here, thanks to the well-stocked kiosks of water sports pavilions, umbrella rentals, and food stands, selling any wares you might need for a long day at the beach.

A one-mile crescent that arcs along the island's northern coast, Pine Grove provides a taste of the Atlantic's stronger waves, making it one of Puerto Rico's most popular surf spots for those just starting out. Especially during the month of December, the east side of this beach tends to catch consistent three-to-four-foot swells, making it a great place for beginners to learn how to surf. The convenient location is a welcome bonus; as a beach in Isla Verde, Pine Grove is a mere five minutes away from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport (SJU), so you can hit the sands as soon as you're wheels down in the Caribbean.

Where to stay near Pine Grove Surfing Beach:

Vieques is a six-mile skip to the southeast of the main island, and once dubbed, “La Isla Nena” by Puerto Rican poet Luis Llorens Torres—this island plays the role of darling little sister perfectly. And where better to experience the island's charms than on one of its beaches? La Chiva is a part of the Vieques National Wildlife Refuge, where a few steps to your left may lead you to a forest of mangroves, a few to the right, a stunning coastal lagoon. Take it all in surrounded by the friendly company of wild horses, sea turtles, manatees, and diving seabirds. Stretching out for one and a half miles, this is a leisurely walk along the beach that's begging to be taken. If you're enticed to do more in the clear-as-glass turquoise waters, head off to nearby Chiva Bay, one of the best snorkeling spots in Puerto Rico.

Also known as Balneario La Monserrate, Luquillo Beach is so much more than its 12 miles of golden sands, tranquil waters, and fanning palms—though all of the above are fabulous. The beach borders El Yunque National Forest, the only rainforest registered in the US National Parks system. If you're searching to pack your itinerary with more than swimming, surfing, and snorkeling, head for the mountains: For can't-miss sights, journey up the main road to La Coca waterfall for a cool mist and Yokahú Tower, an observation tower where you can behold the entire forest floor before you.

Technically, La Parguera has no beaches. But you won't miss any other shores after spending a day at these cays. Rent out a small boat or book with a local tour operator to explore the mild seas. Cays like Mata La Gata have shaded picnic areas for a casual lunch in paradise, while the gin-clear waters at Cayo Caracoles have natural walking paths lined with mangroves. Pressed for time and only able to visit one? Plan an after-hours trip to La Parguera's bioluminescent bay—one of three in Puerto Rico, and the only one visitors are permitted to swim in—which lights up an electric blue as you swim through the clouds of plankton that sparkle like glitter against the dark blue water.

This is one for the snorkelers. For a strong chance of seeing bus-sized manta rays, sea turtles, and marine life in every other form and flavor, look no further than in Tamarindo's welcoming waters. For those who aren't looking to paddle too far, the serene ocean in these parts is ideal for young families and those of all ages who'd rather just dip their feet in. While the entertainment and dining scene is virtually nonexistent, the opportunities for relaxation and reconnecting with nature are unparalleled.

#6292. The Best Ski Resorts in the US and Canada: 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards

For our 39th annual Reader’s Choice Awards, voters weighed in on their favorite ski resorts in North America—including the US and Canada. Big Sky’s decade-long transformation has paid off, landing the Montana resort in the top spot this year. But Colorado reigns as the top US ski destination, with 10 resorts making our top 30. Meanwhile, six East Coast resorts were recognized, including Mont-Tremblant in Quebec, Canada. And in the western US, new enhancements at Alyeska Resort helped get Alaska back on the list.

From Taos to Telluride and Stowe to SilverStar, these ski resorts were picked by our readers as the best in North America for their trails, lodges, lifts, and après-ski scenes. Whether you’re a powder hound or après ski devotee, these ski resorts ticked all your boxes.

View the 2025 Readers' Choice Awards winners for best ski resorts as a list with scores for the United States here and Canada here.

Aspen-Snowmass’s four mountains are each wildly unique, and Buttermilk might be the most playful. More like one giant terrain park, it’s home to seven different parks for everyone from beginners to pros. Its 22-foot Zaugg-cut Superpipe is the stage for star-studded sporting competitions including X Games Aspen and The Snow League. But Buttermilk is also the mountain for easygoing beginner terrain and awesomely intense trails for uphillers—those showoffs practicing the cardio-busting trend of trekking up a mountain on skis.

Where to stay: Just a free, five-minute shuttle ride away in downtown Aspen at your pick of great hotels, including the Little Nell, Limelight Aspen, St. Regis Aspen, and Hotel Jerome.

Stats: 8 lifts and 44 trails. One-day lift tickets average from $189; on the Ikon Pass and Mountain Collective.

The longest continually operating ski resort in Colorado, Winter Park is a Rocky Mountain playground known for its varied terrain and consistent snowfall (roughly 350 inches a year). It’s also one of Colorado’s most accessible mountains. Located just 67 miles west of Denver, it’s an easy drive from the airport, or take the Amtrak Winter Park Express ski train and get dropped off just steps from the lifts. This season, the resort is more than doubling snowmaking on a key base trail, again improving upon its recent $40 million snowmaking system upgrade. Families continue to find tons of value. Back this season, kids can nab a free ski or snowboard rental with a three-day adult gear rental package and every kid 14 and younger who signs up for a Winter Park Ski and Ride School lesson gets a free lift ticket for the day. The Gondola is free to everyone after 4 p.m. every Thursday through Saturday from mid-December through the end of March. That means you can wrap up the day at Mountaintop Après at Sunspot Lodge whether you skied or not.

Where to stay: Zephyr Mountain Lodge has studios, 1, 2, and 3-bedroom condos with full kitchens. In town, Gravity Haus Winter Park offers co-working spaces as well as gear demos and rentals. A-Frame Club is an Instagram-sensation with its 31 A-Frame cabins and historic saloon.

Stats: 23 lifts, 171 designated trails and 1,212 acres of off-piste terrain. One-day lift tickets from $108; on the Ikon Pass.

Where to stay: The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek Resort and Spa is fresh off a $20 million renovation. Other favorites include The Westin Riverfront Resort & Spa Avon, Vail Valley, The Osprey, a RockResort, and the Ritz-Carlton, Bachelor Gulch.

Stats: 24 lifts for 167 trails. One-day lift tickets from $116; on the Epic Pass.

Skiing in Alaska is a different experience than anywhere in the lower 48. Located just 40 miles southeast of Anchorage, Alyeska’s terrain is uniquely Alaskan, boasting everything from high alpine to the steep faces the 49th state is known for. Experts can push their limits, but with over 55 percent intermediate terrain, tree skiing, wide open groomed runs, and a lower mountain venue perfect for beginners, Alyeska caters to all ability levels. Aside from resort skiing, Alyeska serves as a backcountry basecamp offering guided ski touring, cat skiing, or heli skiing with top-notch outfits like SMG Alaska. And when it comes to après-ski, a trip to the mountaintop Bore Tide Bar for an off-menu Fizz cocktail is an Alyeska ritual.

Where to stay: The 299-room Alyeska Resort has eight dining venues, including stellar sushi spot Sakura and fine dining restaurant, Seven Glaciers, with its panoramic views. The eighth-floor Black Diamond Club feels like a hotel-within-a-hotel thanks to perks like a private lounge that serves complimentary breakfast and après bites. The resort’s 50,000-square-foot, indoor-outdoor Nordic spa is the perfect place to spend a down day.

Stats: 7 lifts for 76 runs, with an additional 1,400 vertical feet accessible via hike-to terrain when conditions allow. One-day lift tickets from $77; on the Ikon Pass.

Tamarack’s primarily east-facing slopes receive an average of 300 inches of snowfall annually. Readers love the diversity of terrain, which welcomes everyone from beginners and families to experts and powder chasers. The resort’s 2,000 mountain acres and 2,800 feet of vertical deliver everything from open bowls, steeps and signature cornice drops to high-speed corduroy groomers, natural tree-skiing glades and three terrain parks. At 6,700 feet, the new Mid-Mountain Lodge crowns the top of Tamarack Express with panoramic dining and event space, while a vibrant alpine-style village anchors the base with lodging, dining, and après. And Tamarack's Nordic trail system winds through open meadows and forested terrain for classic and skate skiing, snowshoeing, and fat biking.

Where to stay: Tamarack Resort has accommodations ranging from studios to four-bedroom penthouses plus amenities such as a pool, hot tubs and gear valet. The Lodge at Osprey Meadows is steps from the lifts and has studios and two- and three-bedroom condos.

Stats: 7 lifts for 59 runs. One-day lift tickets from $99; Ikon Pass Bonus Mountain

Founded by the late Robert Redford in 1969, Sundance Mountain Resort is a beloved escape tucked into Utah’s Wasatch Mountains at the base of the 12,000-foot Mount Timpanogos in Provo Canyon. Steep bowls give experienced skiers a thrill, while a third of the runs are green and beginner-friendly. Just an hour from Salt Lake City (hello, easy airport access!), the 5,000 acres of protected wilderness that surround the resort will help you find solitude. This season’s debut of Electric Horseman, a high-speed quad, marks the first phase of Sundance’s back mountain expansion, adding 60-plus acres of terrain and bringing the resort to 605 skiable acres. At the heart of the terrain expansion is Storyteller, a new signature ridgeline run carved from the terrain formerly known as the Far East Ridgeline. An additional 100 acres of terrain are planned for the 2027-2028 winter season. Off the slopes, guests can explore the resort’s renowned Art Studio & Gallery (think silversmithing and pottery classes), or unwind at the Spa and The Springs.

Where to stay: The Inn at Sundance Mountain Resort, which opened in January 2026, introduced ski-in/ski-out hotel accommodations to the resort for the first time, with 63 thoughtfully designed rooms in the heart of the village.

Stats: 10 lifts for 72 trails. One-day pass is $169.

Spanning six peaks and over 3,000 acres in the Yampa Valley, Steamboat is revered for its tree skiing, trademarked Champagne Powder snow, and family-friendly amenities. But many folks keep coming back for its deep Western roots and a down-home vibe that extends from the mountain to the town. A multiyear, multimillion-dollar redevelopment has reimagined Steamboat. The base area now features Wild Blue, a high speed ten-person gondola that takes skiers and riders from the base to the top of Sunshine Peak in 13 minutes, plus Skeeter's ice rink, and the Range Food & Drink Hall. Beginners can hone their skills mid-mountain at Greenhorn Ranch with natural feature-based instruction, while experts can test their mettle on 655 acres of challenging terrain in Mahogany Ridge and Fish Creek Canyon. One of the most accessible resorts in the Rockies, Steamboat is served by 18 major U.S. cities including Portland, Austin, and Houston.

Where to stay: The Steamboat Grand is a favorite for its massive heated pool and hot tubs. Ski-in/ski-out Sheraton Steamboat Resort Villas is conveniently located next to Christie Peak Express. Gravity Haus is an affordable, slopeside boutique stay. The Amble opened this summer and has 42 residences and resort amenities.

Stats: 23 lifts for 184g trails. One-day lift tickets from $131; on the Ikon Pass.

Of the four mountains that make up Aspen Snowmass, the ultimate rite of passage is here at Aspen Highlands’ massive Highland Bowl. Here’s how to do it: Hike some 45 minutes to the top of the bowl, soak in rewarding 360-degree views that include the twin-peaked Maroon Bells and own the drop into almost 2,500 feet of steep bowl skiing. Reward yourself at mid-mountain with the Merry-Go-Round’s signature Boomerang Burger, topped with onion rings, pastrami bacon and grilled cheese buns.

Where to stay: The Little Nell for five-star service and a great spa or its more casual sister property, Limelight Aspen. That Gant for apartment-style residences with full kitchens.

Stats: 5 lifts for 144 trails. One-day lift tickets from $189; on the Ikon Pass and Mountain Collective pass.

With nearly 5,000 acres of diverse terrain, Heavenly offers the best of both California and Nevada skiing and riding including wide-open groomers, glades, and 1,600-foot mogul runs. Sparkling Lake Tahoe views, an average of 300 days of sunshine a year, and high-energy events and après make Heavenly a dream getaway for your party crew that is always looking for the next adventure. The unique Skyline Trail is a must-do run, taking in majestic mountain landscapes, flat valleys, and lake panoramas while crossing from California to Nevada. Plus, the Heavenly Village is located in the heart of South Lake Tahoe, surrounded by snow-based activities and restaurants, and fun events throughout the winter season. If the views of Lake Tahoe inspire you on the slopes, a trip to the shore is just minutes away.

Where to stay: Basecamp Tahoe South is just a four-minute walk to the gondola and offers a variety of rooms from bunks to luxe tents. Zalanta Resort at the Village is steps away from Heavenly Village and residence-style rooms include gourmet kitchens and private balconies. Lakefront Edgewood Tahoe Resort has a partnership with Ski Butlers to have gear delivered directly to your room.

Stats: 27 lifts for 111 trails. One-day lift ticket from $115; on the Epic Pass.

A winter haven for East Coasters, this Poconos resort’s snow-making capacity could cover the George Washington Bridge with one foot of snow in 24 hours. The mountain’s 900-foot vertical drop is great training before venturing to bigger mountains in the West. More than half of the mountain, however, is covered in beginner-friendly greens. Families love the amenities, including one of the country’s largest snow-tubing park, an indoor water park, and a plethora of dining options including ski-in/ski-out Trail’s End Pub & Grille, known for its creative burgers and craft beer, and Alpine Outpost, a new grab-and-go spot along the Coolmoor teaching trail.

Where to stay: Camelback Lodge, the only ski-in/ski out resort in the Poconos, recently refurbished 453 guest rooms that come in 16 different configurations including bunk rooms and a suite that can sleep up to 14 guests.

Stats: 14 lifts for 45 trails. One-day lift tickets from $78; on the Ikon Pass.

Hard-core skiers who live for hike-to terrain and super steeps have always been fans of Taos Ski Valley. But a revitalized base area with an ice-skating rink, improvements to beginner and intermediate terrain, and $3 million in glading and expanding snowmaking capacity have made this New Mexico mountain destination way more family friendly. Taos Ski Valley leans into sustainability, equity, and inclusivity as the first ski resort in the world to have been B-Corp certified, and one of a few to be Certified CarbonNeutral®. The challenging terrain of Kachina Peak and the moguls of Al’s Run are the big draw for experts. This season ups the resort’s luxury appeal with the introduction of Taos by Belvedere, a fully hosted, all-inclusive mountain experience that features slopeside penthouse accommodations, a private chef, privately guided skiing, restorative wellness therapies, and insider access to local experiences. For dining, the Bavarian is an institution known for its brats and German beers (they also host a sleigh ride dinner during the winter), and newcomer Corner Office gives the state its first natural wine bar. Down days are far from dull thanks to surrounding cultural attractions including the Taos Pueblo UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Where to stay: Located adjacent to Lift 1, The Blake offers a variety of accommodation options that include hotel rooms, suites, penthouses, and condos; decor blends rustic European architecture with one of North America’s finest collections of Southwestern art, including original works by Georgia O’Keeffe.

Stats: 13 lifts for 110 trails. One-day lift tickets from $75; on the Ikon Pass and Mountain Collective pass.

The largest of the SkiBig3 resorts in UNESCO-designated Banff National Park earns its keep with 4,200 acres spanning four different mountain faces and a solid mix of beginner, intermediate, and expert runs from every chair. Here’s what else makes it a dream for all walks of skiers: steeps backed by an awe-inspiring wilderness, bowls dusted in famously dry powder, four terrain parks for beginners to experts, and long cruisers—one of which winds on for five miles. The ‘West Bowl’ is a freeride playground with some 480 wilderness acres to explore. And the recent addition of the Juniper Express Quad provides an ideal learning zone for beginner and intermediate skiers and riders looking to advance their skills. This season, Lake Louise is enhancing its recently opened Richardson’s Ridge terrain with new groomed runs, glades, and improved snowmaking, alongside a major Top of the World chair upgrade designed to increase capacity and reliability.

Where to stay: Located lakeside in Banff National Park, Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise looks like a fairytale castle and its new Basin Glacier Waters Thermal Wellness Spa will have you wishing for a down day to spend soaking in its healing waters. A member of Relais & Châteaux, Post Hotel & Spa has a saltwater pool and is known for its extensive wine cellar and talented culinary team.

Stats: 13 lifts for 169 runs and back bowls. One-day SkiBig3 lift tickets from $172; on the Ikon Pass and Mountain Collective pass.

Nestled on the northern edge of British Columbia’s North Okanagan wine region, SilverStar is one of Canada’s best-kept secrets, with 3,065 skiable acres that receive 275-plus inches of annual snowfall. Guests can skip the rental car and take one of the regular shuttles from Kelowna International Airport, just 55 minutes away. The resort has exceptionally groomed terrain for all abilities and families appreciate that kids age 5 and under receive free lift tickets all season. Alpine skiing is just one of many winter activities on offer. You’ll also find 65 miles of groomed cross-country ski trails, 9 miles of fat-tire bike trails, 4 snow tubing lanes, and a natural skating pond. The dining experiences, such as the Ravenwood snowshoe raclette dinner and the Paradise Camp snow cat dinner tour, are not-to-be-missed. And La Stella, a new Italian spot with wood-fired pizzas debuts this season.

Where to stay: SilverStar’s mid-mountain location means most accommodations are ski-in/ski-out. Snowbird Lodge, Silver Creek Lodge, and Lord Aberdeen have prime locations in the heart of the village, steps from the Summit Express Gondola. Firelight Lodge offers convenient access to the Nordic trail heads.

Stats: 10 lifts for 132 runs. One-day lift ticket from $119; on the Ikon Pass.

Originally known as Little Gap Ski Area when it opened in 1977, the resort changed its name in 1989 to better reflect the grandeur of our mountain. With a vertical drop of 1,082 feet, Blue Mountain boasts the highest elevation in Pennsylvania. Whether you’re a beginner or expert, you’ll find the perfect challenge on the mountain’s 171 acres. You can conquer 15 green, 6 blue, 16 black diamond, and 3 double black diamond trails across the region’s most varied terrain. Home to the East Coast’s largest snowmaking system, the mountain delivers some of the most consistent conditions all season long in the mid-Atlantic region. For lunch with gorgeous views, pop into Slopeside Pub & Grill for wood-fired pizzas and hearty sammys like chicken cheesesteaks. For a quick, grab-and-go bite, swing by the new spud truck, serving up loaded baked potatoes.

Where to stay: Blue Mountain-area Airbnb rentals are the way to go here.

Stats: 15 lifts for 40 trails; One-day lift ticket from $48; on the Ikon Pass.

#6290. United Airlines Finally Plans Boeing 757-300 Makeover With Seatback Screens And Bigger Bins

United Airlines plans to give its Boeing 757-300 fleet a long-overdue cabin update, adding larger overhead bins, entertainment screens at every seat, and power throughout the cabin. These aircraft have needed attention for years and were always included in the United Next refresh plan, though I am somewhat surprised to see United keep these workhorses in the fleet.

United Airlines 757-300 aircraft will be modified in accordance with the United’s “United Next” strategy, which includes installation of new Boeing Space Bins, Panasonic Audio Video On Demand (AVOD), In Flight Entertainment at every seat location, full cabin In-Seat Power Supply System (ISPS), new class dividers and cabin headers, and new UAL branding elements. Additionally, all seats and monuments will be refreshed throughout the cabin.

United:“United Airlines 757-300 aircraft will be modified in accordance with the United's "United Next" strategy, which includes installation of new Boeing Space Bins, Panasonic Audio Video On Demand (AVOD), In Flight Entertainment at every seat location, full cabin In-Seat…

As I mentioned above, the surprise is not that United is refreshing its entire narrwobody fleet, which it has promised for years now, but that it is actually moving forward with the 757-300s rather than phasing them out. However, I also understand that an A321neo or 737 MAX is not necessarily a direct replacement for this workhorse.

My understanding is that one reason this project took longer to get moving was the lack of a certified larger-bin option for this particular aircraft. United had to work through that certification hurdle rather than simply order an existing installation, which puts the delay in context.

United listed just 21 Boeing 757-300s in its year-end 2025 fleet disclosure, each with 234 seats. Undertaking a specialized modification for a fleet that small is a more substantial commitment than fitting the same equipment across hundreds of aircraft. For passengers, however, the size of the subfleet is beside the point. If your flight is operated by a 757-300, the overhead storage and cabin condition are part of your United experience.

More useful bin space should make boarding less stressful: currently there are far too many bags that must be gate checked because the smaller overhead bins force larger (but standard) carry-on bags to be placed on their sides.

I will also be happy to see entertainment screens included throughout the aircraft. When traveling with my children, individual screens are especially useful.

JonNYC also mentions power and it will be great to have USB-C, but the aircraft already have universal A/C power outlets in every cabin.

But what JonNYC does not mention and I consider most important is that these aircraft will get Starlink. Currently, most 757-300s still have an ancient Panasonic Wi-Fi system that often does not work. I specifically avoid the 757-300 for this reason and have been burned almost every time I have flown it with non-operable Wi-Fi. Some 757-300s have been upgraded with Viasat, but I am unwilling to fly on the 753s unless absolutely necessary. The new cabins will be welcomed, but Starlink is the most important upgrade.

I do not object to an aircraft simply because it is older: Delta has shown that a 30-year-old aircraft with mood lighting, fast Wi-Fi, and seatback screens can feel just as comfortable as a more modern aircraft. Refreshed seating and better amenities can change that experience substantially, even when the aircraft itself has been flying for decades.

This investment suggests United sees a continuing role for the 757-300 for many years in the future.

The Boeing 757-300 is finally in line for the kind of cabin attention it has long needed. Larger bins, seatback entertainment, and Starlink Wi-Fi will make a noticeable difference. I figured these aircraft would just be retired, but it appears they will fly the “Friendly Skies” for many years to come.
