#6274. Singapore Airlines Unveils the ‘Largest Double Bed in the Sky’ As Part of a $1.6 Billion Redesign

Getting a good night's sleep on a long-haul flight isn't easy, even when you're lucky enough to be flying first class. But Singapore Airlines—consistently voted as one of the best airlines in the world by CNT readers—is taking things to a whole new level, unveiling what it claims will be “the largest double bed in commercial aviation” as part of a major revamp of its long-haul cabins.

The airline announced the $1.6 billion redesign on Friday, November 6, with the first aircraft expected to enter service in the second half of 2027.

Singapore Airlines's new first class cabin

And the luxury doesn't stop there. The new suites will feature Italian Poltrona Frau leather upholstery, personal wardrobes, dedicated dining spaces, and 32-inch 4K entertainment screens. Passengers can also expect proper bedding, including cotton sheets, duvets, a choice of pillows, and mattress toppers from German bedding specialist Paradies.

The new business class seats also come with adjoining seats, offering the option to sleep alongside a traveling companion.

But what about those of us traveling farther back? Premium economy will benefit from additional personal space, adjustable leg rests, dedicated storage, and larger entertainment screens. Meanwhile, economy passengers can look forward to redesigned seats with more leg space, adjustable headrests, and new storage compartments.

The new economy class will feature more leg space, adjustable headrests, and new storage compartments.

The upgrades will be introduced gradually across Singapore Airlines's new Boeing 777-9 aircraft and 41 retrofitted Airbus A350-900 aircraft, including its ultra-long-range fleet. The latter will also receive first class cabins for the first time.

There's no confirmed date yet for when passengers will be able to try the new double beds, but one thing is certain: cuddling up at 35,000 feet has just become a little more appealing.

#6273. Lufthansa Takes Delivery of Its First A350-1000

Lufthansa this week took delivery of its first Airbus A350-1000, a type it says will offer a better customer experience while reducing operating costs.

The aircraft was formally handed over to the carrier on Tuesday in the presence of Lufthansa Group CEO Carsten Spohr and Lars Wagner, CEO of commercial aircraft at Airbus. Nicknamed “Deutschland,” the jet is Lufthansa’s 700th Airbus airplane, and the seventh in a special commemorative fleet bearing 100th anniversary liveries.

The white and dark blue designs feature an oversized crane, a symbol first used by predecessor Deutsche Luft Hansa.

Lufthansa Group has ordered a total of 15 A350-1000s. The first 10 will operate for the Lufthansa core brand, and will be based at its Munich hub.

“Deutschland” will fly to Munich on Wednesday, officials said, and operate its inaugural flight, to Tokyo-Haneda, on Dec. 3. The aircraft will also be Lufthansa’s first long-haul airplane equipped with Starlink satellite internet service.

“The fact that, as the world’s largest Airbus customer, we are taking delivery of our 700th Airbus aircraft exactly 50 years after the first Airbus delivery to Lufthansa, and in the year of our 100th anniversary, makes this a very special moment for us,” Spohr said in a statement. “Our partnership is a prime example of what Europe can achieve when it works together.”

Lufthansa’s -1000s will seat 300 passengers in four cabins – First, Business, Premium Economy, and Economy.

#6272. This Is The Summer To Tick Santorini Off The Bucket List

It’s June, and for perhaps the first time in modern history, Santorini isn’t crowded. Those earthquakes a good few months ago? Not even a flower pot was tipped over, yet incessant clickbait headlines managed to have a lasting impact.

And that’s a shame, because there’s been a lovely tourism revolution brewing there, where local hoteliers are bringing back the kind of experience and hospitality that you want to come back for over and over again.

As someone who goes at least once or twice a year, and will again very shortly, I can only advocate to tick it off the bucket list this summer, because you’ll never find prices, availability or an experience quite like it again for a while.

In the last 20 years, Santorini got totally overrun. Cruise tourism and day trip mania somewhat ruined a once idyllic, low-key fishing island and then Instagram and TikTok lit the match.

But now the TikTok crowd is in Mykonos and Santorini, as unequalled in beauty as ever, is lovely again. Hotels like The Vasilicos and Santorini Sky bring wildly different, delightfully luxurious and hospitality driven experiences to the island.

Beach clubs, yes Santorini’s beaches are underrated, have made a nice little mark on quieter coasts with great effect too. Assyrtiko, the local grape has hit the world stage as a darling of sommeliers in top restaurants and vineyards like Vassaltis offer stunning tasting experiences.

And the food? There’s no Nobu, or Scorpios here, so there are plenty of places to feel the benefit of European pricing, including a personal favorite at Kantouni.

The trouble with Santorini has historically been that many of the best hotels are small, they fill up quickly, and as they do, they charge a fortune. For the best, like the ones mentioned above, it’s still worth it. But this season, all across the board, prices are lower and even if you don’t care about price, many of the best which might typically be sold out for the season have rooms.

As an additional tailwind for travelers, flights between the US and Europe are quieter this summer, which means there’s deals to be had with both points and cash from major markets to Santorini. If you don’t see cheap flights to Santorini, try a major hub and booking an onward ticket separately.

Naturally, precaution is a good thing in life. But fear mongering for the sake of clicks is another beast and I can’t help but be fairly appalled by the many weeks and months of coverage and follow up coverage, reiterating a narrative of fear… despite no damage to anything, anywhere.

If you do bag a great deal this summer and visit one of my very favorite places, and use this great Santorini guide to make the most of your time, you can thank the media.

#6271. United Airlines Bans AI Booking Agents, But Who Is It Really Protecting?

In a November 11 announcement, United said it is restricting unauthorized third-party personal AI agents across its digital platforms and through travel agencies and aggregators.

The airline warns that sharing credentials with these tools could expose sensitive information or lead to unwanted purchases and account changes. It also raises regulatory concerns, pointing to the acknowledgment passengers must make concerning hazardous materials during check-in.

Those concerns deserve consideration. But they do not adequately explain why an assistant should be prohibited from making a change that I understand, authorize, and could make myself.

United has added the following to its prohibited ticketing practices:

“The use of AI Agents to make, modify or service a Ticket, and/or to purchase any service or product.”

The definition encompasses autonomous and semi-autonomous assistants, including those whose actions a passenger supervises or approves.

We already have tools that monitor airfare and notify us when prices change. I use fare alerts myself. But receiving an alert still leaves me with work to do. I must examine the offer, check the restrictions, and determine whether changing the ticket actually leaves me better off.

Imagine an assistant doing that work continuously, then completing an authorized change whenever the savings justify it based on the parameters I input at the start of the process…something I would happily use.

Consider a hypothetical $800 ticket whose rules allow you to rebook at a lower fare and retain the difference as a future flight credit, with no change fee.

The price drops to $650. Your AI assistant identifies the same flight and fare conditions, completes the permitted change, and secures a $150 credit.

Later, the price drops to $575. It does the calculation again and captures another $75.

You still take the flight you intended to take, but now have $225 available toward future travel.

That is not a cash refund on a nonrefundable ticket, and the actual opportunity depends on the fare rules. But evaluating those complications is precisely what would make the technology useful. Tell it what you want to preserve and when it may act. Let it calculate whether the lower price represents actual savings.

Airline revenue management benefits from passengers behaving differently. Some book early, some wait, and some keep checking after buying. Many understandably consider the transaction finished once the confirmation email arrives.

An assistant that keeps shopping changes that calculation.

A brief fare reduction that I would otherwise miss becomes an opportunity and a small saving that would not justify 20 minutes of my time may become worthwhile when software handles the work. Multiply that across millions of reservations and you can understand why an airline might become uncomfortable.

It would put serious pressure on the ability to retain a higher fare from someone whose ticket permits a lower-price exchange. The airline could still set its prices and restrictions, but fewer customers would leave available savings unclaimed merely because they were busy living their lives.

I suspect United understands this very well. This strikes me as a preemptive move to control who can manage a reservation before automated consumer tools become an ordinary part of travel.

These new rules do not suggest that United intends to eliminate every fare alert: the more consequential restriction is preventing the assistant from acting on what it finds.

I would not hand any application unrestricted control of my MileagePlus account and yes, I do not want software canceling an important trip because it misunderstood an instruction. But those are reasons to establish permissions and accountability.

United’s hazardous-materials example is particularly weak as a justification for prohibiting reservation management. The federal passenger-notification rule requires disclosures and passenger acknowledgment in specified circumstances. Reading that requirement, I do not see why an assistant could not stop and ask the traveler to complete the necessary acknowledgment personally.

More to the point, checking whether my ticket can be exchanged for a lower fare does not require an assistant to make a declaration about what is inside my suitcase. A responsible system should require approval where needed and limit what software can do. United’s restriction still encompasses an assistant whose actions I supervise and approve.

So no, I do not accept the customer-protection explanation.

Scott Kirby offered a more revealing observation at a Chicago event, according to The Wall Street Journal:

“To be honest, I don’t want to create another middleman.”

I understand why United would prefer to control the customer relationship, but my interests are not identical to United’s. I may want someone working for me, comparing the options and continuing to look after my reservation once United has collected payment.

I recently examined Kirby’s argument that technology helps make United the best airline in the world. I agree that its app is excellent. Better technology has made my United travel easier. But I also want technology that helps me spend less. An assistant that understands my preferences and captures an eligible fare reduction would be doing exactly that.

United should explain what secure, authorized access would require. Simply blocking an AI assistant carte blanche protects the airline’s control much more clearly than it protects my interests.

United says its restrictions on third-party AI agents protect customers. I think they also–and primarily–protect United from a future in which passengers can monitor and manage reservations far more effectively than they do today.

Just as airlines use complex algorithms to extract the highest fare fro Mme, I want to use technology to help capture savings without having to babysit every reservation.

To me, this looks like a cheap shot dressed up as customer protection. United is entitled to secure its systems, but I am far less sympathetic to using that explanation to block an authorized assistant from helping me obtain a better deal.

#6270. 14 Best Steakhouses in New York City for Old-School Chops, Wagyu, and the Perfect Martini

No single steakhouse can beat out all the others in NYC. Each has its strengths, and some are certainly better than others. There are the classics—Keens and Gallaghers in Midtown, Delmonico's in the Financial District, Peter Luger over in Williamsburg—that have been here for a hundred years or more, and for good reason. They are dimly-lit, tavern-like, with walls clad in wood. The menus do not change. The new and newish guard variously emulate and do their own thing. Increasingly, we are seeing steakhouses taking the basic assignment—red meat and sides in a formal dining room—and running with it in various cultural directions. Below, we've rounded up our favorites across this board. What's most important is their shared ability to make its diner feel important, a feat that goes beyond (but does require) the ability to gorge on good steak.

Read our complete New York City guide here, which includes:

Seagram Building, 99 E 52nd St, Midtown Manhattan

I am forming the opinion that a steakhouse's cardinal function is to make its diners feel important. No place has succeeded so impeccably in this mission as The Grill, where I was whisked from a downstairs lobby into the glamorous dining room as though a visiting board member come to town to be courted and impressed. I went for lunch, so the metal chain curtains that undulate (yes, they are ever-moving) over the massive windows shimmered in the daylight. Everyone except for me, it seemed, as there on very important business. I was the only male diner that I could see not in a jacket. The menu is very spendy (you cannot get a cocktail for less than $26) and therefore especially reserved for special occasions. Peppered filet mignon and martini, I'd say, are the way to go, but if it's lunch and the prime rib roast beef sandwich is being served, it's a worthy detour. —C.H.

The best thing that happened to me at 4 Charles Prime Rib was that I made a new friend. Steak and martinis and burgers, they're all fabulous—make no mistake. But sometimes it’s the life that comes at you in pursuit of those delicious menu items that leaves you feeling the most full. Too corny? Allow me to elaborate.

4 Charles is one of the toughest tables in town. Like Torrisi, it’s practically a private members' club where the only people who can land a reservation are those who’ve eaten there before. Hopeful walk-ins start lining up over an hour before opening at 4 p.m., and I got there at 2:45 p.m. to find myself second in line. I sat on the West Village townhouse stoop and enjoyed the day, enjoyed the sight of the staff puttering around setting up, glared at the people with reservations who we in line agreed were “line cutters.” When the host began seating people around 3:45 p.m., she told me that I was the first single walk-in and would therefore enjoy the one table by the door that they reserve for such parties. The man behind me, who arrived nary five minutes after I did, was told he would therefore have to wait until I was done. “Can’t I just sit with him?” he asked in earnest bewilderment. “Sure!” I responded.

And so together we unhinged our jaws and ate the 10-ounce double wagyu smash burger with thick slabs of bacon, his with an egg, and together we poured the beef jus over the pink center of the titular 4 Charles Cut and expressed our unexpected delight with the horseradish cream accoutrement. Together we drank martinis—I, a perfect vesper; he, an espresso; and then a chocolate each. If you’re going to try to go, I recommend you do so in this way. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

Peter Luger isn't just the Brooklyn steakhouse. It just might be the New York City steakhouse, especially if history carries any weight with you, dear reader. This fine establishment has sat at the same address in the Williamsburg Bridge's shadow since 1887, and the interiors carry about as many frills as your average public house—dark wood, plaster walls, and so on. The menu is just as unadorned, with the most popular menu items being the dry-aged steak for two, steak for three, or steak for four. You can also, rest assured, get a single steak, lamb chops, salmon, or filet of sole. The Luger's sizzling bacon is not to be missed, nor are the sliced tomatoes and onions with Luger's Own sauce (pro tip: they go quite well together.) If you're there before 3:45 p.m., you'd also be wise to order the over-½-lb Luger burger, which is so simple and bloody with optional American cheese that your eyes will roll back in your head. —C.H.

This summer, the Montecito and Malibu staple Lucky's Steakhouse came to roost on a bustling street in New York’s Soho—and has been a fun addition to the city’s oft-stodgy steakhouse landscape ever since. Importantly, it’s a cool counterpoint—with its intimate size, Jazz Age-y murals, sexy date-night vibe, and a menu that accommodates non-steak eaters (i.e. me, a pescatarian). I know what you’re thinking: Why is a non-meat eater reviewing Lucky’s? Well, precisely for the fact that steakhouses can be wincingly non-inclusive, despite often being the restaurant of choice on special occasions. And Lucky’s feels different, not least because of its ambience. On a recent night, we started with the oysters, the peaky-toe crab cocktail, house chips, and Jimmy’s Greek salad (named after a family member of the owner). I then got the salmon, initially a perverse choice—because it usually plays poor country cousin at most steakhouses—but it was excellent. And we really dug into the sides—onion rings, market vegetables, and creamed corn. Both times I ate there, my companions ordered the 10-oz Gene’s Filet and I heard murmurs of firm approval. Whatever your dietary preference, don’t miss Lucky’s martini service, for which multiple servers will shake (or stir) your drinks table-side and in unison—because a little theatre hurts no one.

Head 10 blocks south of New York’s Koreatown (see an itinerary of the neighborhood here), and you'll find Cote, a Korean steakhouse and one of the city’s best and buzziest restaurants. There’s no shortage of a la carte options, but the prix-fixe Butcher’s Feast is where diners should start. For $74 a person, you're treated to seasonal ban-chan, savory egg soufflé, two stews (including spicy kimchi stew), and the house selection of beef, including USDA Prime and Wagyu, cooked on the table with smokeless grills. The restaurant’s award-winning wine list features an impressive Champagne selection, and all by-the-glass pours come from Magnums, the large-format bottles that sommeliers say keeps wines younger and fresher. There's also a second location at 550 Madison that's a bit grander, should that suit you. —D.F.

Gallaghers is the best steakhouse to eat at before a Broadway show. Wood paneled walls covered in framed old photographs (one of singer Perry Comon had to be labeled “this is not Jeffrey Epstein” due to those two men’s shared resemblance) offset the inhumane Midtown environment just beyond the front door. This is a place that’s as good for steak (and it really is good for steak) as it is for all of the accoutrements one expects of a good steakhouse—beyond the bovine, highlights include the old fashioned, the creamed spinach, the house-smoked bacon, and the beautifully browned veal chop parmigiana. Putting it all over the edge is the people watching—real live businesspeople drowning their sorrows at the bar alongside the theatergoers, and haughty waiters doing buttoned-up to the max. —C.H.

The only difficult choice to make when entering Keens is where to look first. Is it up, at the 90,000 pipes lining the ceiling? To the glass cases, where the most famous churchwardens—15-inch pipes—smoked by the likes of Babe Ruth and General MacArthur are stored? In the bar, are you mesmerized by the Miss Keen painting (a nude, lounging on her bear rug) right away, or are you too distracted by the New-York-ad-men-in-the-'50s vibe? This steakhouse, open since 1883, delivers something new to look at every time you go. Keens was originally called a chop house, in recognition of its famous mutton chop, and although that is good and musty and intense, most people are ordering steak. There’s the porterhouse for two or three, the chateaubriand, and the filet mignon—which is actually fabulous here. You want the béarnaise or au poivre sauce on the side, and the creamed spinach, which is less a vegetable than it is dessert. There's also the matter of the burger, which can be ordered up to the dining room from the more casual bar menu. —Alex Van Buren

1271 Avenue of the Americas, Midtown Manhattan

From the moment you walk into Cuerno, there's a sense of importance—the crowd, in suits and slicked back hair, is well-dressed; the dining room is always bustling and full, necks turning to see who else has walked in; and tableside preparations are happening left and right. This is Northern Mexican meat at its finest, in a space that feels true to that spirit—big leather booths, a colorful tile mural of a skeleton riding a bull—and with a menu that won't let you down. There are expected starters, like fresh guac and queso fundido, but also a chicarrón de pulpo bursting with flavor, and a charcoal-roasted cauliflower complemented by truffle and habanero. The main event, of course, are the steaks, like the decadent Taco Taquero with perfect skirt steak, and fire-roasted bone marrow scooped onto each tortilla tableside, or the Norteño-style arrachera served with chiltepin butter and avocado salsa.

Portions are generous, so come in a group of four people minimum to actually try different sections of the menu. And though most steakhouses focus on wine (and the wine list is good here), I like the chance to pair smoky mezcal and tequila cocktails with the heavier food. —Megan Spurrell

355 Metropolitan Ave, Williamsburg, Brooklyn

Not just in Williamsburg, not just in New York City, but truly one of the coziest, best-value steakhouses I’ve ever been to, St. Anselm manages a rare balance: laid-back yet elevated, intimate without trying too hard, and consistently delicious. The space feels like a hidden tavern—dark wood, low light, and just enough buzz and energy to make it feel like a special night out. The Butcher’s Steak is the standout—charred to perfection, tender and juicy inside, and ideal for sharing (for two) alongside fingerling potatoes and long green beans. Go for a group lunch or, better yet, settle in after dark when the candles are lit and the place feels like a warm, secret pocket of the city. Ask your server—or better yet, belly up to the bar—and you’ll get a wine recommendation that pairs not just with the food, but with your mood. —Jessica Chapel

513 E 6th Street, East Village, Manhattan

Buenos Aires earns major points for nostalgia: The tiny dining room is adorned in hanging soccer jerseys, televisions showing live games and commentary, and scarfs and pendants for teams like the Boca Juniors. There are couples on dates, families with kids, and even, in my case, a dude who came in alone and ordered his regular with his headphones in. (Ask about celebrities and they'll bring out an iPad with photos of grinning staff beside countless Latin America soccer players, American actors, and even Matt Damon who apparently hosted two birthday parties here in the early 2000s.) All to say, this isn't the place to bring the corporate account or close the deal, but it is the place to roll up your sleeves and tuck into a massive skirt steak, expertly cooked, and served no-frills—just a great piece of meat on a plate. Do save room for the empanadas (carne cortada a cuchillo, of course); on my next visit, I'm planning to order the sweetbreads as well. —M.S.

Glam, glam, glam with a capital G. Golden Steer's New York iteration—the original is in Vegas, and little of that location's trademark opulence has been sacrificed in adapting the brand for New York. We're not in Midtown either, but in the West Village, and this is a fitting addition to that neighborhood as it increasingly wears its wealth on its sleeve. Entering this crimson bunker is a cinematic experience—long hallways flanked by side quests like the capacious but moody bar. What to get? Sink into your plush booth and go full Sin City: the bloody bull oyster shooter (where a rich beef broth-spiked shot of bloody mary chases the slime), the big ole baked potato, and a Caesar dotingly mixed tableside. Any cut of meat will do. —C.H.

56 Beaver St, Financial District, Manhattan

The definitive downtown steakhouse is also New York City's oldest. Its home since 1837 is 56 Beaver Street, a dramatic triangular lot at the intersection of Beaver, William, and South William in the Financial District. When I visited on a mid-May evening, the exterior was bedecked in American regalia—they were to film an episode of The Gilded Age there the next day (the new season is currently airing on HBO) depicting the ticker tape parade welcoming the Statue of Liberty to the city. All of this history would be moot were the steakhouse inside not very good, which it is from top to bottom—superlative, doting service in the mural-clad dining room, stiff drinks, perfect cuts of meat. As with every steakhouse, there are a couple of signature items beyond steak that you should consider. Here, it's wedge salad and buttery Lobster Newberg, said to have been invented there. Don't miss either, but steak is still the thing, namely the titular flagship cut—a glistening 18-ounce ribeye that stands alone on the plate, needing no accoutrements. —Charlie Hobbs

Dinner and a show in New York City’s midtown sounds fabulous, but in practice usually means settling for a meal that delivers more on convenience than cuisine or atmosphere. Carvesteak, a newish steakhouse on the west side of 48th street, stepped up to all these qualities after I saw The Rocky Horror Show earlier this year. Designed by David Rockwell and the Rockwell Group, it’s moody, mirrored interiors are filled with little nods to the Broadway history it shoulders—including a dramatic velvet curtain that the bartender at the martini bar told me was once part of the set for Andrew Lloyd Webber’s Phantom of the Opera (even if untrue, it certainly looked the part). Speaking of the martini bar, it’s not to be missed: a pocket-sized station to post yourself up at before or after dinner. Food-wise, this is a classic steakhouse menu, but with a little bit of flashiness thanks to the restaurant’s Las Vegas origins (it debuted at Resorts World Las Vegas in 2021): think, prime cuts and aged rib eyes with all the sides and sauces you would expect, but also the option to order a potato and caviar “popsicle.” There’s a pre-theater menu, too, but for the full experience I suggest coming hungry and catching the last call before 10 p.m. —Lale Arikoglu

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6269. Wander.com: Best Luxury Take On Airbnb (With Real Value Too?)

At first, the big hotel chains of the world laughed off Airbnb and vacation rentals. No seriously, they did. Now, they all compete in the vacation rental business and act like it was always the plan.

The problem for the traveler, is that almost all of the newer entrants just plug into a massive pipeline of already existing vacation homes and apartments and pop them on their own branded website with no added luxury, differentiation, amenity or expertise in curation.

There’s no huge unlock of new places or highly curated places that you could virtually always stamp as worth recommending to a friend, the way you’d rate an Aman, St. Regis, or Four Seasons hotel.

This is precisely where Wander.com comes in, and it’s by far my favorite luxe vacation rental platform to date. The fact that it’s boutique and limited is what makes it, at least for me. And, the $350 off Wander promo code doesn’t hurt either.

Wander is a vacation rental company which truly hand picks every property that it lists, and has the exclusive listing on. Crucially, each of the vacation properties undergoes a sort of ‘Wander’ transformation to conform with brand standards for wifi, amenity, style and vibe.

It’s above my pay-grade as a blogger on this topic, but it seems like Wander co-invests in the real estate portfolio’s, or partners with owners in a unique way that’s far more integrated than others.

Where are they? Most Wander.com properties are scattered across the US, from the shores of Malibu to the great National Parks in Wyoming and all along the Eastern seaboard too. Hawaii is also a recent addition. New destinations keep popping up!

Each of their properties feels uniquely wonderful and aspirational, and I’d say all have a very modern and contemporary slant to luxury. Grandma’s cabinets are not in any of these homes, but Tesla chargers are. One nice touch: each Wander offers a dedicated workspace with desk, chair, monitors and lightning fast wifi.

I completely respect that all tastes are individual, but the interiors and setups of these homes much more reflect my personal tastes, more minimalist chic, than many less curated vacation rental options.

Most Wander properties are around $1000 a night. Some will be half that, some will be double. On its face, that’s intimidating to many, but when you factor in the number of bedrooms and features it’s really reasonable. Families, or multi-family get togethers… amazing.

All Wander.com properties are at least two bedrooms and many are four, five or even twelve. One is an entire island with multiple residential complexes. For me, I love these sort of getaways for catching up with family or friends, and I never mind when other people are contributing too.

We’ve had some of our best ever vacations renting a house in Palm Springs for weeks or months at a time. Often, family or friends want in too, so we split the house and end up with two bedrooms each for under $500 per night.

We’ve used these bonus rooms and features to socialize or catch up with people in the serenity of the home, not annoyed by service, crowded pools or tight room setups. For a longer stay, I absolutely hate having to rely on a hotel kitchen for every meal. I love to hit a local market and grill with family or guests.

Wander is offering $350 off first bookings, which is a great way to get started. To browse the homes, you simply download the Wander app and start doom scrolling. When you find one you’re ready to book, the process is very self explanatory and easy to share with others.

I’m personally a fan of virtually California vacation and the properties offered on the platform cover everything from Palm Springs to Napa and all in between in stunning form. The $350 off is a solid discount and combined with new property discounts, which are frequent, there is a lot to love. You can browse Wander and download the app here.

If you don’t see the Wander.com discount in your account, you can add promo code AKFVDFD7 once the app is downloaded.

Alaska Airlines is rolling out a new invite-only status level called Atmos Global Concierge. Like the other major U.S. airlines that have such a tier, Alaska is not publicly disclosing what it takes to earn an invitation — though you can be sure it will require a lot of spending.

News of Alaska's new invite-only tier began spreading across aviation blogs Tuesday, and the company confirmed the move to TPG.

"Atmos Global Concierge is a new, invitation-only program," said Alaska in a statement, " ...  that, in addition to all the award-winning benefits of Atmos Rewards membership, provides personalized travel support when you need it the most."

For now, this is a beta program rollout, so it's likely to change over time.

In addition to published top tiers, like American Airlines' AAdvantage Executive Platinum, Delta's Diamond Medallion and United Airlines' Premier 1K, all three major U.S. carriers offer an even higher level of status generally saved for the elites who spend the most with the airline (and some travel providers and C-level executives and celebrities).

American Airlines has ConciergeKey, Delta Air Lines has 360, and United Airlines has Global Services. And now Alaska has Atmos Global Concierge.

None of these airlines publicly disclose the exact qualification requirements for their invitation-only programs, which makes pontificating about what it takes to qualify something of an unofficial pastime for loyalty die-hards.

Among the theories: Invites are tied not only to flight spending, but also to credit card spending and even to your home airport. For example, an American Airlines frequent flyer based at the carrier's Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) hub might have a harder time securing an invitation than a similarly high-spending traveler based in a more competitive market.

Alaska isn't revealing the full list of benefits that come with its new status, but it did share some details with TPG.

"Members are supported by a dedicated Concierge team throughout their journey, including proactive trip monitoring and travel assistance, along with exclusive benefits and curated experiences," Alaska said.

That means help with travel disruptions, such as a next-flight guarantee and dedicated, specialized assistance.

Reports suggest other benefits include the ability to gift Gold status, a free Clear+ membership and Avis Chairman's Club status. Those invited are also reportedly being given Atmos Titanium status, even if they haven't already qualified organically this year.

If Alaska follows the lead of its larger competitors, additional perks could include VIP airport transfers, higher upgrade priority and expanded lounge access. However, Alaska has not confirmed those benefits.

As for what it might take to get invited to this special club, it will likely require spending tens of thousands of dollars on tickets. Some reports suggest the invitations appear to be targeted at potential customers for Alaska's new international routes with lie-flat business class. On the flip side, some Titanium-level Alaska flyers haven't been invited even after earning as many as 250,000 Alaska Atmos status points and buying international business-class tickets.

"Through this beta program, we’re creating new ways to recognize some of our most loyal members as our global network grows," Alaska told TPG.

While this won't mean much for most of us, it's still exciting to see a new layer of potential perks for some of Alaska's most loyal flyers. Alaska has been one of the most innovative U.S. airlines when it comes to loyalty, so it's an interesting development to see the carrier recognize its highest-value customers with an invite-only tier that matches what the other big global U.S. airlines have done.

Alaska is also now the only major U.S. airline that lets you earn elite status from actual flight miles (though you can choose to earn status by spending). A new top-tier status level is another way the airline is differentiating itself.

#6267. A Thief Grabbed His Backpack From A Delta Carousel At JFK, But A Friend Tracked Him Down In Washington, DC

A stolen backpack at New York JFK could have been the start of a miserable few weeks for travel writer JT Genter. Instead, it became an interstate detective story involving a luggage tracker, a bus number, and fellow travel writer Jamie Larounis riding in a Washington, D.C. police car. This one has a happy ending…and Jamie deserves a huge round of applause.

JT, who writes about points and miles and nomadically travels full-time with his wife Katie, reported that his checked bag had been stolen from Delta’s baggage claim belt at JFK Terminal 4. Before leaving the terminal, he filed a missing-baggage claim with Delta and a police report.

Ugh. Checked baggage stolen off of @Delta baggage claim belt in JFK Terminal 4.

Delta missing baggage claim and police report filed before leaving the terminal.

Never had this happen before. Happy for any tips on what to do next.

— JT Genter (@JTGenter) November 11, 2026

He subsequently explained that the backpack contained his clothing, medication, toiletries, and irreplaceable mementos. He was also decidedly unimpressed by the response from Delta employees.

For someone who lives on the road, that is considerably more than losing a suitcase of vacation clothes. Understandably, his bag contains much of his daily life. Replacing the contents becomes another job, and some things cannot simply be purchased again.

But there was something JT had deliberately left out of his initial account.

People understandably suggested that he should have put a tracker inside. In a subsequent update, JT revealed that he already had one. He had kept that information private while police were tracking the man.

And to be precise, this was a Tile tracker, rather than an Apple AirTag.

I appreciate the restraint. When something like this happens, the temptation is to post every development, especially when people are offering advice (and condemnation) about the precaution you already took.

But the more useful audience for those location updates was the people who could actually help recover the bag.

According to Jamie’s account, the man took the stolen backpack from New York to Washington, DC on Amtrak.

Using the Tile location, Jamie found a man with the bag at a bus station. Then the man boarded a bus.

That could have been the end of the opportunity, but Jamie caught the bus number and found two police officers willing to help. The officers located the suspect a few blocks away and apprehended him.

They then asked Jamie to ride in the police car to identify the man. Afterward, they went to the station to retrieve the items.

Jamie summed up his unexpected afternoon rather nicely:

“Gotta say, I didn’t have being in a Metropolitan Police cop car on my bingo card today”

https://twitter.com/TheForwardCabin/status/2120615885626835334?a=hFcZDL9PoGdHYVjUzks&s=20

Usually when someone ends up in a police car, the story has taken a less encouraging turn. This was a very welcome exception!

I also love that the bus number became such a useful detail. The tracker got Jamie close enough to spot the bag, but paying attention when the man boarded gave the officers something concrete to work with.

I know Jamie, and I am delighted to see him get credit for this.

There is a considerable difference between feeling sorry for someone who has lost a bag and going out to help find it. Jamie gave his time and followed through when the situation became more complicated than simply spotting a backpack.

The police officers deserve credit too. A location on a tracking app is useful, but recovering stolen property still requires someone to act on that information and I don’t consider it very smart to confront a thief directly. In this case, Jamie found officers who helped turn a promising lead into an actual recovery.

JT’s response to Jamie was understandably enthusiastic:

He also expressed amazement at how much had been recovered. A great story involving two people I consider friends.

A backpack stolen from a JFK baggage carousel ended up in Washington, where a tracker and a determined friend helped police catch the suspect and recover belongings.

What a satisfying ending. So many missing-bag stories conclude with a claim number and a disappointing reimbursement discussion. This one concluded with Jamie doing some excellent detective work and JT getting back possessions he thought he might never see again.

Well done, Jamie. That is friendship in action!

Good work Jamie. Glad the police gave you a safe assist!

If he’s such an experienced traveler why is he checking his backpack with medication and “momentos?”

I’m sure the Delta baggage people reminded him of his amateur move which is why he claims that they weren’t helpful.

But, more importantly…why didn’t he post a picture of the thief?

Some of us travel in and out of T4 at JFK and it would be helpful to know who the real garbage is.

Did I miss the part where he says he has a picture of thief? Or do you mean Jamie?

He took and posted pictures of the stolen bag.

It would have been really helpful to have taken a picture of the thief at the same time.

In lieu of that…a nice follow up from him could be a link to the publication of the thief’s official mugshot.

Well, I do have photos of the thief from the JFK security cams and from Jamie’s pursuit. But I’m going to let justice play itself out in the courts, not online.

JT is full time global nomad and does carry several weeks of meds in his carry on. This backpack contains pretty much everything else he travels the world with. This is a little different than a normal vacationer.

“Once again, when the crunch is on, Delta Airlines Staff prove to be absolutely indifferent to the travelers’ plight”.

Just ask the 1.3 million travelers stranded for days during Crowdstrike.

I disagree…the Delta baggage services people gave him some much needed tough love.

Never put medications or “irreplaceable mementos” is checked bags.

The key momento was too large to fit in our carry-on bags, or it would’ve been in there with the others.

As far as medications go, I carry a few weeks’ worth in my carry-on bags. But, since we live on the road and can’t always get an easy refill, I typically have additional meds in my checked bag — along with over-the-counter meds and suppliments.

I had someone steal a brand new shirt, still in the plastic bag, from an outside pocket of a checked carryon (yes, it should have been in the case, but it was a last minute purchase). I reported it to Delta and periodically received “we’re looking for your bag” updates. I must have told them 10 times, I have my bag, someone stole a shirt from the bag itself. Finally, they closed the case, saying “sorry, we cannot locate your bag.” I went to the baggage office at my local airport, explained that the item had been stolen from the checked luggage. The agent asked how much it cost and I showed her the receipt. She wrote me a check on the spot. Delta’s online baggage claims service is terrible.

How did Jamie have the location? Is that something JT shared with him?

Yes, I was able to share a link with Jamie that had the live-updating Tile tracking information.

#6266. The Best Stocking Stuffer for Jet-Setters Is This Viral Handbag Accessory

If there’s one thing I love almost as much as planning a trip, it’s having a cute lineup of travel gear to help me get there. The perfect carry-on, a reliable travel tote, a passport holder that doesn’t look like everyone else’s—and, as of late, a bag charm (or three). The accessory du jour has officially made its way from our handbags to our airport ensembles, and I can’t think of a more delightful stocking stuffer for the traveler in your life.

Commerce writer Jessica Chapel is showing off Coach's signature cherry bag charm

Bag charms have a longer fashion history than their current moment suggests: Jane Birkin famously adorned her namesake Hermès with personal keepsakes. Hermès then introduced its Rodeo charm in 2005, and Fendi sent its furry Monster charms down the runway in 2013. After a runway revival at Miu Miu and Balenciaga shows in 2024, the look made its way back to stylish travelers everywhere.

It makes sense, really: We put so much thought into what we pack and what we carry, so why not have a little fun with the bags that get us there? A bag charm is an easy way to give a well-loved weekender a fresh look, or make that familiar canvas tote feel a bit more like your own. There are colorful beads, mini leather accessories, nostalgic trinkets, whimsy characters, and even designs with a practical purpose. Some bag charms are simply there to look good; others offer a clever place to tuck away small essentials. And when your suitcase is circling the baggage carousel among a sea of lookalikes, a fun, personal detail is hardly a bad thing.

Beyond the styling, I like to think of bag charms as a new kind of travel keepsake. We’re always bringing pieces of our trips home: a street market find, a knickknack from a beach town, some wonderfully impractical souvenir that means everything to us and very little to anyone else. Rather than tucking them away on a shelf, clip these charms onto a tote or suitcase, and they’ll join you for the next adventure. The same goes for a charm gifted by a friend or one that reminds you of home. Nothing says, “think of me on the road,” quite like this.

Bag charms add a pop of color to a neutral bag or suitcase

And there’s no shortage of ways to make the look your own. Layer a few bag charms together, mixing colors, textures, and shapes, or keep things more understated with a single leather accent or jewelry-like detail. Think of it as accessorizing your luggage with the same consideration you give the rest of your travel outfit. Whether you’re shopping for the friend who’s always planning a weekend away, the family member with an enviable vintage luggage collection, or the frequent flier who appreciates thoughtful detail, there’s something in the mix for just about every kind of traveler.

Bag charms are small, they’re personal, they’re wonderfully extra, and truthfully, a whole lot more exciting to unwrap than another pair of compression socks. (Sorry, compression socks). Ahead, I’ve rounded up the best bag charms to gift this season, from playful fashion finds and colorful conversation starters to travel-friendly designs that do a little more than just look pretty.

A little cherry on top, quite literally. Made from glittery resin and metal, this bright red pick brings a playful pop of color to a tote, backpack, or set of keys. It’s a particularly good choice for the friend whose wardrobe could always use one more fun thing.

For the person who prefers their accessories a little more understated—but still appreciates a good detail—this bad boy pairs deep green beads with gold-tone hardware and a lobster clasp, offering their favorite bag a subtle hit of color and texture.

For the New Yorker in your life, here's some Big Apple nostalgia to take on the road. Kate Spade pays homage to its hometown with this mini MetroCard-inspired design—and for those who remember the ol’ swipe of a subway card, it's a fun yet tasteful piece of the city to carry along.

I’m adding this gold boot gem to my cart. For a little Western flair—minus the need to break in a new pair of boots—the iconic brand Tecovas has turned its Loretta boot into a mini accessory crafted from solid brass with an antique finish. It comes with both a key ring and a D-ring, so it can go wherever its owner does—whether that’s a road trip, a dude ranch weekend, or simply the daily commute.

Talk about chic! Sézane’s Juliette keychain has a caramel-color resin exterior with delicate white lace detailing, but the real treat is inside: a pocket mirror that opens with a pivoting mechanism. It’s ideal for a quick lipstick check before stepping off the train or heading out to dinner.

For the friend who has approximately 1,000 photos of their dog on their phone—and would happily add one more to the rotation. This little Jack Russell is embroidered onto supple full-grain leather, with a debossed Lauren Ralph Lauren logo on the back. A rather handsome stand-in for a four-legged travel buddy.

A handbag for your handbag? I’m listening. This mini zippered pouch is styled like a classic carryall, with leather construction and gold-tone hardware, and clips onto a larger bag to keep small essentials close. It’s available in red, cobalt blue, and silver, and can be personalized with a foil-debossed monogram—making it an especially sweet gift for a loved one.

A little luck for the road never hurts! This Madewell design brings together a wishbone, stone, and moon motif in a red-and-gold-toned cluster, and is finished with a dog-clip closure. It’s a playful pick for the friend who loves a meaningful trinket—or could use a little good fortune on their next big adventure.

For the friend who's always planning their next trip, this miniature version of Away’s signature hard-shell carry-on is made from the same durable polycarbonate shell and opens into two little compartments for small essentials like a spare key or folded cash. It clips onto a bag or backpack, and the Coast Blue shade is a nice nod to the real thing.

Meet the mini-me of one of our editors' favorite travel bags. Calpak's best-selling Luka duffel—this compact zip pouch comes in a pearlescent finish and clips onto a larger bag with a carabiner-ready loop. Better yet, it actually earns its keep: There’s room for keys, earbuds, cash, or whatever small essentials you’d rather not fish around for at the bottom of your tote.

A flower that doesn’t need watering—or a vase. Inspired by the marigolds of Diwali, this three-dimensional design is made from layered Italian leather petals and comes in yellow or orange. The leather leaf can also be monogrammed, making it a thoughtful gift with a personal touch. It’s a lovely way to bring a little color to someone’s everyday bag.

#6265. My First “New” Chase Sapphire Reserve Travel Redemption Blew My Mind

There’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the new changes.

The changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

Chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

Which leads me to the important bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a new “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

Previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the new version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

I am in New York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

Typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

If I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive…

Yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

For the first time I can remember, transferring points to Hyatt was not the best option here and that’s something to stand up and take notice of.

If Chase can keep up this Points Boost game, it can really send ripples through rewards. For the first time, people can easily receive tremendous value for their points through a credit card portal while still earning elite status and points with the hotel or airline of their choosing.

You can check out the new 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.

#6264. 13 Travel Slippers That Are Comfier Than the Ones From Your Favorite Hotel

After a full day of sightseeing—or an even longer one spent in and out of airports—few things feel better than kicking off your shoes and sliding on a cozy pair of slippers. The complimentary slippers at a luxury hotel are always tempting to take home, but if we're honest, they rarely last beyond a few wears. Fortunately, plenty of more durable—and more comfortable—options exist, from plush, shearling slides and classic wool slip-ons to lightweight travel slippers that barely take up any room in your suitcase. Some have cushioned footbeds and rubber soles sturdy enough for a quick trip outside; others feature soft, suede soles better suited to padding around the house.

Whether you want a warm, fluffy pair by your bed or a foldable option for your next long-haul flight, there’s a slipper for everyone on this list. Read on for the very best pairs to pick up this season from Bombas, Cozy Earth, Ugg, and more.

⁠These lightweight, fuzzy slippers feature a soft, wool-like polyester upper, a breathable lining, and a memory foam footbed for a cushy feel underfoot. The nonslip soles are sturdy enough for quick trips outside to grab the mail or take out the trash, but they're best suited for indoor wear. Even better, they're machine washable, so you can easily keep them in pristine condition all season long. Available in five colors and backed by more than 10,000 Amazon reviews, they're an affordable option for wearing around the house or packing for a weekend away.

It's easy to see why this under-$25 Amazon find has racked up more than 23,000 five-star ratings. Not only are these slippers ridiculously soft (and just the right amount of over-the-top), but they're also pretty practical, thanks to the thick memory foam insole that retains its shape even after daily wear.

While your winter wardrobe likely contains a cashmere sweater or two, don’t sleep on these cashmere slides from Garnet Hill. Thanks to the slip-on slides’ sumptuous cashmere construction and breathable, thermal-insulating fibers, they’ll keep your feet warm and toasty—but not sweaty—all winter long. The padded footbed provides an extra layer of pillowy-soft comfort.

After a long day on your feet, you'll be glad to have these Quince slippers waiting by your bed. They have a soft suede leather upper and thick Australian shearling lining that feels plush against bare feet. And unlike some fuzzy slippers that leave your feet sweaty, the shearling material naturally wicks away moisture and regulates temperature, so you can wear them year-round.

The soft, moisture-wicking sheepskin wool lining of this classic shoe has made it an all-time favorite from the nostalgic Australian brand. The Scuff comes with a thin rubber sole that has just the right amount of support and stability for being on your feet in the kitchen or just puttering around the house on the weekend. Colors include the popular chestnut (shown above), dark gray, and black.

This luxury slide keeps your feet dry and cool, thanks to its moisture-wicking and temperature-regulating design. They're fluffy and warm, and so easy to slip on when you first wake up in the morning. Plus, they feature a slip-resistant sole, making them one of the sturdiest picks on the list.

One of the little luxuries of a hotel stay is slipping into the plush robes and slippers hanging in the closet. Now you can capture that vacation-level comfort at home with The Ritz-Carlton Frette slippers. Crafted from ultra-soft microfiber, they feel cozy and spa-like, while the nonslip soles make them practical for everyday wear around the house. The embroidered hotel logo adds a touch of opulence, and when they need a refresh, simply toss them in the wash.

These striped slippers from Parachute look like something you'd find at a cool boutique hotel. Made in Turkey from thick, absorbent cotton terry, they're soft underfoot and comfortable to slip on after a shower or while lounging at home. The stripes add a little more personality than your typical spa slippers, and the rubber soles grip slippery floors effortlessly. They're durable enough for everyday wear, too, though you may want to size up for a roomier fit.

Made with ultra-soft sheep fur and a plush shearling lining, these chic slippers provide plenty of warmth on chilly fall and winter mornings. As warm as they are, they're also naturally odor-resistant and breathable, so you don't have to worry about your feet getting too hot. They offer a grippy, durable outsole, so while they're best suited for lounging indoors, they can also be worn outside if necessary; you'll feel a little more secure wearing them out on the Airbnb's deck or down to the hotel lobby than in other pairs. They come recommended by commerce editor Meaghan Kenny, who regularly turns to them for extra warmth on cold weekend mornings at home.

Bombas has quite a few solid slippers from which to choose—including the Gripper Slipper that really blurs the line between sock and shoe. But the Sunday Slipper, with its super-soft faux fur and slip-on, slip-off capability, sits at the top of the heap when it comes to versatility. If you're stumped on what to gift someone for the holidays, the best-selling style is foolproof.

Birkenstock manufactures footwear of fabulous durability and quality, from the popular sandals and clogs that you can wear here, there, and everywhere to the more indoor-friendly Zermatt shearling slipper. Despite being supremely soft, the latex sole offers a boost of support, which is why they make such a great house shoe. They come in men's and women’s sizes, and you can pick between wide or narrow fits for optimal comfort.

The Ugg Tasman slipper might be the most recognizable slipper on this list, and it's popular for good reason: The closed-back design makes it a more practical alternative to the brand's classic Scuff slipper; the plush sheepskin lining and durable suede upper ensure coziness and durability; and the Fair Isle–inspired Tasman braid around the trim adds a hint of character.

L.L.Bean fans rave about these clog-like slippers for their arch support, heel cushioning, and playful patterns, featuring designs ranging from turtles to moose to ombré forest trees. They have a fleece lining and rubber anti-slip sole, and are roomy enough to wear your thickest socks underneath in colder months, making them our top pick for cold feet.

What are the best brands for travel slippers?

Bombas and EverFoams design lightweight slippers that are conveniently packable, while Ugg and Quince offer cozy shearling options that take up a bit more suitcase space. If you love the slippers you usually find at luxury hotels, The Ritz-Carlton also sells its signature Frette spa slippers online, so you can bring five-star comfort right to your home.

Slippers can be a welcome change from sneakers or boots on a long-haul flight, especially if you’re hoping to get some sleep. Choose a lightweight, packable pair with nonslip soles, but switch back to shoes when walking around the cabin or using the bathroom.

What should you look for in the best indoor slippers?

When shopping for indoor slippers, fit and material matter most: Wool and shearling provide warmth without trapping too much heat, while memory foam adds cushioning. Look for a soft, flexible sole with enough grip to keep you from slipping on hardwood or tile floors.

#6263. Singapore Airlines CEO May Rethink New Business Class Colors, And He Should

Singapore Airlines has made a mistake with the colors of its new business class cabin. The gray and black surfaces with bright yellow accents look more like a cheap hybrid of Spirit Airlines and Scoot than the premium airline whose name is on the aircraft. Now CEO Goh Choon Phong has left the door open to changes. I hope Singapore Airlines takes that opportunity.

When I covered the new Singapore Airlines business class seat, I welcomed several functional improvements, particularly the redesigned footwell. Singapore has addressed complaints about sleeping comfort and added features passengers increasingly expect.

I keep looking at the photographs and wondering how this particular color scheme made it through the approval process. Singapore Airlines has spent decades cultivating an identity associated with understated luxury. Its warmer, muted cabin colors help communicate that identity before a “Singapore Girl” even shows up to offer a welcome drink.

The new business class looks disconnected from it. The yellow accents against the gray and dark surfaces suggest a budget airline or a gaming chair. Neither association strikes me as particularly useful for Singapore Airlines.

During the launch Q&A, executives defended the decision to move in a different visual direction.

A post shared by Brandon · The Points Wanderer (@thepointswanderer)

Vice President of Product Experience Ong Wah Li said customer research had identified a desire for a more contemporary appearance. She described the resulting palette as “modern and refreshed, yet elegant and refined.”

Chief Commercial Officer Lee Lik Hsin emphasized that the Singapore Airlines experience extends beyond cabin colors. He defended the different palette, saying:

“We do not feel that a different colour palette creates any kind of inconsistency.”

Of course the Singapore Airlines experience involves more than colors. Service and comfort are far more consequential over a long flight. But the airline does not invest in cabin design because appearance is irrelevant. It understands that the surroundings help establish what passengers think they are buying.

Asking for something “modern” does not mean asking for this. Singapore Airlines could refresh its interiors while preserving the warmth and restraint that make them recognizable. I simply do not understand why contemporary design should require such a sharp departure from the brand. Plenty of modern interiors feel inviting and expensive without a bright yellow accent running through the seat.

At a November 11 employee town hall, Goh acknowledged the negative reaction. According to The Business Times, he said:

“We’ll look at it, we’ll see what is feasible.”

He also expressed confidence that passengers would appreciate the seats once they experienced their comfort and practical features.

They may well do so. I hope I do too. But enjoying the seat would not make the color choice better. I can appreciate a more comfortable bed while wishing the cabin looked like Singapore Airlines…and the fact that I say that underscores what a brand Singapore has built and should be careful not to fritter away over idiotic consultants who are out of touch with Singapore’s customer base.

Goh has not promised a redesign, and I would not describe this as a reversal. Still, his willingness to consider what can be changed is welcome. We all make mistakes. There is considerably more dignity in acknowledging one and correcting it than spending years defending it.

The contrast with the new Singapore Airlines first class suite makes the business class decision even stranger.

PriestmanGoode designed first class, while Designworks, a BMW Group company, designed business class. Factorydesign handled premium economy and economy.

First class looks like a natural evolution of Singapore Airlines. The warmer finishes and batik details give the new suite a connection to the airline without making it look old. It demonstrates that you can introduce a substantially different product while retaining a recognizable identity.

I worked closely with PriestmanGoode during my time at Star Alliance and have a great appreciation for its work. Looking at these two cabins, I would ask the firm to help bring the business class finishes into the same visual family.

Designworks does have aviation experience, including work with STARLUX and EVA Air. Nevertheless, I think it has badly misjudged this assignment. The BMW association does not automatically make the result luxurious, and this particular result does not look worthy of Singapore Airlines.

I am not particularly impressed with the new premium economy aesthetic either, though that is a different firm’s work. Ultimately, Singapore Airlines approved all these designs. The responsibility for how they fit together belongs to the airline.

There is nothing inherently wrong with yellow. It works for Scoot because Scoot has a different identity and sells a different proposition. It worked for Spirit Airlines (until it didn’t…).

But Singapore Airlines has little reason to make its premium cabin evoke its own budget subsidiary. Nor does the comparison with Spirit help communicate the experience it wants passengers to pay for, right?

That is particularly strange in Southeast Asia, where travelers have plenty of experience distinguishing a full-service premium carrier from a budget airline. Singapore Airlines should reinforce what makes it different.

The yellow stripe will not suddenly send loyal passengers to another carrier: I don’t think people will book away from Singapore because they don’t like the seat color. But why should that be even a consideration? Singapore Airlines has the resources to deliver both comfort and an interior that reflects its reputation.

The earthy, muted colors have worked because they convey quality. This new palette feels like a needless attempt to be different, with too little consideration for what is being lost.

I welcome the functional improvements in the new Singapore Airlines business class seat and look forward to trying it. But the color scheme is a mistake. Sorry, it is. To my eyes, it cheapens the appearance of a product intended to command a premium.

Goh has indicated that the airline will consider what is feasible. My suggestion is straightforward: retain the improvements to comfort, ask PriestmanGoode to help reconsider the finishes, and give business class an appearance consistent with the airline passengers have chosen. Dark brown would work well.

Singapore Airlines does not need to spend the next decade explaining why a cabin that reminds people of Scoot actually represents luxury. It has time to reconsider. I hope it does.

The color scheme looks crap. They could have asked a 100 of their PPS and Solitaire customers to pick from a few option and they would have had a pretty good clue of how things are supposed to look like.

A yellow strip. A color palette. My god, seriously? Do you all stand there and stare at the seat for hours to gain some sort of energy transference? Personally, I sit down on it, eat the food, sleep and arrive somewhere I need to be. It’s a tiny cocoon of transport. Not a hotel room. Yes, I want comfort and decent things to pass the time. But anyone who obsesses over feeling less comfortable given a yellow stripe needs to seriously assess priorities.

#6262. Aeromexico Adds New U.S. Routes, Flights

Aeromexico is again expanding its footprint in the U.S. with assistance from longtime partner Delta.

The carrier announced Monday that it will connect Mexico City with Nashville, Tennessee, New Orleans, and San Juan, Puerto Rico. None of the three cities currently has nonstop service to the Mexican capital.

All three connections will operate four times weekly. Service to Nashville will launch first, on June 13, 2027, followed by New Orleans on June 17 and San Juan on June 24.

Flights to Nashville and New Orleans will use Embraer E190 aircraft with 99 seats. For the route to San Juan, the airline will operate Boeing 737 MAX 8s with 166 seats.

Aeromexico will also launch a second daily service between Mexico City and Austin, Texas, on June 3.

“The addition of Nashville, New Orleans, and San Juan to our network will allow us to provide more connectivity options, bringing our customers closer to destinations known for their unique identity and remarkable attractions,” Giancarlo Mulinelli, senior vice president of global sales at Aeromexico, said in a news release. “Together with Delta, we continue to open markets and create more opportunities that strengthen tourism and ties between Mexico and the United States.”

Last month, the partners announced new routes from Mexico City to Orange County, California, Fort Lauderdale, Florida, and Portland, Oregon.
